# The distribution of prime values of random polynomials

**Authors:** Noah Kravitz Address: St John’s College, Oxford and Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford; St Giles’, Oxford OX1 3JP, UK Email address: noah.kravitz@maths.ox.ac.uk , Katharine Woo Address: Stanford University, 450 Serra Mall, Stanford, CA 94306 Email address: katywoo@gmail.com and Max Wenqiang Xu Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, 251 Mercer Street, New York 10012, USA Email address: maxxu1729@gmail.com

## Abstract

The Bateman–Horn Conjecture predicts how often an irreducible polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ assumes prime values. We demonstrate that with sufficient averaging in the coefficients of $f$ (viz. exponential in the size of the inputs), one can not only prove Bateman–Horn results on average but also pin down precise information about the distribution of prime values. We show that 100% of polynomials (in an $L^{k}$ sense for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ ) satisfy the Bateman–Horn Conjecture, and that that 100% of polynomials (in an $L^{2}$ sense) satisfy an appropriate polynomial analogue of the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture. We use the latter to prove that 100% of polynomials satisfy the appropriate analogue of the Poisson Tail Conjecture, in the sense that the distribution of the gaps between consecutive prime values around the average spacing is Poisson.

We also study the frequencies of sign patterns of the Liouville function evaluated at the consecutive outputs of $f$ ; viewing $f$ as a random variable, we establish the limiting distribution for every sign pattern. The Chowla problem along random polynomials is a special case. A key input behind all of our arguments is Leng’s recent quantitative work on the higher-order Fourier uniformity of the von Mangoldt and Möbius functions (in turn relying on Leng, Sah, and Sawhney’s quantitative inverse theorem for the Gowers norms).

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Prime values along (random) polynomials

A notorious number-theoretic problem is determining whether a given polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ assumes prime values at infinitely many positive integer inputs. It is clear that $f$ fails to achieve prime values if it factors, if it is uniformly zero modulo some prime (e.g., $x^{2}+x+2$ is always even), or if it is eventually always negative. In 1854, Bunyakovsky [5] conjectured that these are the only three things that can go wrong: If an irreducible polynomial has positive leading coefficient and its outputs have no common factor, then it should be prime for infinitely many integer inputs. Dirichlet’s Theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions proves this conjecture for linear polynomials. There is no non-linear polynomial for which the conclusion of Bunyakovsky’s Conjecture is known to hold.

In 1962, Bateman and Horn [3] refined Bunyakovsky’s Conjecture by predicting how frequently such prime values should occur. Using quasirandomness heuristics for the distribution of primes, they predicted that if $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is an irreducible polynomial, then

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))\sim\mathfrak{S}_{f}X, $$

where $\Lambda$ denotes the generalized von Mangoldt function

$$ \Lambda(n):=\begin{cases}\log(p),&\text{if }n=\pm p^{k}\text{ for some prime }p;\\
0,&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases} $$

and $\mathfrak{S}_{f}$ denotes the singular series

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}:=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right). $$

Using the same heuristics, they also predicted the asymptotic frequency with which several irreducible polynomials simultaneously achieve prime values; the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture is a special case. The Bateman–Horn Conjecture, even more than Bunyakovsky’s Conjecture, seems far out of reach with current methods.

A related family of problems concerns sums of the Liouville function along polynomials. Recall that the Liouville function $\lambda:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ is the completely multiplicative function that equals $-1$ at all of the primes. Cancellation in sums of the Liouville function are closely related to the density of primes and the Riemann Hypothesis. In 1965, Chowla [6] conjectured that

$$ \sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))=o(X) $$

for any $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ that cannot be written as a constant times the square of another polynomial. The problem in general is still wide open, although there has been some recent progress in the case where $f$ is a product of linear factors. See the further discussion in Section 2.3.

Although we cannot prove the Bateman–Horn Conjecture or the Chowla Conjecture for particular polynomials $f$ , we are able to describe what happens for a “random” $f$ . For our model, we fix $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and consider a uniformly random polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at most $d$ with integer coefficients of size at most $H$ . With a sufficiently large amount of averaging in $f$ , we can prove an “almost-all” version of the Bateman–Horn Conjecture, and we can precisely describe the lower-order fluctuations for the Chowla Conjecture. Our averaged Bateman–Horn results also let us show that 100% of polynomials $f$ satisfy a suitable polynomial analogue of the Poisson Tail Conjecture. The moral of this paper is that all of the usual “prime number quasirandomness” heuristics hold, and to great precision, if one includes enough averaging. This can be viewed as weak evidence towards the original non-averaged versions of the conjectures.

The main technical idea, which we will expand on shortly, is that while the expression $a_{0}+\ldots+a_{d}x^{d}$ is a degree- $d$ polynomial in $x$ , it is linear in $a_{0},\ldots,a_{d}$ for each fixed $x$ . In our proofs, we will be able to switch the order of summation so that the quantities of interest are expressed as average correlations of $\Lambda$ or $\lambda$ evaluated at such linear forms (for various $x$ ’s). At this point the tools of higher-order Fourier analysis can be fruitfully deployed. A particularly important input is Leng’s work [25] on the higher-order Fourier uniformity of the von Mangoldt and Möbius functions, which combines the techniques of Green and Tao [14, 16, 15] with recent quantitative improvements on the Green–Tao–Ziegler machinery [13] due to Leng [24] and Leng, Sah, and Swahney [23]. This idea also occurs in the work of Teräväinen [43]; it is more potent in our work because of recent quantitative improvements that were not available at the time of [43].

### 1.2. Averaged Bateman–Horn

The earliest averaged Bateman–Horn result is due to Skorobogatov and Sofos [38], who in 2020 proved that asymptotically 100% of fixed-degree polynomials satisfy (1.1); among the arithmetic applications of this breakthrough is the fact that as a positive proportion of generalized Châtelet surfaces and a positive proportion of a family of conic bundles have rational points. Let us state the result of [38]. Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\delta>0$ be a small constant, and set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta})$ . Let $\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ denote the set of integer-coefficient polynomials of degree at most $d$ where all coefficients have absolute value at most $H$ . Skorobogatov and Sofos showed that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))-\mathfrak{S}_{f}^{\prime}\right|\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log X}}, $$

where $\mathfrak{S}_{f}^{\prime}$ is a suitable truncated version of the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{f}$ . It is desirable to prove such an inequality with $H$ growing more slowly in terms of $X$ (corresponding to less averaging). Browning, Sofos, and Teräväinen [4] later achieved this with $H:=X^{c}$ for $c>\frac{19d}{5}$ with polylogarithmic savings; their work also handles the setting where the coefficients of $f$ are constrained to certain combinatorial cubes. See [1] for further work in this direction.

This brings us to our first result, which provides more precise information in the regime of $H$ exponential in $X$ . We are able to control not only the first moment of the expression of interest but also all higher moments.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $0<\delta<1$ be a real. Set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta})$ . Then for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))-\mathfrak{S}_{f}\left(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\right)\right)^{k}=O_{d,\delta,k}((\log X)^{-1+o(1)}), $$

where the truncated singular series is given by

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}\left(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\right):=\prod_{p\leq(\log X)/(\log\log X)}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right). $$

Let us pause to highlight a few aspects of this theorem statement; these remarks also apply to our later results.

- (1) Recall that the heuristic (1.1) pertains only to irreducible polynomials $f$ . It has been known since the work of van der Waerden [44] that a uniformly random polynomial $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ is irreducible with probability $1-\exp(-\Omega_{d}((\log H)/(\log\log H)))$ . Thus reducible polynomials $f$ make a negligible contribution to (1.2).

- (2) The truncated singular series is nonzero as long as there is no prime $p\leq(\log X)/(\log\log X)$ such that $f(x)\equiv 0\bmod p$ for all $x$ . For $p>d$ , we have $f\equiv 0\bmod p$ if and only if $p$ divides all of the coefficients of $f$ , so our truncated singular series is nonzero for a positive proportion (depending on $d$ ) of polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ . In particular, (1.2) provides a meaningful statement about the $\mathfrak{S}_{f}\neq 0$ case.

- (3) We truncate our singular series because of issues related to its absolute convergence; at the present, such a truncation seems necessary. The authors of [38, 4] also truncate their singular series, but at different spots ( $\log X$ and $\exp(\sqrt{\log X})$ , respectively) from ours. We chose the truncation spot $\log X/\log\log X$ in order to make our computations cleaner.

- (4) Our proof would still work if instead of averaging over all of $\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ , we fixed all but two of the coefficients of $f$ and then averaged over just the last two coefficients. The work of [4] has the same feature, even though their proof techniques there are quite different.

- (5) There is no real difference between averaging over polynomials of degree exactly $d$ and averaging over polynomials of degree at most $d$ , since only a $O(1/H)$ -fraction of polynomials in $\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ have degree strictly smaller than $d$ .

- (6) We can obtain the same conclusion with $H(X)$ as large as around $\exp(X/(\log X)^{k+1})$ .

#### Remark 1.2.

Browning, Sofos and Teräväinen [4] proved a version of Theorem 1.1 in the (more interesting and difficult) polynomial regime where $X\in[H^{c},2H^{c}]$ for $0<c<19d/5$ . This does not immediately imply our result in the exponential regime, due to the upper bound needed on $H$ .

### 1.3. Averaged Prime Tuples and Poisson Tail

Theorem 1.1 pertained to the one-polynomial case of the Bateman–Horn Conjecture. Our methods also are applicable to many instances with multiple polynomials. We will focus on what might be termed the “Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture along polynomials” because this case has interesting consequences for gaps between prime values of polynomials. Our averaged version goes as follows.

#### Theorem 1.3.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer and let $0<\delta<1$ be a real. Set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta})$ . Let $1\leq k<1/\delta$ be an integer, and let $\alpha>0$ be a real. Then for any distinct integers $\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{k}$ of size $|\ell_{i}|\leq X^{\alpha}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,\left(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\right)\right|^{2}=O_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}((\log X)^{-1+o(1)}), $$

where the truncated singular series is given by

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,\left(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\right):=\prod_{p\leq\log X/(\log\log X)}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall 1\leq i\leq k\}}{(1-1/p)^{k}}\right). $$

#### Remark 1.4.

A standard diagonalization argument produces a function $\delta(X)=\delta_{d,\alpha}(X)$ , tending very slowly to $0$ as $X\to\infty$ , such that the following holds with $H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta(X)})$ : For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and any distinct integers $\ell_{1}<\cdots<\ell_{k}$ of size at most $X^{\alpha}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,\left(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\right)\right|^{2}=O_{d,\alpha,k}((\log X)^{-99/100}). $$

This inequality holds uniformly in the $\ell_{i}$ ’s for each fixed $k$ (but of course it is non-uniform in $k$ ). This formulation is useful because it sets us up to study gaps between prime values assumed by $f$ ; we emphasize that the uniformity in the shifts $\ell_{i}$ will be important for this application.

Gallagher [10] and Montgomery and Soundararajan [33] showed that if one assumes a strong form of the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture, then one can show that primes are distributed like Poisson random variables in short intervals and like Gaussian random variables in longer intervals. Given a polynomial $f$ , one can ask about the distribution of integer inputs on which $f$ achieves prime values; of course the general case of this problem is even more difficult than the case $f(x)=x$ that we just described.

By combining the approach of Gallagher with the (diagonalized version of) Theorem 1.3, we are able to establish unconditional almost-all results for this polynomial prime gaps problem. The setup is a bit delicate. For $f$ a polynomial and $X,L$ natural numbers, define the counting function

$$ P_{f}(X,L;k):=\#\{1\leq x\leq X:f([x,x+L))\textrm{ contains exactly $k$ primes}\}. $$

We obtain a probability distribution $\rho_{f,X,L}$ on $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ by setting $\rho_{f,X,L}(k):=X^{-1}P_{f}(X,L;k)$ . Since $f(X)\asymp HX^{d}$ for typical $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ , the Poisson Tail Conjecture heuristic suggests that $\rho_{f,X,L}$ should be close to the Poisson distribution with mean

$$ \mathcal{L}:=\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f}\left(w(X)\right)L}{\log(HX^{d})}, $$

where $w(X)$ is a suitable slowly-growing function and $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w(X))$ is a truncated singular series as in Theorem 1.1. We will show that this is indeed the case asymptotically for 100% of polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ . Note that $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)$ is nonzero with a positive probability; of course, on the positive-probability event that $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)$ does vanish, determining $\rho_{f,X,L}$ is trivial.

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $\delta(X)=\delta_{d,1}(X)$ be the function from Remark 1.4. Let $\mathcal{L}>0$ . Let $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots$ be a sequence of natural numbers satisfying $X_{i}\geq\exp(i^{1+\gamma})$ for some $\gamma>0$ . Set $H_{i}:=\exp(X_{i}^{\delta(X_{i})})$ and $w_{i}:=\delta(X_{i})(\log X_{i})/(\log\log X_{i})^{2}$ ; for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$ , sample $f_{i}$ uniformly at random from the polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H_{i})$ with $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w_{i})\neq 0$ , and set $L_{i}:=\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(H_{i}X_{i}^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f_{i}}(w_{i})}$ . Then with probability $1$ , for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{P_{f_{i}}(X_{i},L_{i};k)}{X_{i}}=\frac{e^{-\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{L}^{k}}{k!}. $$

#### Remark 1.6.

The conclusion of this conjecture also implies the following weaker statement along the lines of what sometimes goes under the name of the Poisson Tail Conjecture. For each $i$ , let $n_{i,1}<\cdots<n_{i,R_{i}}$ be the integers $1\leq n\leq X_{i}$ such that $f_{i}(n_{i,j})$ is prime. Then for any $\lambda>0$ , with probability $1$ we have

$$ \#\{1\leq j<R_{i}:|f(n_{i,j+1})-f(n_{i,j})|\geq\lambda\log(H_{i}X_{i}^{d})\}\asymp e^{-\lambda}\frac{X_{i}}{\log(H_{i}X_{i}^{d})}. $$

In the regime where $\mathcal{L}$ tends to infinity, one would expect $\rho_{f,X,L}$ to be close to a Gaussian distribution with mean $\mathcal{L}$ . We can, once again, establish that this is the case asymptotically asymptotically 100% of polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ , for a reasonably wide range of parameters.

#### Theorem 1.7.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer, let $\alpha>0$ , and let $\delta(X)=\delta_{d,\alpha}(X)$ be the function from Remark 1.4. Let $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}(X)>0$ be a function tending to infinity with $X$ and satisfying $\log\mathcal{L}(X)=o(\log(\delta(X)(\log X)/(\log\log X)^{2}))$ . Let $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots$ be a sequence of natural numbers satisfying $X_{i}\geq\exp(i^{1+\gamma})$ for some $\gamma>0$ , and and set $H_{i}:=\exp(X_{i}^{\delta(X_{i})})$ and $w_{i}=\delta(X_{i})(\log X_{i})/(\log\log X_{i})^{2}$ ; for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$ , sample $f_{i}$ uniformly at random from the polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H_{i})$ with $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w_{i})\neq 0$ , and set $p_{i}:=\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f_{i}}(w_{i})}{\log(H_{i}X_{i}^{d})}$ and $L_{i}:=p_{i}^{-1}\mathcal{L}(X_{i})$ . Then with probability $1$ , for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{k\leq p_{i}L_{i}+t\sqrt{(p_{i}-p_{i}^{2})L_{i}}}P_{f_{i}}(X_{i},L_{i};k)}{X_{i}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,dx. $$

#### Remark 1.8.

In the classical setting of primes in short intervals, it is expected that

$$ \#\{1\leq x\leq X:[x,x+L]\textrm{ contains exactly $k$ primes}\}=0 $$

if $L$ is sufficiently large with respect to $k$ and $X$ . Moreover, this quantity should become harder to estimate when $L$ is larger relative to $k$ . Our work corresponds to the regime $L=\log X\cdot(\log\log\log X)^{A}$ for arbitrary $A>0$ in the classical setting.

If for a suitable choice of $w(X)$ one could replace the upper bound in Theorem 1.3 with square-root cancellation, namely,

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w(X))\right|^{2}=O_{d,\delta,\alpha}(X^{-1/2+o(1)}), $$

then we could extend the range of $\mathcal{L}$ to $\mathcal{L}(X)\ll X^{A\delta(X)}$ for any $A>0$ . This would correspond to $L=\log X\cdot(\log\log X)^{A}$ for $A>0$ in the classical setting. It may be of interest to note that Montgomery and Soundararajan [33] work with a similar uniform square-root cancellation hypothesis in their study of the Gaussian range in the classical setting.

### 1.4. Averaged polynomial Chowla

We now turn our attention from the von Mangoldt function $\Lambda$ to the Liouville function $\lambda$ . In the Bateman–Horn-type problems above, we identified main terms (via singular series) in various averages of $\Lambda$ . In Chowla-type problems, the main term is typically zero, and the interesting problems concern the rate of decay and the “shape” of lower-order terms. Instead of establishing “almost-all” results as we vary the polynomial $f$ , we will view $f$ as a random variable and study the limiting distributions (over $f$ ) of various Liouville sums involving $f$ .

The overarching theme of this subsection is that one should expect $\lambda$ to behave like a uniformly random $\{-1,1\}$ -valued sequence, and one can compare its statistics to the corresponding statistics of a truly random $\{-1,1\}$ -valued sequence. For example, the sum of $N$ independent uniformly random $\pm 1$ ’s is typically of size $\asymp N^{1/2}$ , and the limiting distribution of these fluctuations (after normalization) is Gaussian.

The first results in this direction were due to Browning, Sofos, and Teräväinen [4] and Teräväinen [43]; Wilson [47] later studied the higher moments of the expression

$$ \frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n)), $$

considered as a random variable depending on the random polynomial $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ . Since the Gaussian distribution is determined by its moments, one can deduce that the random variable $X^{-1/2}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))$ converges to a Gaussian (as a distribution) if one knows that all of its individual moments converge to the corresponding moments of a Gaussian. Wilson made progress towards this goal by using the circle method to show that indeed the first $d+1$ moments of $X^{-1/2}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))$ approach the first $d+1$ moments of a Gaussian of variance $1$ .

We mentioned previously that one can view a collection of polynomials $\{a_{0}+\ldots+a_{d}n_{i}^{d}\}_{i=1}^{t}$ as a system of linear form in the variables $a_{0},\ldots,a_{d}$ . The overdetermination of this system for $t>d+1$ limits Wilson’s circle-method approach to the first $d+1$ moments. By replacing Wilson’s Fourier-analytic approach with higher-order Fourier-analytic tools, we are able to obtain all moments. Let $C_{k}:=k!!\cdot{\bf 1}_{\text{$k$ even}}$ denote the $k$ -th moment of the Gaussian of mean $0$ and variance $1$ .

#### Theorem 1.9.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer. Suppose $H=H(X)\geq\exp(X^{\delta})$ for some real $\delta>0$ . Then for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))\right)^{k}=C_{k}+O_{d,\delta,k}(X^{-1}). $$

An immediate corollary is that $X^{-1/2}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))$ converges in distribution to a Gaussian of mean $0$ and variance $1$ , i.e.,

$$ \lim_{X\to\infty}\Pr_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))\leq t\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,dx $$

for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ .

Theorem 1.9 is a special case of a more general result about sign patterns of the Liouville function sampled along a random polynomial. Recall that the sign-pattern instance of the Chowla Conjecture asserts that the sequence $\lambda(n+1),\ldots,\lambda(n+s)$ assumes each of the $2^{s}$ possible sign patterns for $(1+o(1))2^{-s}X$ values of $1\leq n\leq X$ . For a polynomial $f$ that is not a constant times a square of another polynomial, one can make the analogous conjecture about the sign patterns of the sequence

$$ \lambda(f(n+1)),\lambda(f(n+2)),\ldots,\lambda(f(n+s)). $$

As usual, we are able to address this conjecture only on average; as in Theorem 1.9, we show not only that the main term is as expect but also that the lower-order fluctuations of these counts converge to Gaussians.

#### Theorem 1.10.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer. Suppose $H=H(X)\geq\exp(X^{\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$ . Let $\vec{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\in\{-1,1\}^{s}$ be a sign pattern. Then for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{\#\{n\leq X:(\lambda(f(n+1)),...,\lambda(f(n+s)))=\vec{\epsilon}~\}-2^{-s}X}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}=\sigma(\vec{\epsilon})^{k}C_{k}+O_{d,\delta,s,k}(X^{-1}), $$

where the standard deviation $\sigma(\vec{\epsilon})\geq 0$ is given by

$$ \sigma(\vec{\epsilon})^{2}=4^{-s}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\emptyset\neq T_{1},T_{2}\subseteq[s]\\
\text{translates}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in T_{1}}\epsilon_{i}\cdot\prod_{i\in T_{2}}\epsilon_{i}\right). $$

Of course, it follows that the main quantity under consideration is distributed as a Gaussian of mean $0$ and variance $\sigma(\vec{\epsilon})^{2}$ in the limit. The $s=1$ case corresponds to Theorem 1.9 (via the identity $\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))=X-2\#\{n\leq X:\lambda(f(n))=-1\}$ ).

In the course of the proof of Theorem 1.10, we will see that if $y(1),y(2),\ldots$ is a sequence of independent uniformly random $\pm 1$ ’s, then the limiting distribution of the count

$$ \frac{\#\{n\leq X:(y(n+1),\ldots,y(n+s))=(\epsilon_{1},...,\epsilon_{s})\}-2^{-s}X}{X^{1/2}} $$

is also a Gaussian of mean $0$ and variance $\sigma(\overline{\varepsilon})^{2}$ , in accordance with the heuristic from the beginning of this subsection. The latter fact follows from a more general classical result of Hoeffding and Robbins [19] on $m$ -dependent random variables.

### 1.5. Related questions

There are several ways in which one could hope to extend our results. Our argument for Theorem 1.3 should also give $L^{q}$ -bounds with $q>2$ , possibly under further restrictions among $\delta,k,q$ ; we worked out only the $L^{2}$ -bounds because these suffices for our Poisson Tail applications. The hypotheses $\delta<1$ in Theorem 1.1 and $\delta<1/k$ in Theorem 1.3 seem to reflect a technical limitation of our methods, and it would be interesting to remove or weaken these assumptions.

A natural follow-up question is whether Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 can be established with $H(X)$ growing more slowly, e.g., polynomially in $X$ . [4, Theorem 1.2] directly implies a version of Theorem 1.1 where $H(X)$ grows polynomially in $X$ . Indeed, their result shows that for $0<c<5/(19d)$ and for $H\asymp X^{1/c}$ , for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A>0$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))-\mathfrak{S}_{f}(\exp(\sqrt{\log X}))\right)^{k}=O_{d,c,k,A}((\log X)^{-A}). $$

The techniques of Browning, Sofos and Teräväinen differ greatly from ours; one topic for future work could be seeing what their methods say about analogues of the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture and the Poisson Tail Conjecture. Another possible path towards decreasing $H(X)$ is utilizing the “Siegel zero model” for the von Mangoldt function (described explicitly in [31]) and exploiting the fact that we are averaging over many linear systems (indexed by the variables $n_{i}$ below).

### 1.6. Structure of the paper

In Section 2 we gather notation, our singular series conventions, and other preliminaries and background. In Section 3 we explain the necessary inputs from higher-order Fourier analysis. Section 4 contains our on-average result about the polynomial Chowla problem and Liouville sign patterns. We upper-bound all moments for Bateman–Horn in Section 5. We prove our almost-all prime tuples result in Section 6, and in Section 7 we establish our almost-all results on Poisson and Gaussian tails.

## 2. Preliminaries and heuristics

### 2.1. Notation

Throughout this paper, $\Lambda,\lambda,\mu$ denote the von Mangoldt, Liouville, and Möbius functions, respectively. We extend each of these functions to all of $\mathbb{Z}$ by declaring it to be equal on $n,-n$ for all $n$ . We write $\mathscr{P}$ for the set of primes (again both positive and negative).

We will always treat the degree $d$ as fixed, and we will often treat the moment or tuple length $k$ as fixed as well. In proofs, we will sometimes omit the dependence on $d,k$ in our asymptotic notation $O(\cdot)$ , $o(\cdot)$ , $\ll$ when there is no risk of confusion.

### 2.2. Singular series

In general, we will write $\mathfrak{S}$ for a singular series and $\mathfrak{S}(w)$ for a truncation of it. Singular series depending on polynomials $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ often need to be truncated due to issues about absolute convergence.

Let us write down some singular series that we will encounter later. First,the Bateman–Horn heuristic involves the singular series

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}:=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right). $$

Second, the singular series from the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture is

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{\vec{\ell}}:=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:x+\ell_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{|\vec{\ell}|}}\right). $$

Third, our “hybrid” problem about prime tuples along polynomials corresponds to the singular series

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{|\vec{\ell}|}}\right). $$

We will work with truncated versions of the first and third of these singular series, viz.

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}(w):=\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right), $$

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w):=\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{|\vec{\ell}|}}\right), $$

where the truncation point $w$ is a slowly-growing parameter. We need the following basic bounds.

#### Lemma 2.1.

Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ , and let $\vec{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}^{k}$ be a tuple of distinct integers. Then

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\ll\log w\quad\text{and}\quad\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\ll(\log w)^{k}. $$

#### Proof.

From $\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\},\,\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}\leq p$ we deduce that

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\leq\prod_{p\leq w}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{-1}\ll\exp\left(\sum_{p\leq w}\frac{1}{p}\right)\ll\log w $$

and likewise

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\leq\prod_{p\leq w}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{-k}\ll\exp\left(k\sum_{p\leq w}\frac{1}{p}\right)\ll(\log w)^{k}.\qed $$

#### Lemma 2.2.

Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ . If there is a prime $p\leq w$ dividing $f(n)$ for all integer inputs, then $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)=0$ . Otherwise, we have the lower bound

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\gg_{d}(\log w)^{1-d}. $$

#### Proof.

For each prime $p$ , if $f$ modulo $p$ is not the zero polynomial, then it vanishes on at most $d$ elements of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . In particular, $\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}$ is either $0$ or at least $p-d$ . If the former occurs for some $p\leq w$ , then $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)=0$ . Otherwise we have

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\geq\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{1-\min(d,p-1)/p}{1-1/p}\right)\gg_{d}\prod_{p\leq w}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{d-1}\gg_{d}(\log w)^{1-d}.\qed $$

Finally, we record the singular series that appears in the main term of the asymptotic results of Green and Tao [14, 15, 16], and Green, Tao, and Ziegler [13] on linear equations in primes. Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{k})$ denote a set of linear forms in $n$ variables with finite complexity. The corresponding singular series is

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}:=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-n}\#\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:\psi_{i}(\vec{x})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{k}}\right). $$

Observe that $\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}$ converges absolutely. Indeed, for all but finitely many primes $p$ , we have

$$ \#\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:\psi_{i}(\vec{x})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}=p^{n}-kp^{n-1}+O_{\Psi}(p^{n-2}) $$

from the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle and the fact that each equation $\psi_{i}(\vec{x})=0$ cuts out a plane.

### 2.3. Heuristics for sign patterns of the Liouville function

It is believed that the sequence of Liouville values $\lambda(n)$ should behave “similarly” to a random $\pm 1$ -valued sequence. A concrete conjecture in this direction is that a length- $s$ subinterval of Liouville values with a random starting point is equally likely to see each of the $2^{s}$ possible sign patterns.

#### Conjecture 2.3 (Chowla).

Let $s\geq 1$ and let $(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\in\{-1,1\}^{s}$ be a sign pattern. Then the set $\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\lambda(n+i)=\epsilon_{i}~\forall i\}$ has natural density $2^{-s}.$

The $s=1$ case is equivalent to the prime number theorem. Hildebrand [18] showed that each sign pattern of length at most $3$ occurs infinitely often, and in 2015 Matomäki, Radziwiłł, and Tao [29] established that these sign patterns occur with positive natural lower density. The same authors [28] studied the distribution of the tuple $(\lambda(n+h_{1}),\ldots,\lambda(n+h_{s}))$ when the $h_{i}$ ’s are averaged over an interval.

In a related direction, there has been much recent progress on the logarithmically-weighted form of Chowla’s Conjecture, namely, the statement that

$$ \frac{1}{\log X}\sum_{n\leq X}\frac{\lambda(n+1)\cdots\lambda(n+s)}{n}=o_{s}(1) $$

as $X\rightarrow\infty$ . This conjecture is strictly weaker than Conjecture 2.3. Tao [42] proved the logarithmically-weighted Chowla Conjecture for $s=2$ , and Tao and Teräväinen [39] later proved it for all odd $s$ . The same authors showed that for $s=4$ all sign patterns occur with positive lower density. See also [17, 34]. Recent work towards the higher-uniformity conjecture [27, 30, 26, 45, 46] is approaching the range that would establish the logarithmically-weighted Chowla conjecture for all $s$ . Sawin [37] has explained potential obstructions to obtaining more detailed information on sign patterns using this line of thought.

The full polynomial Chowla Conjecture generalizes the above sign pattern conjecture.

#### Conjecture 2.4 (Chowla).

Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ . If $f$ is not a constant times the square of another polynomial, then as $X\rightarrow\infty$ we have

$$ \frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))=o_{f}(1). $$

Teräväinen [43] showed that if $f$ factors as a product of linear and quadratic polynomials and is not a constant times a perfect square, then $\lambda(f(n))$ attains each of $-1,1$ for a positive proportion of inputs. He also established an averaged version of the polynomial Chowla problem; this was improved upon quantitatively by [4]. These results hold more generally for nonpretentious multiplicative functions and can be understood as multiplicative analogues of the work of Skorobogatov and Sofos [38]. In the function-field setting, this question has been resolved by the work of Sawin and Shusterman [36]. Another recent development [21] is that for a fixed polynomial $f$ , there is square-root cancellation when $\lambda$ is replaced by a random multiplicative function.

### 2.4. Distribution of gaps between primes

Most of this section is based on the survey of Funkhouser, Goldston and Ledoan [9] on the distribution of gaps between consecutive primes; any mistakes are, of course, our own.

Based on Cramér’s model, one expects the average gap between two consecutive prime numbers $p_{n}$ , $p_{n+1}$ to be of size $\sim\log p_{n}$ . Works of Zhang [48], Maynard [32], and independently Tao (in unpublished work), and the Polymath project [35] exhibit explicit constants $c$ such that there are infinitely many prime gaps of size at most $c$ . It is less clear what to expect regarding the largest gaps between consecutive primes. Building on the work of [8, 32], the authors of [7] showed that there are gaps of size at least

$$ \gg\frac{(\log p_{n})(\log\log p_{n})(\log\log\log\log p_{n})}{\log\log\log p_{n}}. $$

The folklore Poisson Tail Conjecture predicts that the distribution of prime gaps should be roughly Poisson at scale $\log p_{n}$ .

#### Conjecture 2.5.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ . For $1\leq H\leq(\log X)^{2-\varepsilon}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p_{n+1}\leq X\\
p_{n+1}-p_{n}\geq H\end{subarray}}1\asymp e^{-H/\log X}\cdot\frac{X}{\log X}; $$

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p_{n+1}\leq X\\
p_{n+1}-p_{n}\geq H\end{subarray}}(p_{n+1}-p_{n})\asymp\left(1+\frac{H}{\log X}\right)\cdot e^{-H/\log X}\cdot X. $$

For $H>(\log X)^{2+\varepsilon}$ and $X$ sufficiently large, both of the above quantities vanish.

Gallagher [10] studied the regime $H(X)=\lambda\log X$ , with $\lambda>0$ constant, under the assumption of a uniform version of the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture.

#### Theorem 2.6 (Gallagher).

Let $\lambda>0$ , and set $H(X):=\lambda\log X$ . Assume that for each fixed integer $k\geq 2$ and each admissible tuple $\vec{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}^{k}$ , we have

$$ \#\{1\leq n\leq X:n+\ell_{i}\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}=(1+o_{k}(1))\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{\ell}}\,\cdot\frac{X}{(\log X)^{k}} $$

uniformly for $\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{k}$ of size at most $H$ . Then the quantity

$$ P(X,H;k)=\#\{1\leq n\leq X:(n,n+H]\textrm{ contains exactly $k$ primes}\} $$

satisfies the asymptotic (as $X\to\infty$ )

$$ P(X,H;k)\sim\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!}\cdot X. $$

Montgomery and Soundararajan [33] showed that under the assumption of a strong form of the Hardy–Littlewood Prime Tuples Conjecture —more precisely, one with both a uniformity assumption and square-root cancellation—the $2k$ -th moments of the gaps between primes are consistent with the prediction of the Poisson Tail Conjecture in the range $\log X\leq H\leq X^{1/2k}$ . They found that in this range of $H$ , the lower-order fluctuations are slightly smaller than what the Crámer model would predict. There is no such “unexpected smaller variance” phenomenon in our work, essentially because our averaging parameter $H$ is so large that the averaging “covers up” more subtle lower-order behavior.

Finally, we mention the thematically related work of Balog [2] and Kawada [20] (see also the references therein) on an averaged version of the Prime Tuples Conjecture where one averages over the shifts.

## 3. Higher-order Fourier analysis input

In this section we recall the necessary tools from higher-order Fourier analysis. This area originated in Gowers’s new proof of Szemerédi’s Theorem [11, 12]. The work of Green and Tao [14, 15, 16], and later Green, Tao, and Ziegler [13], used higher-order Fourier analysis to study the asymptotic frequency with which linear forms simultaneously assume prime values. In general, the circle method is useful for problems of this type when the number of variables exceeds the number of linear forms. Higher-order Fourier analysis allows one to access the regime where the number of linear forms exceeds the number of variables; it is this shift in perspective that lets us overcome the limitations of Wilson’s circle-method approach [47].

Much of the early work in higher-order Fourier analysis came with poor quantitative dependences, and a major theme has been obtaining “reasonable” quantitative bounds. We will use the strongest known quantitative bounds for arithmetic functions evaluated along linear forms. The main tool is Leng’s recent breakthrough [25] on the higher-order Fourier-uniformity of the von Mangoldt and Möbius functions; as we mentioned above, this work builds on quantitative improvements for the inverse theory of the Gowers norms, as developed by Leng [24] and Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [23].

### 3.1. Leng’s quantitative result on linear equations in primes

We cannot quite use Leng’s main result out-of-the-box because it is stated for multilinear systems with constant coefficients, whereas we work with multilinear systems with slowly-growing coefficients. We will instead use the following variant.

#### Theorem 3.1.

Let $m,t,A\in\mathbb{N}$ , and let $N\in\mathbb{N}$ be a large parameter. Let $\Omega\subseteq[-N,N]^{m}$ be a convex set, and let $\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t}:\mathbb{Z}^{m}\to\mathbb{Z}$ be affine linear forms of the form

$$ \psi_{i}(\vec{n})=\vec{n}\cdot\dot{\psi}_{i}+\psi_{i}(0), $$

where $\dot{\psi}_{1},\ldots,\dot{\psi}_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$ are pairwise linearly independent with coefficients of size at most $(\log N)^{A}$ , and each $|\psi_{i}(0)|\leq(\log N)^{A}$ . Then the following holds.

First, we have the asymptotic

$$ \sum_{\vec{n}\in\Omega\cap\mathbb{Z}^{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\vec{n}))=\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}\cdot\vol(\Omega)+O_{m,t,A}\left(N^{m}(\log N)^{-A}\right), $$

where the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}$ is given by

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}:=\prod_{p}\frac{p^{-m}\#\{\vec{n}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}:\psi_{i}(\vec{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{t}}. $$

Second, we have the cancellation

$$ \sum_{\vec{n}\in\Omega\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mu(\psi_{i}(\vec{n})),\quad\sum_{\vec{n}\in\Omega\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\lambda(\psi_{i}(\vec{n}))\ll_{m,t,A}N^{m}(\log N)^{-A}. $$

There are two differences between this theorem and [25, Theorem 5]:

- • Leng assumes that the $\dot{\psi}_{i}$ ’s have coefficients of constant size.

- • Leng states his results only for $\Lambda$ and $\mu$ (not for $\lambda$ ).

It is well-known to experts that one can obtain the statement of Theorem 3.1 from the arguments in [25]. We will briefly indicate the necessary modifications of the proof.

The main work in [25] is establishing the Gowers-norm control

$$ \|\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\ll_{s,B}(\log N)^{-B},\quad\|\mu\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\ll_{s,B}(\log N)^{-B} $$

for all $s\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B>0$ . Here $\Lambda_{\cramer,z}$ denotes the Cramér approximant of the von Mangoldt function (where $z=z(N):=\exp((\log N)^{1/10})$ is an auxiliary parameter); its exact form is not relevant here. Leng’s deduction of these bounds goes by way of certain Siegel zero approximants $\Lambda_{\siegel},\mu_{\siegel}$ of $\Lambda,\mu$ , whose particular forms are (again) not relevant for us. Leng shows in his Theorem 7 that for each $s\in\mathbb{N}$ there is some $c_{s}>0$ such that

$$ \|\Lambda-\Lambda_{\siegel}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]},~\|\mu-\mu_{\siegel}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\ll_{s}\exp(-(\log N)^{c_{s}}). $$

He then applies11 1 Leng inserts Siegel’s Theorem into his application of [40, Theorem 2.5], so the version that he uses in his paper looks slightly different from the version stated in [40]. This use of Siegel’s Theorem makes the implied constants ineffective. a result of Tao and Teraväväinen [40, Theorem 2.5] which says that

$$ \|\Lambda_{\siegel}-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]},~\|\mu_{\siegel}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\ll_{s,B}(\log N)^{-B}. $$

The desired Gowers-norm control then follows from the Triangle Inequality for Gowers norms.

Unsurprisingly, we also need the analogous statement

$$ \|\lambda\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\ll_{s,B}(\log N)^{-B} $$

for the Liouville function. This can be deduced from the Gowers-norm control for the Möbius function as follows. As usual, choose a prime $5N\leq M\leq 10N$ , and work in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ instead of $\mathbb{Z}$ ; for ease of notation, write $\lambda^{\prime}:=\lambda\cdot{\bf 1}_{[N]}$ and $\mu^{\prime}:=\mu\cdot{\bf 1}_{[N]}$ . Then

$$ \|\lambda\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\asymp_{s}\|\lambda^{\prime}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\asymp_{s}\|\lambda^{\prime}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}, $$

and likewise for $\mu$ (where we evaluate the functions on $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ by first lifting to $[M]\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ ). Using the formula $\lambda(n)=\sum_{r:r^{2}|n}\mu(n/r^{2})$ (which applies equally well to the truncations $\lambda^{\prime},\mu^{\prime}$ ), we expand

$$ \displaystyle\|\lambda^{\prime}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s+1}} \displaystyle=\E_{n,h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}\in\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}}\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(n+\epsilon\cdot h) \displaystyle=\E_{n}\lambda^{\prime}(n)\E_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}}\prod_{0\neq\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(n+\epsilon\cdot h) \displaystyle=\E_{n}\sum_{r:r^{2}|n}\mu^{\prime}(n/r^{2})\E_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}}\prod_{0\neq\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(n+\epsilon\cdot h) \displaystyle=M^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{m=1}^{M/r^{2}}\mu^{\prime}(m)\E_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}}\prod_{0\neq\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(mr^{2}+\epsilon\cdot h). $$

Let $C>0$ be a constant to be chosen later. By the Triangle Inequality, the total contribution of $r>(\log M)^{C}$ is at most

$$ M^{-1}\sum_{r=(\log M)^{C}}^{\infty}\frac{M}{r^{2}}\ll(\log M)^{-C}\ll(\log N)^{-C}. $$

Now, the contribution of a single value $r\leq(\log M)^{C}$ is

$$ M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M/r^{2}}\mu^{\prime}(m)\E_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}}\prod_{0\neq\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(mr^{2}+\epsilon\cdot h)\\
=\E_{m\in\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}}\mu^{\prime}(m)\cdot{\bf 1}_{[M/r^{2}]}(m)\E_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{s+1}}\prod_{0\neq\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{s+1}}\lambda^{\prime}(r^{2}(m+\epsilon\cdot h)); $$

in passing to the second line we replaced the variables $h_{i}$ with the variables $h^{\prime}_{i}:=r^{-2}h_{i}$ , which still range over $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ . The Gowers–Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality (see, e.g., [41, Exercise 1.3.19]), applied to the function $\mu^{\prime}\cdot{\bf 1}_{[M/r^{2}]}$ and the dilated functions $\lambda^{\prime}(r^{2}\times\cdot)$ , gives that the last centered quantity is of size at most

$$ \|\mu^{\prime}\cdot{\bf 1}_{[M/r^{2}]}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}\cdot\|\lambda^{\prime}(r^{2}\times\cdot)\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s+1}-1}\leq\|\mu^{\prime}\cdot{\bf 1}_{[M/r^{2}]}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}. $$

Recalling that $\log(M/r)\asymp_{C}\log N$ and using the Gowers-norm control on $\mu$ , we find that

$$ \|\mu^{\prime}\cdot{\bf 1}_{[M/r^{2}]}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}\asymp_{s}r^{-(s+1)}\|\mu\|_{U^{s+1}[M/r^{2}]}\ll_{s,C,\kappa}r^{-(s+1)}(\log N)^{-\kappa} $$

for all $\kappa>0$ . The sum over $r\leq(\log M)^{B}$ is easily $\ll_{s,C,\kappa}(\log N)^{-\kappa}$ . Taking $C=\kappa:=2^{s+1}B$ , we conclude that $\|\lambda\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\asymp_{s}\|\lambda^{\prime}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})}\ll_{s,B}(\log N)^{-B}$ , as desired.

The aforementioned Gowers uniformity bounds are stated for $\Lambda,\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\mu$ defined to vanish on negative inputs. The Triangle Inequality for the Gowers norms immediately gives bounds of the same quality for the extensions of these functions to negative integers via $\Lambda(-n):=\Lambda(n)$ , etc.

We now have the setup for the deduction of Theorem 3.1. Consider the multilinear operator

$$ F(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}):=\sum_{\vec{n}\in\Omega\cap\mathbb{Z}^{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(\vec{n})). $$

Set $Y=Y(N):=(m+1)(\log N)^{A+1}N$ , so that $\psi_{i}([-N,N]^{m})\subseteq[-Y,Y]$ for all $i$ . Standard applications of the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality and monotonicity properties of box norms (see, e.g., [41, Exercise 1.3.23] for the Cauchy–Schwarz applications, [14, Appendix C] for handling the convex body, and [22, Lemma 3.5(iv)] for the polynomial dependence on the coefficient sizes) show that for any functions $f_{i}:[-Y,Y]\to\mathbb{C}$ , we have

$$ F(f_{1},\ldots,f_{t})\ll_{t}N^{m}(\log N)^{O_{t}(A)}\min_{1\leq i\leq t}\left(\|f_{i}\|_{U^{t-1}[\pm Y]}\cdot\prod_{j\neq i}\|f_{j}\|_{L^{\infty}}\right). $$

Inserting the Gowers uniformity bounds on $\mu,\lambda$ from above, we deduce that

$$ F(\mu,\ldots,\mu),~F(\lambda,\ldots,\lambda)\ll_{t,B}N^{m}(\log N)^{O_{t}(A)}\cdot(\log N)^{-B,} $$

which is $\ll_{t,A}N^{m}(\log N)^{-A}$ if $B$ is sufficiently large depending on $t,A$ . This completes the proof of the second statement of Theorem 3.1.

It remains to prove the von Mangoldt part of Theorem 3.1. By expanding $\Lambda=\Lambda_{\cramer,z}+(\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z})$ , we can write $F(\Lambda,\ldots,\Lambda)$ as $F(\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\ldots,\Lambda_{\cramer,z})$ plus a sum of $O_{t}(1)$ term of the form $F(g_{1},\ldots,g_{t})$ , where each $g_{i}\in\{\Lambda,\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}\}$ and there is at least one index $i$ with $g_{i}=\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}$ . The functions $\Lambda,\Lambda_{\cramer,z}$ are pointwise $\ll\log Y$ (the latter due to [40, Lemma 2.4]). Thus the considerations of the previous paragraph, the Triangle Inequality, and our Gowers uniformity bound on $\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}$ (with $B$ suitably large in terms of $t,A$ ) together give

$$ \displaystyle F(\Lambda,\ldots,\Lambda) \displaystyle=F(\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\ldots,\Lambda_{\cramer,z})+O_{t}(N^{m}(\log N)^{O_{t}(A)}(\log Y)^{t-1}\|\Lambda-\Lambda_{\cramer,z}\|_{U^{t-1}[\pm Y]}) \displaystyle=F(\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\ldots,\Lambda_{\cramer,z})+O_{t,A}(N^{m}(\log N)^{-A}). $$

Tao and Teräväinen [40] have used sieve methods to estimate this main term to good precision. In particular, their Theorem 5.2 (the coefficients of our linear forms are comfortably small enough) gives that

$$ F(\Lambda_{\cramer,z},\ldots,\Lambda_{\cramer,z})=\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}\cdot\vol(\Omega)+O_{m,t}(N^{m}\exp(-(\log N)^{4/5})). $$

Combining the last two equations completes the proof of Theorem 3.1.

### 3.2. Application to random polynomials

Theorem 3.1 is related to average correlations of random polynomials because for $n$ a fixed natural number and $f(x)=a_{d}x^{d}+\cdots+a_{0}$ a random degree- $d$ polynomial, we can interpret $f(n)$ as a linear form in the random variables $a_{0},\ldots,a_{d}$ whose coefficients are powers of $n$ . The following theorem is the technical tool underpinning the arguments in the rest of the paper. The division into residue classes for the von Mangoldt statement will be useful for later computations involving truncated singular series.

#### Theorem 3.2.

Let $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $d\geq 1$ , and let $\delta,A>0$ . Let $X>0$ be a large parameter, and set $H:=\exp(X^{\delta})$ . Let $n_{1},\ldots,n_{t}$ be distinct positive integers of size $|n_{i}|\leq X$ , and let $M\leq(\log H)^{A}$ be a natural number. Then the following holds.

First, for any polynomial $f_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at most $d$ , we have the asymptotic

$$ \E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod M\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(f(n_{i}))=\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod M}+O_{t,d,\delta,A}((\log H)^{-A}), $$

where the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod M}$ is defined by

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod M}:=\left(\prod_{p\mid M}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{i})\neq 0\bmod p}}{1-1/p}\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{p\nmid M}\frac{p^{-(d+1)}\#\{\vec{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d+1}:a_{0}+a_{1}n_{i}+\ldots+a_{d}n_{i}^{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{t}}\right). $$

Second, we have the cancellation

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\lambda(f(n_{i}))=O_{t,d,\delta,A}((\log H)^{-A}). $$

#### Proof.

We start with the Liouville statement since it is simpler. Write $f(x)=a_{d}x^{d}+\cdots a_{0}$ , where $a_{0},\ldots,a_{d}$ range over the integers in $[-H,H]$ . Then we can express

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\lambda(f(n_{i}))=\frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\vec{a}\in[-H,H]^{d+1}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\lambda(\psi_{i}(\vec{a})), $$

where the homogeneous linear forms $\psi_{i}=\dot{\psi}_{i}$ are given by

$$ \psi_{i}(\vec{a}):=a_{0}+n_{i}a_{1}+\cdots+n_{i}^{d}a_{d}. $$

Since the $n_{i}$ ’s are distinct, the non-vanishing of the Vandermonde determinant guarantees that $\dot{\psi}_{i}$ ’s are in fact jointly linearly independent (not merely pairwise linearly independent). The coefficients of the linear forms have size at most $X^{d}=(\log H)^{\delta^{-1}d}$ , where we view $\delta^{-1}d$ as a constant. Thus, for $A\geq\delta^{-1}d$ , Theorem 3.1 tells us that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\lambda(f(n_{i}))=O_{t,d,\delta,A}((\log H)^{-A}), $$

as desired.

We now turn to the von Mangoldt statement. Without loss of generality, we may take $f_{0}$ to be of the form $f_{0}(x)=b_{d}x^{d}+\cdots+b_{0}$ for some integers $1\leq b_{0},\ldots,b_{d}\leq M$ . Then we can express $f$ as

$$ f(x)=(b_{d}+Ma_{d})x^{d}+\cdots+(b_{0}+Ma_{0}), $$

where each $a_{j}$ ranges over the integers in $I_{j}=I_{j}(H,f_{0}\bmod M):=\left[\frac{-H-b_{j}}{M},\frac{H-b_{j}}{M}\right]$ . Thus we can express

$$ \E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod M\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(f(n_{i}))=(1+O(M/H))\left(\frac{M}{2H}\right)^{d+1}\sum_{\vec{a}\in\prod_{j=0}^{d}I_{j}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\vec{a})), $$

where now our linear forms are given by

$$ \psi_{i}(\vec{a}):=Ma_{0}+Mn_{i}a_{1}+\cdots+Mn_{i}^{d}a_{d}+(b_{0}+b_{1}n_{i}+\cdots+b_{d}n_{i}^{d}). $$

Again the homogeneous parts are linearly independent by Vandermonde, and the coefficients are of size $\ll MX^{d}=(\log H)^{A+\delta^{-1}d}$ . Applying Theorem 3.1 with $N=2H/M$ (say) and some $A^{\prime}\geq A+\delta^{-1}d$ , we find that

$$ \E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod M\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(f(n_{i}))=(1+O(M/H))\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}+O_{t,d,\delta,A}((\log H)^{-A})=\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}+O_{t,d,\delta,A}((\log H)^{-A}). $$

It remains only to observe that the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod M}$ is a rewriting of the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\Psi}$ from Theorem 3.1. ∎

## 4. Averaged polynomial Chowla

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.10. To illustrate our methods in a simpler setting, we start with a proof of Theorem 1.9.

### 4.1. Liouville sums

For the proof of Theorem 1.9, we need the following combinatorial fact about Gaussian moments (proven, e.g., in [47]).

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then as $X\rightarrow\infty$ , we have

$$ \frac{1}{X^{k/2}}\sum_{u=1}^{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{u}\geq 1\\
2\mid\ell_{i}\\
\sum_{i=1}^{u}\ell_{i}=k\end{subarray}}\frac{k!}{\ell_{1}!\cdots\ell_{u}!}\sum_{1\leq n_{1}<\ldots<n_{u}\leq X}1=C_{k}+O_{k}(X^{-1}). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.9.

Fix $d\geq 1$ . We expand the quantity of interest as

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))\right)^{k}=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{1}{X^{k/2}}\sum_{u=1}^{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{u}\geq 1\\
\sum_{i=1}^{u}\ell_{i}=k\end{subarray}}\frac{k!}{\ell_{1}!\cdots\ell_{u}!}\sum_{1\leq n_{1}<\ldots<n_{u}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{u}\lambda(f(n_{i}))^{\ell_{i}}. $$

Since $\lambda(n)^{2}=1$ for all $n$ , we care only about the parities of the $\ell_{i}$ ’s. We split the sum according to whether or not there is some odd $\ell_{i}$ : Write

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\lambda(f(n))\right)^{k}=M_{k}(X;H)+\sum_{v=1}^{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v}\geq 1\\
2\nmid\ell_{i}\\
\sum_{i=1}^{v}\ell_{i}\leq k\end{subarray}}E_{k}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v};X;H), $$

where the main term is

$$ M_{k}(X;H):=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{1}{X^{k/2}}\sum_{u=1}^{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{u}\geq 1\\
2\mid\ell_{i}\\
\sum_{i=1}^{u}\ell_{i}=k\end{subarray}}\frac{k!}{\ell_{1}!\cdots\ell_{u}!}\sum_{1\leq n_{1}<\ldots<n_{u}\leq X}1, $$

and for for odd $\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v}$ we have defined the error term $E_{k}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v};X;H)$ to be

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{1}{X^{k/2}}\sum_{v^{\prime}=1}^{k-v}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\ell_{v^{\prime}}^{\prime}\geq 1\\
\sum_{i=1}^{v^{\prime}}\ell_{i}^{\prime}+\sum_{j=1}^{v}\ell_{j}=k\\
2\mid\ell_{i}^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\frac{k!}{\ell_{1}!\cdots\ell_{v}!\cdot\ell_{1}^{\prime}!\cdots\ell_{v^{\prime}}!}\sum_{1\leq n_{1}<\ldots<n_{v}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{v}\lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

Lemma 4.1 tells us that

$$ M_{k}(X;H)=C_{k}+O_{k}(X^{-1}), $$

and we will be done once we bound the error terms (of which there are only $O_{k}(1)$ ) as

$$ E_{k}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v};X;H)\ll_{d,\delta,k}X^{-1}. $$

The main idea is that we can swap the order of summation and then apply Theorem 3.2 to the resulting averages over $f$ . To this end, write

$$ E_{k}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v};X;H)=\frac{1}{X^{k/2}}\sum_{v^{\prime}=1}^{k-v}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v^{\prime}}^{\prime}\geq 1\\
\sum\ell_{i}^{\prime}+\sum\ell_{j}=k\\
2\mid\ell_{i}^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\frac{k!}{\ell_{1}!\cdots\ell_{v}!\cdot\ell_{1}^{\prime}!\cdots\ell_{v^{\prime}}^{\prime}!}\sum_{1\leq n_{1}<\ldots<n_{v}\leq X}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{v}\lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

Due to the choice of $H$ and the upper bound on the $n_{i}$ ’s, Theorem 3.2 lets us control the inner averages over $f$ as

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{v}\lambda(f(n_{i}))\ll_{d,\delta,v,A}(\log H)^{-A}, $$

which is $\ll_{d,\delta,k,B}X^{-B}$ (by choosing $A$ suitably depending on $\delta,B$ ). Summing over the at most $X^{v}$ possibilities for the $n_{i}$ ’s and the $O_{k}(1)$ choices for the remaining parameters, we conclude that each

$$ E_{k}(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{v};X;H)\ll_{d,\delta,k,B}X^{-k/2+v-B}, $$

which is safely $\ll_{d,\delta,k}X^{-1}$ for a suitable choice of $B$ (e.g., $B=k+1$ ). This completes the proof.
