### 4.2. Sign patterns

The proof of Theorem 1.10 follows the same general strategy as the proof of Theorem 1.9, but we must replace Lemma 4.1 with more complicated counting arguments. The connection goes as follows. It is straightforward to show that the equidistribution of Liouville sign patterns is equivalent to Chowla’s Conjecture for polynomials of the form $f(x)=(x+a_{1})\cdots(x+a_{t})$ ; more precisely, the equidistribution of Liouville sign patterns of length $s$ is equivalent to Chowla’s Conjecture for all polynomials $f(x)=(x+a_{1})\cdots(x+a_{t})$ with $1\leq a_{1}<\cdots<a_{t}\leq s$ . The forward implication is immediate, and the backward implication follows from the important observation that for any $(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\in\{-1,1\}^{s}$ , we have

$$ 2^{-s}\prod_{i=1}^{s}(1+\epsilon_{i}\lambda(n_{i}))=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\lambda(n_{i})=\epsilon_{i}\text{ for all $i$};\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

In the setting of Theorem 1.10, this identity implies that

$$ \#\{n\leq X:(\lambda(f(n+1)),\ldots,\lambda(f(n+s)))=(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\}=2^{-s}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{s}(1+\epsilon_{i}\lambda(f(n+i))); $$

the advantage of this maneuver is that expanding out the product and averaging over $f$ gives a sum of several expressions, each of the type that we analyzed in the previous subsection.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.10.

We wish to estimate the moments of

$$ \frac{\#\{n\leq X:(\lambda(f(n+1)),\ldots,\lambda(f(n+s)))=(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\}-2^{-s}X}{X^{1/2}} $$

as $f$ ranges over $\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ . Expanding the product in (4.2), we can express this quantity as

$$ \frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\sum_{n\leq X}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T\subseteq[s]}\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_{i}\lambda(f(n+i))); $$

notice that $T=\emptyset$ corresponds to the “main term” $2^{-s}X$ that we subtracted off. Now the $k$ -th moment of this random variable is

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\sum_{n\leq X}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T\subseteq[s]}\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_{i}\lambda(f(n+i)))\right)^{k}, $$

which we can expand as

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\sum_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}\leq X}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}\subseteq[s]}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\lambda(f(n_{j}+i)). $$

For each fixed choice of $n_{1},\ldots,n_{k},T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ , we will estimate the contribution of the term

$$ \prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\cdot\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\lambda(f(n_{j}+i)). $$

As in the proof of Theorem 1.9, whether this contribution goes towards a main term or towards an error term depends on the form of the multiset $\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}$ . Say that a multiset is even if all of its elements appear with even multiplicity. Theorem 3.2 tells us that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\lambda(f(n_{j}+i))=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if the multiset $\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}$ is even;}\\
O_{d,\delta,s,k,A}((\log H)^{-A}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Since there are at most $X^{k}2^{sk}$ choices of $n_{1},\ldots,n_{k},T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ , the total contribution to (4.4) of the non-even multisets is

$$ \ll_{d,\delta,s,k,A}\left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}X^{k}2^{sk}\cdot(\log H)^{-A}, $$

which is comfortably $O_{d,\delta,s,k}(X^{-1})$ if we choose $A$ sufficiently large in terms of $\delta,k$ . We are left with the contribution of the even multisets, and we conclude that (4.4) is equal to

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}\subseteq[s]}\left(\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\right)\cdot\Bigl|\Bigl\{\begin{subarray}{c}\displaystyle(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}):\text{ the multiset}\\
\displaystyle\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}\text{ is even}\end{subarray}\Bigr\}\Bigr|+O_{d,\delta,s,k}(X^{-1}). $$

We pause to consider the analogous problem with $\lambda(f(1)),\lambda(f(2)),\ldots$ replaced by a sequence of independently random $\pm 1$ ’s. Let $y(1),y(2),\ldots\in\{-1,1\}$ be chosen independently and uniformly at random. The same argument that led to (4.4) tells us that the $k$ -th moment of the quantity

$$ \frac{\#\{n\leq X:(y(n+1),\ldots,y(n+s))=(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{s})\}-2^{-s}X}{X^{1/2}} $$

is precisely

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\E_{\vec{y}}\left(\sum_{n\leq X}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T\subseteq[s]}\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_{i}y(n+i))\right)^{k}, $$

where $\E_{\vec{y}}$ denotes the expectation over $\vec{y}=(y(1),\ldots,y({X+s}))$ drawn uniformly at random from $\{-1,1\}^{X+s}$ Expanding and swapping the order of summation gives

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\sum_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}\leq X}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}\subseteq[s]}\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\cdot\E_{\vec{y}}\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}y(n_{j}+i). $$

The inner expectation is $1$ when the multiset $\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}$ is even, and it is $0$ otherwise, so we can rewrite this $k$ -th moment as

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\sum_{\emptyset\neq T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}\subseteq[s]}\left(\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\right)\cdot\Bigl|\Bigl\{\begin{subarray}{c}\displaystyle(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}):\text{ the multiset}\\
\displaystyle\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}\text{ is even}\end{subarray}\Bigr\}\Bigr|, $$

which agrees (up to $+o(1)$ ) with what appeared in the Liouville setting.

Thus, if one of the quantities in (4.3), (4.5) has a limiting distribution as $X\to\infty$ that is determined by its moments, then these two quantities have the same limiting distribution. Indeed, it is a consequence of the so-called “ $m$ -dependent central limit theorem” of Hoeffding and Robbins [19] that the limiting distribution of the quantity in (4.5) is a Gaussian with mean zero; since Gaussians are determined by their moments, it follows that the quantity in (4.3) has the same limiting distribution. The result of Hoeffding and Robbins also provides a way to compute the variance of this Gaussian in terms of certain covariances, and one can conclude the proof of Theorem 1.10 by appealing to their work. For the sake of completeness and simplicity, we will also provide a direct combinatorial argument for estimating the moments in (4.6).

It will be convenient to use some language from graph theory for bookkeeping. Fix a choice of $T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ , and consider the complete multipartite graph $G=G(T_{1},\ldots,T_{k})$ with partite sets $T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ . For each choice of $n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}$ , we can obtain a subgraph $G^{\prime}=G^{\prime}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{k},n_{1},\ldots,n_{k})$ of $G$ by keeping the edge between the vertex $i_{1}$ in part $T_{j_{1}}$ and the vertex $i_{2}$ in part $T_{j_{2}}$ if and only if $n_{j_{1}}+i_{1}=n_{j_{2}}+i_{2}$ . In this language, the multiset $\{n_{j}+i:i\in T_{j}\}$ is even if and only if the graph $G^{\prime}$ has a perfect matching. Such a perfect matching can exist only when $|T_{1}|+\cdots+|T_{k}|$ is even, so we restrict our attention to choices of $T_{1},\ldots,T_{k}$ for which this is the case.

Fix a subgraph $G^{*}$ of $G$ that contains a perfect matching. We will estimate the number of tuples $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k})$ for which $G^{\prime}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{k},n_{1},\ldots,n_{k})=G^{*}$ . Consider the auxiliary graph $J$ with the vertex set $[k]$ , where vertices $j_{1},j_{2}$ are adjacent if and only if $G^{*}$ contains an edge connecting $T_{j_{1}}$ and $T_{j_{2}}$ . It is clear that $J$ has no isolated vertices (due to $G^{*}$ containing a perfect matching), so $J$ has some number $c\leq k/2$ of connected components. The connected components of $J$ partition $[k]$ . For any connected component of $J$ with vertex set $U\subseteq[k]$ , the corresponding edges of $G^{*}$ place linear constraints on $\{n_{j}:j\in U\}$ , and specifying the value of $n_{j}$ for any single $j\in U$ determines the value of $n_{j}$ for every other $j\in U$ ; thus there are at most $X$ possible choices for the tuple $(n_{j})_{j\in U}$ . In total, the number of tuples $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{j})$ with $G^{\prime}=G^{*}$ is at most $X^{c}$ . There are $O_{s,k}(1)$ possibilities for graphs $G,G^{*}$ , so the contribution to (4.6) of the $G^{*}$ ’s with $c<k/2$ is

$$ \ll_{s,k}\left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}X^{k/2-1}\ll_{s,k}(X^{-1}). $$

It remains to consider the contribution of the graphs $G^{*}$ such that the auxiliary graph $J$ has exactly $c=k/2$ connected components. In this case, the graph $J$ must be a perfect matching, and for each each edge $(j_{1},j_{2})$ in $J$ , the graph $G^{*}$ must contain a perfect matching between the vertex sets $T_{j_{1}},T_{j_{2}}$ . This is possible exactly when the sets $T_{j_{1}},T_{j_{2}}$ are translates of one another, in which case there are $X-O_{s}(1)$ choices for the pair $(n_{j_{1}},n_{j_{2}})$ . (The corresponding edges of $G^{*}$ match the $\ell$ -th smallest element of $T_{j_{1}}$ with the $\ell$ -th smallest element of $T_{j_{2}}$ for all $\ell$ .) This gives $(X-O_{s}(1))^{k/s}$ choices for $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{s})$ such that $G^{\prime}$ contains $G^{*}$ , and by the considerations of the previous paragraph the contribution where $G^{\prime}$ properly contains $G^{*}$ is negligible. Thus, the contribution to (4.6) of each such $G^{*}$ is

$$ \left(\frac{2^{-s}}{X^{1/2}}\right)^{k}\left(\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\right)\cdot(X-O_{s}(1))^{k/2}+O_{s,k}(X^{-1})=2^{-sk}\left(\prod_{(i,j):i\in T_{j}}\epsilon_{i}\right)+O_{s,k}(X^{-1}). $$

The total number of possibilities for the graph $J$ is the number of perfect matchings of $[k]$ , namely, $C_{k}=(k-1)!!$ . Consider the contribution to (4.6) of all of the choices of $T_{1},\ldots T_{k}$ corresponding to a given perfect matching $J$ ; this is independent of $J$ (since the elements of $[k]$ can be relabeled), so we can estimate (4.6) as $C_{k}$ times the contribution from a single fixed $J$ , say, the graph $J_{0}$ with the edges $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,(k-1,k)$ . The sum over such tuples $(T_{1},\ldots,T_{k})$ splits as a product over the edges of $J_{0}$ , and we can write (4.6) as

$$ C_{k}\cdot 2^{-sk}\cdot\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\emptyset\neq T_{1},T_{2}\subseteq[s]\\
\text{translates}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in T_{1}}\epsilon_{i}\cdot\prod_{i\in T_{2}}\epsilon_{i}\right)^{k/2}+O_{s,k}(X^{-1}),\vskip-7.11317pt $$

as desired. ∎

## 5. Moments for averaged Bateman–Horn

In this section we establish Theorem 1.1. The methods are similar to those of the previous section, but the computation is considerably more involved due to the presence of a main term. Recall that $H=\exp(X^{\delta})$ for some $0<\delta<1$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Set $w=w(X):=(\log X)/(\log\log X)$ . We want to bound the $k$ -th moment

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left(\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))-\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\right)^{k}=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k-j}X^{-j}\sum_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\Lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

Switching the order of summation, we can rewrite this as

$$ \sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}X^{-j}S_{j}(X;H), $$

where for each $0\leq j\leq k$ we have set

$$ S_{j}(X;H):=\sum_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k-j}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\Lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

Our intermediate goal is to show that for each $j\geq 1$ , the sum $S_{j}(X;H)$ is dominated by the contribution where $n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}$ are all distinct. This distinctness will then facilitate the application of our main tool Theorem 3.2. The final step of the argument consists of exhibiting cancellation in the resulting sums of singular series. The details are as follows.

For $1\leq\ell\leq j$ , consider the contribution

$$ S_{j,\ell}(X;H):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X\\
\#\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\}=\ell\end{subarray}}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k-j}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\Lambda(f(n_{i})) $$

from tuples $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{j})$ containing exactly $\ell$ distinct numbers. There are at most $X^{\ell}$ choices for the set $\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\}$ , and each such set corresponds to $O_{k}(1)$ tuples $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{j})$ , so in total we are summing over $O_{k}(X^{\ell})$ tuples. Lemma 2.1 tells us that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , we have $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\ll_{d,k,\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon/k}$ for all $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ , so certainly $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k-j}\ll_{d,k,\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon}$ . Finally, we have

$$ \Lambda(f(n))\leq\log(2HX^{d})\leq X^{\delta}+d\log X+\log(2)\ll_{d,\delta}X^{\delta} $$

for all $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ and $n\leq X$ . In total we have

$$ S_{j,\ell}(X,H)\ll_{d,\delta,k,\varepsilon}X^{\ell+\varepsilon+j\delta}. $$

If $\ell<j$ , then this exponent is at most $j-1+\varepsilon+k\delta$ ; since $k\delta<1$ by assumption, we can choose $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small (depending on $\delta,k$ ) that the exponent is strictly smaller than $j$ , which gives

$$ S_{j,\ell}(X;H)\ll_{d,\delta,k}X^{j-\gamma} $$

for some $\gamma=\gamma(\delta,k)>0$ .

Our next goal is to evaluate $S_{j,j}(X;H)$ using Theorem 3.2. Fix a tuple $\vec{n}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{j})$ of distinct positive integers of size at most $X$ , and consider the average

$$ S_{j}(X,H;\vec{n}):=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k-j}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\Lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

Again splitting the expectation modulo $P=P(w)$ (see Section 2.1), we obtain

$$ S_{j}(X,H;\vec{n})=\E_{f_{0}\bmod{P}}(1+O_{d}(P/H))\cdot\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod P\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\Lambda(f(n_{i})). $$

From $P\sim\exp(\log X/\log\log X)\ll X$ we see that $P,n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\ll_{\delta}\log(H)^{A^{\prime}}$ for some $A^{\prime}>0$ , so we can use Theorem 3.2 (with $M=P$ ) to evaluate the inner expectation. We obtain

$$ \displaystyle S_{j}(X,H;\vec{n}) \displaystyle=\E_{f_{0}\bmod{P}}(1+O_{d}(P/H))\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}(\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}+O_{d,k,A}((\log H)^{-2A})) \displaystyle=\E_{f_{0}\bmod{P}}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}+O_{d,k,A}((\log H)^{-A}), $$

where we used Lemma 2.1 to pass to the second line. Putting everything together gives

$$ \displaystyle S_{j,j}(X;H) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X\\
\textrm{distinct}\end{subarray}}S_{j}(X,H;\vec{n}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X\\
\textrm{distinct}\end{subarray}}\E_{f_{0}\bmod{P}}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}+O_{d,k,A}(X^{j}\log(H)^{-A}). $$

Since $\log(H)\gg X^{\delta}$ , a suitable choice of $A$ lets us bound the error term by $O_{d,\delta,k}(X^{j-1})$ .

We now turn to the main term of $S_{j,j}(X;H)$ . We truncate the singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}$ and split the $n_{i}$ ’s into arithmetic progressions modulo $P$ . The key to the calculation will be that the average over $\vec{n}\bmod{P}$ of the truncation of $\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}$ precisely matches $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{j}$ . Since this singular series $\mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}$ converges absolutely, we may safely write

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{\vec{n},f_{0}\bmod P}=(1+O(w^{-1}))\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}; $$

notice that the product depends only on $\vec{n}\bmod{P}$ . So our main term from above can be written as

$$ (1+O(w^{-1}))\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\sum_{\vec{m}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(m_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},\ldots,n_{j}\leq X\\
\textrm{distinct}\\
\vec{n}\equiv\vec{m}\bmod P\end{subarray}}1. $$

For each choice of $\vec{m}$ , the number of $\vec{n}$ ’s in the sum is

$$ (X/P)^{j}+O_{j}(X^{j-1})=(1+O_{k}((\log X)^{-1}))(X/P)^{j} $$

(recall $P\sim\exp(\log X/\log\log X)\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ ), and we can simplify our main term as

$$ (1+O_{k}(w^{-1}))X^{j}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\E_{\vec{m}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k-j}\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(m_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}. $$

Here we have again used (the argument from) Lemma 2.1 to upper-bound $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)$ for the error term. Bringing the average over $\vec{m}$ inside the product over $p,i$ , we find that

$$ \E_{\vec{m}\bmod P}\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(m_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}=\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{m_{i}\bmod p:f_{0}(m_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}=\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{j}. $$

Reinstating the average over $f_{0}$ , we conclude that

$$ S_{j,j}(X;H)=(1+O(w^{-1}))X^{j}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k}+O_{d,\delta,k}(X^{j-1/2}) $$

for $j\geq 1$ . Observe that $X^{j-1/2}=O(w^{-1})\cdot X^{j}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k}$ , so we can drop the second error term here.

The only remaining term, corresponding to $j=0$ , is

$$ S_{0}(X;H)=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{k}. $$

Since $P\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ , we easily obtain

$$ S_{0}(X;H)=\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k}+O_{\varepsilon}(H^{-1}X^{\varepsilon}). $$

Recall that $H=\exp(X^{\delta})$ , so this error is much smaller than $O(X^{-1/2}).$

Putting everything together, we have

$$ \displaystyle\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)} \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\Lambda(f(n))-\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\right)^{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}X^{-j}S_{j}(X;H) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}(1+O(w^{-1}))\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k}+O_{d,\delta,k,A}(X^{-1/2}+(\log X)^{-A}). $$

The main terms cancel perfectly due to the identity $\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}=0$ , and the remaining error terms have size

$$ \ll_{d,\delta,k}w^{-1}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)^{k}+(\log X)^{-1}. $$

Lemma 2.1 gives $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0}}(w)\ll\log w$ pointwise, and (with plenty of room to spare) we obtain the desired upper bound $O_{d,\delta,k}(w^{-1+o(1)})=O_{d,\delta,k}((\log X)^{-1+o(1)})$ . ∎

## 6. Prime tuples on average

Our goal is to prove the following refinement of Theorem 1.3; the latter corresponds to the special case $w(X)=(\log X)/(\log\log X)$ .

#### Theorem 6.1.

Let $d\geq 1$ be an integer and let $0<\delta<1$ be a real. Set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta})$ , and suppose that $w=w(X)\leq(\log X)/(\log\log X)$ . Let $1\leq k<1/\delta$ be an integer, and let $\alpha>0$ be a real. Then for any distinct integers $\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{k}$ of size at most $X^{\alpha}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}=O_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}(w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}). $$

#### Proof.

Unsurprisingly, we first expand the square as

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}=\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n_{1}+\ell_{i}))\Lambda(f(n_{2}+\ell_{i}))\\
-\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{2}{X}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))+\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}. $$

We will see that the second term is approximately twice the size of the last term. Again, set $P:=P(w)$ and recall that $\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)$ depends only on $f\bmod P$ ; with this in mind, we will split the expectation over $f$ into residue classes modulo $P$ . Recall that $P\ll\exp(\log X/\log\log X)=X^{o(1)}$ . Hence an application of Theorem 3.2 gives

$$ \frac{2}{X}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))\\
=\frac{2}{X}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\sum_{n\leq X}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod P\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))+O_{d}(P/H)\\
=\frac{2}{X}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\sum_{n\leq X}\mathfrak{S}_{n+\vec{\ell},f_{0}\bmod P}+O_{d,\delta,\alpha,k,A}(\log(H)^{-A}). $$

Since $H=\exp(X^{\delta})$ , we can bound the error term by $O_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}(X^{-1})$ .

The next task is evaluating the sum of singular series. Recall that we may truncate $\mathfrak{S}_{n+\vec{\ell},f_{0}\bmod P}$ since the singular series converges absolutely. In particular, we have

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{n+\vec{\ell},f_{0}\bmod P}=(1+O_{k}(w^{-1}))\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}, $$

where (for fixed $f_{0}$ ) the product depends only on $n\bmod P$ . Hence

$$ \frac{2}{X}\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\sum_{n\leq X}\mathfrak{S}_{n+\vec{\ell},f_{0}\bmod P}\\
=\frac{2(1+O_{k}(w^{-1}))}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0},n_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{1-1/p}\cdot\frac{1}{X}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq X\\
n\equiv n_{0}\bmod P\end{subarray}}1\\
=\frac{2(1+O_{k}(w^{-1}))}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{n\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f_{0}(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{k}}\right)+O_{k}(X^{-9/10})\\
=2(1+O_{k}(w^{-1}))\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}+O_{k}(X^{-9/10}). $$

In obtaining the error term we used the fact that $P\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ and the pointwise upper bound on $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)$ from Lemma 2.1. At the same time,

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}=(1+O_{d}(P/H))\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
f\equiv f_{0}\bmod P\end{subarray}}1=\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}+O(H^{-1/2}). $$

Thus, inserting the pointwise bound $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\ll(\log w)^{k}=w^{o_{k}(1)}$ from Lemma 2.1, we find that the quantity in the statement of Theorem 6.1 is equal to

$$ \frac{1}{X^{2}}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n_{1}+\ell_{i}))\Lambda(f(n_{2}+\ell_{i}))-\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}+O(w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}); $$

it remains to bound this quantity

We separate the diagonal and off-diagonal contributions in the first sum. The diagonal terms are the pairs $(n_{1},n_{2})$ satisfying

$$ \{n_{1}+\ell_{i}:1\leq i\leq k\}\cap\{n_{2}+\ell_{i}:1\leq i\leq k\}\neq\emptyset. $$

We can bound the diagonal contribution by

$$ \frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\log(HX^{d})^{j}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
|(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})|=j\end{subarray}}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n_{1}+\ell_{i}))\prod_{n_{2}+\ell_{i}\not\in n_{1}+\vec{\ell}}\Lambda(f(n_{2}+\ell_{i})). $$

Using either Theorem 3.2 or an upper-bound sieve, we can bound the latter by

$$ \ll_{k,\varepsilon}\frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\log(HX^{d})^{j}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
|(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})|=j\end{subarray}}X^{\varepsilon}\ll_{\delta,k}X^{\delta k-1+\varepsilon}. $$

Since $\delta<1/k$ , the diagonal contribution is $\ll_{k,\varepsilon^{\prime}}X^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}$ .

The off-diagonal terms are those with $(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})=\emptyset$ . In this case, a direct application of Theorem 3.2 gives

$$ \frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})=\emptyset\end{subarray}}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n_{1}+\ell_{i}))\Lambda(f(n_{2}+\ell_{i}))\\
=\frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})=\emptyset\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{S}_{n_{1}+\vec{\ell},n_{2}+\vec{\ell}}\,+O_{d,k,A}((\log H)^{-A}), $$

where the singular series is given by

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{n_{1}+\vec{\ell},n_{2}+\vec{\ell_{2}}}:=\prod_{p}\left(\frac{p^{-d-1}\#\{f_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]:\deg(f_{0})\leq d;f_{0}(n_{1}+\ell_{i}),f_{0}(n_{2}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}\}}{(1-1/p)^{2k}}\right). $$

As $d\geq 1$ , this singular series converges absolutely, and truncating it at $w$ yields the estimate

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{n_{1}+\vec{\ell},n_{2}+\vec{\ell}}=(1+O(w^{-1}))\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{1}{p^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod p}~\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{1}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{2}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}. $$

This product depends only on $n_{1},n_{2}\bmod P$ , so the main term of the off-diagonal contribution can be written as

$$ (1+O(w^{-1}))\frac{1}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod P}\sum_{n_{1}^{\prime},n_{2}^{\prime}\bmod P}\prod_{p\leq w}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{1}^{\prime}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{2}^{\prime}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}\times\frac{1}{X^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
n_{i}\equiv n_{i}^{\prime}\bmod P\\
(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})=\emptyset\end{subarray}}1. $$

Since $P\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ , this inner sum is

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\leq X\\
n_{i}\equiv n_{i}^{\prime}\bmod P\\
(n_{1}+\vec{\ell})\cap(n_{2}+\vec{\ell})=\emptyset\end{subarray}}1=\left(\frac{X}{P}\right)^{2}+O_{k}(X), $$

and the off-diagonal main term is

$$ (1+O(w^{-1}))\frac{1}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod P}\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{1}{p^{2}}\sum_{n_{1}^{\prime},n_{2}^{\prime}\bmod p}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{1}^{\prime}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{f_{0}(n_{2}^{\prime}+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}}{(1-1/p)}+O_{k}(X^{-1/2})\\
=(1+O(w^{-1}))\frac{1}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod P}\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f_{0}(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{k}}\right)^{2}+O_{k}(X^{-1/2})\\
=(1+O(w^{-1}))\frac{1}{P^{d+1}}\sum_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}+O_{k}(X^{-1/2}). $$

Let us return to the main quantity in the statement of Theorem 6.1. Combining the above calculation with (6.1) and recalling that $\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\ll\log w$ , we see that this main quantity is bounded by

$$ \left|\frac{1}{X^{2}}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n_{1}+\ell_{i}))\Lambda(f(n_{2}+\ell_{i}))-\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}\right|+O_{k}(w^{-1+o_{k}(1)})\\
\ll_{\varepsilon}w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}+O(w^{-1})\left|\E_{f_{0}\bmod P}\mathfrak{S}_{f_{0},\vec{\ell}}\,(w)^{2}\right|+O_{k,d,\varepsilon,A}(X^{\delta k-1+\varepsilon}+X^{-1/2}+\log(H)^{-A})\\
\ll_{k,d,\varepsilon}X^{\delta k-1+\varepsilon}+w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}. $$

We conclude on noting that the first error term is negligible since $\delta<1/k$ . ∎

We remark that this argument allows us to bound not just the second moment but also all higher moments. We presented only the second-moment argument here because it will suffice for our applications in the following section.

## 7. Distributions for prime tails

We model our proof of our distributional results Theorems 1.5 and 1.7 on Gallagher’s proof of Theorem 2.6. The main input is Theorem 6.1, our averaged prime tuples result.

### 7.1. From prime tuples to moments

We can use our prime tuples result Theorem 1.3 to deduce information on the typical moments of $\rho_{f,X,L}$ for various ranges of $L$ . To this end, set

$$ M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L}):=\E_{Y\sim\rho_{f,X,L}}[Y^{k}]=X^{-1}\sum_{n\leq X}(\pi_{f}(n+L)-\pi_{f}(n))^{k}, $$

where $\pi_{f}(n)$ denotes the number of $1\leq x\leq n$ such that $f(x)$ is prime. Let $S(k,r)$ denote the Stirling number of the second kind (the number of partitions of $[k]$ into exactly $r$ parts).

#### Theorem 7.1.

Let $d\geq 1$ , let $0<\alpha<2/3$ , and let $\delta(X)=\delta_{d,\alpha}(X)$ be the function from Remark 1.4. Set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta(X)})$ . Let $L=L(X)\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $0<L\leq X^{\alpha}$ and $L(X)\rightarrow\infty$ as $X\rightarrow\infty$ . Let $w=w(X)\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $w(X)\leq\min(\log L(X)/\log\log L(X),\log X/\log\log X)$ . Then for every fixed $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L})-\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|^{2}\ll_{d,\alpha,k}\frac{1}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\left(\frac{L}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{2r}. $$

We remark that our argument would work with any $\alpha<1$ , and we have presented the proof with $\alpha<2/3$ for notational simplicity; this makes no difference in our applications, where $L(X)$ will in fact grow more slowly than any positive power of $X$ .

Theorem 7.1 shows that for most $f$ ’s, the quantity $M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L})$ is very close to the $k$ -th moment of a Poisson random variable of expectation $\mathcal{L}:=\frac{L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}$ . This underpins Theorem 1.5 in the regime of constant $\mathcal{L}$ . In the regime where $\mathcal{L}$ tends to infinity, we deduce Theorem 1.7 from the standard fact that a Poisson distribution with growing expectation limits to a Gaussian after suitable centering and rescaling.

We isolate two steps of the proof in advance. The first lemma records a singular series identity; this is an important component of the argument. The second lemma lets us replace $\Lambda$ with the indicator function of the primes in the conclusion of Theorem 1.3; this maneuver is standard.

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $d\geq 1$ and let $\alpha>0$ . Let $L=L(X)\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $0<L\leq X^{\alpha}$ and $L(X)\to\infty$ as $X\to\infty$ . Let $w=w(X)\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $w(X)\leq\min(\log L(X)/\log\log L(X),\log X/\log\log X)$ . Then for every $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ , irreducible and of degree $d$ , and every $r\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have

$$ (L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w))^{r}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)+O_{r}(L^{r-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}). $$

#### Proof.

We start with the sum on the right-hand side. Again, set $P:=P(w)$ . We have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}\\
=\sum_{\vec{l}\in(\mathbb{Z}/P\mathbb{Z})^{r}}\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}\\
\times\#\{1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L:\ell_{i}\equiv l_{i}\bmod P,~\text{distinct}\}. $$

For each $0\leq j<P$ , let $e_{j}$ denote the number of indices $i$ such that $l_{i}=j$ . Then we know that

$$ \#\{1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L:\ell_{i}\equiv l_{i}\bmod P,~\text{distinct}\}=\prod_{j}\frac{\lfloor(L-j)/P\rfloor!}{\lfloor(L-j)/P-e_{j}\rfloor!}=\left(\frac{L}{P}\right)^{r}+O_{r}(L^{r-1}). $$

Hence, we get that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)=\left(\frac{L}{P}\right)^{r}\sum_{\vec{l}\in(\mathbb{Z}/P\mathbb{Z})^{r}}\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}\\
+O_{r}\left(L^{r-1}\sum_{\vec{l}\in(\mathbb{Z}/P\mathbb{Z})^{r}}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{l}}\,(w)\right). $$

Lemma 2.1 tells us that $\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{l}}\,(w)\ll(\log w)^{r}$ , so the error term is $O_{r}(L^{r-1}P^{r}(\log w)^{r})$ . From $w\leq(\log L)/(\log\log L)$ we get $P=L^{o_{\alpha}(1)}$ , and the error can be bounded by $O(L^{r-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)})$ .

Next, we manipulate the singular series

$$ \sum_{\vec{l}\in(\mathbb{Z}/P\mathbb{Z})^{r}}\prod_{p\leq w}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}=\prod_{p\leq w}\sum_{\vec{l}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{r}}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}. $$

Switching the order of summation, we see that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\vec{l}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{r}}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\} \displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}~\prod_{i=1}^{r}\#\{l_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+\ell_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\} \displaystyle=p\cdot\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}^{r}. $$

Thus we can write

$$ \prod_{p\leq w}\sum_{\vec{l}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{r}}\frac{p^{-1}\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(x+l_{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}~\forall i\}}{(1-1/p)^{r}}=\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right)^{r}. $$

The main term in (7.1) now becomes

$$ L^{r}\prod_{p\leq w}\left(\frac{p^{-1}\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:f(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\}}{1-1/p}\right)^{r}=L^{r}\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)^{r}, $$

and we conclude that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)=(L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w))^{r}+O_{r}(L^{r-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}).\qed $$

#### Lemma 7.3.

Let $d\geq 1$ and let $0<\delta<1$ be a real. Set $H=H(X):=\exp(X^{\delta})$ . Let $1\leq k<1/3\delta$ be an integer and let $0<\alpha<2/3$ be a real. Then for any distinct integers $\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{k}$ of size at most $X^{\alpha}$ , we have

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\right|^{2}\ll_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}\frac{X^{2}w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{2k}}. $$

#### Proof.

Theorem 6.1 tells us that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}\ll_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}. $$

This will give us the desired control once we replace $\Lambda$ with the function

$$ \theta(n):=\begin{cases}\log(|n|),&n\text{ prime};\\
0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

and apply partial summation.

First, we claim that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}\ll_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}. $$

Observe that

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}\\
\ll\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2}+\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right|^{2}. $$

By Theorem 6.1, the second term is $O_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}(w^{-1+o(1)})$ . For the first term, we crudely bound

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2}\\
\ll\log(HX^{d})^{k}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|. $$

Telescoping the product and applying the Triangle Inequality gives

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i})\right)\right|\\
\leq\sum_{j=1}^{k}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{1}{X}\sum_{n\leq X}\left|\prod_{i=1}^{j-1}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\times(\theta(f(n+\ell_{j}))-\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{j}))\times\prod_{i=j+1}^{k}\Lambda(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|. $$

The functions $\theta,\Lambda$ differ only on proper prime powers (that is, numbers of the form $p^{r}$ with $p$ prime and $r>1$ ), so the quantity inside the absolute value is nonzero only when $f(n+\ell_{j})$ is a proper prime power; when this does occur it can be bounded by $\ll_{d,\delta,k}(\log H)^{k}$ . For each fixed $n$ , the quantity $f(n+\ell_{j})$ is a perfect $r$ -th power for at most a $O(H^{-1+1/r})$ -proportion of $f$ ’s; summing over $r\geq 2$ , we conclude that $f(n+\ell_{j})$ is a proper prime power for at most a $O(H^{-1/2})$ -proportion of $f$ ’s. Thus the previous centered equation is at most $\ll_{d,\delta,k}(\log H)^{k}H^{-1/2}$ , which is much smaller than $w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}$ . This completes the proof of (7.2).

With (7.2) in hand, we return to our main quantity of interest, namely,

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\right|^{2}. $$

We can bound this by

$$ \ll\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2}\\
+\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\left(\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))-X\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)\right)\right|^{2}, $$

where (7.2) tells us that the second term is $\ll_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}\frac{w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}X^{2}}{\log(HX^{d})^{2k}}$ . We will handle the first term using partial summation. Let us split the expectation over $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ according to whether $|a_{d}|\geq H/X^{2/3}$ or $|a_{d}|\leq H/X^{2/3}$ . When $|a_{d}|\leq H/X^{2/3}$ , we bound the sum over $n$ trivially as

$$ \frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|\leq H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2}\\
\ll\frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|\leq H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}O(X^{2})\ll X^{2-2/3}. $$

The assumption $k<1/3\delta$ ensures that the power of $X$ in $(\log(HX^{d}))^{2k}\ll_{d}X^{2k\delta}$ is strictly smaller than $2/3$ , so our $X^{2/3}$ saving is acceptable for the conclusion of the lemma.

We now turn to the contribution of $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ with $|a_{d}|\geq H/X^{2/3}$ . Observe that if $t\geq 2X^{2/3}$ then $|f(t)|\asymp|a_{d}|t^{d}$ , i.e., $|f(t)|$ can be small only when $t\leq 2X^{2/3}$ . We thus split our sum

$$ \frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|>H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2} $$

according to the size of $n$ . This quantity is $\ll S_{1}+S_{2}$ , where $S_{1}$ is the small- $n$ contribution

$$ \frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|>H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}\left|\#\{n\leq 2X^{2/3}:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\leq 2X^{2/3}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2} $$

and $S_{2}$ is the large- $n$ contribution

$$ \frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|>H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}\left|\#\{n\in[2X^{2/3},X]:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\in[2X^{2/3},X]}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\right|^{2}. $$

We can trivially dispose of the first term as

$$ S_{1}\ll\frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|>H/X^{2/3}\end{subarray}}X^{4/3}\ll X^{2-2/3}, $$

which is acceptable (as described at the end of the previous paragraph). We use partial summation to handle $S_{2}$ . Writing

$$ \psi_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(t):=\sum_{n\leq X}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i})), $$

we find by partial summation that

$$ \#\{n\in[2X^{2/3},X]:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}=\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{k}}\sum_{n\in[2X^{2/3},X]}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\theta(f(n+\ell_{i}))\\
+O\left(\int_{2X^{2/3}}^{X}\psi_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(t)\cdot\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}\log(f(t+\ell_{i}))}\right)\,dt\right). $$

The lower bound on $t$ (together with the upper bound on the $\ell_{i}$ ’s) ensures that

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}\log(f(t+\ell_{i}))}\right)\ll_{k}\frac{1}{t(\log|f(t)|)^{k+1}}. $$

Putting everything together, we have

$$ S_{2}\ll_{k}\frac{1}{(2H+1)^{d+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)\\
|a_{d}|>H/X^{\beta}\end{subarray}}\left|\int_{2X^{2/3}}^{X}\frac{\psi_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(t)}{t(\log|f(t)|)^{k+1}}\,dt\right|^{2}\\
\ll_{k}\frac{1}{\log(HX^{d})^{2(k+1)}}\int_{2X^{2/3}}^{X}\int_{2X^{2/3}}^{X}\E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\frac{\psi_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(t)}{t}\cdot\frac{\psi_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(t^{\prime})}{t^{\prime}}\,dt\,dt^{\prime}. $$

Since $\delta<1/2k$ , it is straightforward to check (by Cauchy–Schwarz) that the integrand is uniformly $O_{k}(1)$ , so again this error term is acceptable (with room to spare). ∎

With these two ingredients in hand, we can prove Theorem 7.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.1.

Since $\pi_{f}(n+L)-\pi_{f}(n)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}{\bf 1}_{f(n+\ell)\in\mathscr{P}}$ , we can expand

$$ M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L})=\sum_{n\leq X}(\pi_{f}(n+L)-\pi_{f}(n))^{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}. $$

The main idea is that the sums over the $\ell_{i}$ ’s are of the form treated in Theorem 1.3 (via Lemma 7.3). Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality, inserting Lemma 7.2, and applying the Cauchy–Schwar Inequality again, we get

$$ \left|M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L})-X\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|^{2}\\
\leq\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)^{2}\cdot\sum_{r=1}^{k}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\left(\frac{L\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|^{2}\\
\ll_{k}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\left(\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}+O\left(X\frac{L^{-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}\right)\right)\right|^{2}\\
\leq\sum_{r=1}^{k}L^{r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}+O\left(X\frac{L^{-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}\right)\right|^{2}\\
\ll\sum_{r=1}^{k}L^{r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\left[\left|\#\{n\leq X:f(n+\ell_{i})\in\mathscr{P}~\forall i\}-X\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{f,\vec{\ell}}\,(w)}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}\right|^{2}+O\left(X\frac{L^{-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}\right)^{2}\right]. $$

We now average over $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ . Lemma 7.3 lets us bound the the first term’s contribution by

$$ \ll_{d,\delta,\alpha,k}\sum_{r=1}^{k}L^{r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell_{1},...,\ell_{r}\leq L\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\frac{X^{2}w^{-1+o_{k}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{2r}}\ll_{d,\alpha,k}\frac{X^{2}}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\left(\frac{L}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{2r}, $$

as desired. The second term contributes

$$ \ll_{k}\sum_{r=1}^{k}L^{2r}\left(X\frac{L^{-1+o_{r,\alpha}(1)}}{\log(HX^{d})^{r}}\right)^{2}, $$

which is certainly acceptable. ∎

### 7.2. Poisson tail

Theorem 7.1 tells us that, for a suitable range of $L$ , the moments $M_{k}$ typically match the moments of a Poisson distribution. The Poisson distribution, like the Gaussian, is determined by its moments. However, before we can deduce Theorem 1.5, we must address three further points: We need to filter out $f$ ’s with $\mathfrak{S}_{f}=0$ , we need a flexible version of Theorem 7.1 that allows $L$ to depend on $f$ , and we need to obtain convergence for all moments simultaneously. The most important of these is the second: Since the value of $L_{i}$ depends on $f_{i}$ in the statement of Theorem 1.5, we need a statement like Theorem 7.1 for many different values of $L$ . Taking a union bound over all of the possible values of $L$ (corresponding to the possible polynomials $f$ ) is much too expensive, so instead we will apply Theorem 7.1 with a suitable “net” of $L$ -values.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

For now, fix some $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . Lemmas 2.2 and 2.1 provide a constant $C=C(d)>0$ such that

$$ C^{-1}(\log w)^{1-d}\leq\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\leq C\log w $$

whenever the singular series is nonzero. These upper and lower bounds differ by a multiplicative factor of $D=D(X):=C^{2}(\log w)^{d}$ . Now let $\tau=\tau(X)$ be another slowly-growing function; we will later take $\tau$ to grow slightly faster than $\log D$ . For $0\leq j\leq\tau$ , consider the parameter

$$ L(j):=\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{D^{j/\tau}C^{-1}(\log w)^{1-d}}. $$

The $L(j)$ ’s are decreasing from $\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{C^{-1}(\log w)^{1-d}}$ to $\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{C\log w}$ , and consecutive $L(j)$ ’s have quotient $L(j)/L(j+1)=D^{1/\tau}=1+O((\log D)/\tau)$ .

Theorem 7.1 with

$$ w=w(X):=\frac{\delta(X)\log X}{(\log\log X)^{2}}\leq\frac{\log L(\tau)}{\log\log L(\tau)}\leq\frac{\log L(j)}{\log\log L(j)} $$

gives

$$ \E_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left|M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L(j)})-\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L(j)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|^{2}\ll_{k}\frac{1}{w^{1-o(1)}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\left(\frac{L(j)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{2r}\\
\ll_{k}\frac{1}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}\left(1+\left(\mathcal{L}\cdot C(\log w)^{d-1}\right)^{2k}\right)\ll_{k,\mathcal{L}}\frac{1}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}(\log w)^{2k(d-1)}. $$

Markov’s Inequality and a union bound over $j$ give

$$ \mathbb{P}_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left[\left|M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L(j)})-\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L(j)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|\geq\varepsilon\text{ for some $0\leq j\leq\tau$}\right]\\
\ll_{\mathcal{L},k}\frac{\tau\varepsilon^{-2}(\log w)^{2k(d-1)}}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}, $$

uniformly in $\varepsilon>0$ .

Now suppose we pick $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ uniformly at random subject to the constraint $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\neq 0$ . Take the $0\leq j\leq\tau-1$ satisfying

$$ \frac{L(j)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\geq\mathcal{L}>\frac{L(j+1)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}. $$

Since these upper and lower bounds differ by a multiplicative factor of $(1+O((\log D)/\tau))$ , we conclude that they are both $(1+O((\log D)/\tau))\mathcal{L}$ . In particular, we have

$$ \sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L(j)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r},\quad\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\left(\frac{L(j+1)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\mathcal{L}^{r}+O_{\mathcal{L},k}((\log D)/\tau). $$

It follows from the inequality at the end of the previous paragraph that with probability at least

$$ 1-O_{d,\mathcal{L},k}\left(\frac{\tau\varepsilon^{-2}(\log w)^{2k(d-1)}}{w^{1-o_{k}(1)}}\right), $$

we have

$$ M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L(j)}),~M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L(j+1)})=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\mathcal{L}^{r}+O_{\mathcal{L},k}(\varepsilon+(\log D)/\tau). $$

(For the bound on the error probability, note that $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\neq 0$ for a positive proportion (depending on $d$ ) of polynomials $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ , so our conditioning changes the error term by only a constant factor.) Since

$$ L(j+1)<\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}\leq L(j) $$

and $M_{k}(\rho_{f,X,L})$ is monotone in $L$ , this implies that

$$ \displaystyle M_{k}\left(\rho_{f,X;\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}}\right)=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\mathcal{L}^{r}+O_{\mathcal{L},k}(\varepsilon+(\log D)/\tau). $$

This is nearly the desired conclusion. It remains to take a sequence of $f$ ’s and specify $\varepsilon,\tau$ .

Let $X_{i},H_{i},w_{i},f_{i},L_{i}$ be as in the statement of Theorem 1.5. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ . Let $E_{i}$ denote the event that (7.3) fails for $f_{i}$ . Then

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Pr[E_{i}]\ll_{d,\mathcal{L},k}\varepsilon^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\tau(X_{i})(\log w_{i})^{2k(d-1)}}{w_{i}^{1-o_{k}(1)}}. $$

Notice that $w_{i}=(\log X_{i})^{1-o(1)}$ since $\delta(X)$ grows slowly (in fact we can take it to grow arbitrarily slowly). Set $\tau(X_{i}):=\varepsilon^{-1}\log D$ , so that the error on the right-hand side of (7.3) is $O_{\mathcal{L},k}(\varepsilon)$ and

$$ \tau(X_{i})\ll\varepsilon^{-1}\log\log w_{i}\ll\varepsilon^{-1}\log\log\log X_{i}. $$

Now we can bound

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Pr[E_{i}]\ll_{d,\mathcal{L},k}\varepsilon^{-3}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{(\log\log\log X_{i})(\log\log X_{i})^{2k(d-1)}}{(\log X_{i})^{1-o_{k}(1)}}\ll_{k}\varepsilon^{-3}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(\log X_{i})^{1-o_{k}(1)}}, $$

and this sum converges since the sequence $X_{i}$ grows sufficiently quickly. The Borel–Canteli Lemma then tells us that with probability $1$ , the event $E_{i}$ occurs for only finitely many $i$ ’s; in particular, with probability $1$ it will fail for all sufficiently large $i$ . This means that with probability $1$ , we have

$$ M_{k}\left(\rho_{f_{i},X_{i},L_{i}}\right)=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\mathcal{L}^{r}+O_{\mathcal{L},k}(\varepsilon) $$

for all sufficiently large $i$ . Since this holds for all $\varepsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}M_{k}\left(\rho_{f_{i},X_{i},L_{i}}\right)=\sum_{r=1}^{k}S(k,r)\mathcal{L}^{r} $$

with probability $1$ . By a union bound, with probability $1$ this is the case for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ simultaneously.

Finally, since the Poisson distribution is determined by its moments, we conclude that with probability $1$ , the distribution $\rho_{f_{i},X_{i},L_{i}}$ converges to a Poisson distribution with expectation $\mathcal{L}$ . The statement of the theorem follows. ∎

### 7.3. Gaussian counts

The deduction of Theorem 1.7 goes similarly to the deduction of Theorem 1.5. The main difference is that now $\mathcal{L}$ is growing and we must rescale our distributions before taking a limit. We need the following (standard) identity relating rescaled central moments to raw moments for the Poisson distribution. Recall that we write $C_{k}$ for the $k$ -th moment of the Gaussian of mean $0$ and variance $1$ . We use the convention $S(0,0)=1$ and $S(0,r)=0$ for $r>0$ .

#### Lemma 7.4.

Set $m_{\ell}(\lambda):=\sum_{r=0}^{\ell}S(\ell,r)\lambda^{r}$ for $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Then for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have the identity

$$ \frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k}{\ell}m_{\ell}(\lambda)(-\lambda)^{k-\ell}}{\lambda^{k/2}}=C_{k}+O_{k}(\lambda^{-1/2}) $$

as $\lambda\to\infty$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $k$ . For convenience, set

$$ \mu_{k}:=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k}{\ell}m_{\ell}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-\ell} $$

for $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . For the base cases, is easy to check that

$$ \mu_{1}=m_{0}\cdot(-\lambda)+m_{1}=-\lambda+\lambda=0 $$

and

$$ \mu_{2}=m_{0}\cdot\lambda^{2}+2m_{1}\cdot(-\lambda)+m_{2}=\lambda^{2}-2\lambda^{2}+(\lambda+\lambda^{2})=\lambda, $$

as desired. We will show inductively that $\mu_{k}$ satisfies the recurrence

$$ \mu_{k}=\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{k-2}\binom{k-1}{t}\mu_{t}. $$

From this recurrence it follows that each $\mu_{k}$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ , and that the degree of this polynomial is at most $\lfloor k/2\rfloor$ . Isolating the $t=k-2$ contribution and using the induction hypothesis $\lambda^{-(k-2)/2}\mu_{k-2}=C_{k-2}+O_{k}(\lambda^{-1/2})$ , we find that

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{-k/2}\mu_{k} \displaystyle=(k-1)\lambda^{1-k/2}\mu_{k-2}+O_{k}(\lambda^{1-k/2+\lfloor(k-3)/2\rfloor}) \displaystyle=(k-1)(C_{k-2}+O_{k}(\lambda^{-1/2}))+O_{k}(\lambda^{-1/2}) \displaystyle=C_{k}+O_{k}(\lambda^{-1/2}) $$

(since $C_{k}=(k-1)C_{k-2}$ by definition). It remains only to establish (7.4).

We need the combinatorial identity

$$ m_{\ell+1}=\lambda\sum_{s=0}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{s}m_{s}, $$

which is just a restatement of the Stein–Chen identity; we include the short proof for the reader’s convenience. Indeed, inserting the definition of $m_{s}$ , we see that we need to show that

$$ \sum_{r=0}^{\ell+1}S(\ell+1,r)\lambda^{r}=\lambda\sum_{s=0}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{s}\sum_{u=0}^{s}S(s,u)\lambda^{u}. $$

Gathering like powers of $\lambda$ on the right-hand side, we need to show that

$$ S(\ell+1,r)=\sum_{s=r-1}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{s}S(s,r-1) $$

for all $1\leq r\leq\ell+1$ (we can ignore $r=0$ since neither side of the previous centered equation has any constant term). The left-hand side counts the number of ways to partition $[\ell+1]$ into exactly $r$ parts. The data of such a partition consists of the set $X\subseteq[\ell]$ of elements contained in the same part as the element $\ell+1$ , together with a partition of $[\ell]\setminus X$ into exactly $r-1$ parts; this is precisely what the right-hand side counts. We have now established (7.5).

Returning to (7.4), we can use Pascal’s Identity and (7.5) to expand

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{k}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k}{\ell}m_{\ell}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-\ell} \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\left[\binom{k-1}{\ell}+\binom{k-1}{\ell-1}\right]m_{\ell}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-\ell} \displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{\ell}m_{\ell}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-1-\ell}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{\ell}m_{\ell+1}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-\ell-1} \displaystyle=-\lambda\mu_{k-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{\ell}\cdot(-\lambda)^{k-1-\ell}\cdot\lambda\sum_{s=0}^{\ell}\binom{\ell}{s}m_{s}. $$

Setting $t:=k-1-\ell+s$ and noting that

$$ \binom{k-1}{\ell}\binom{\ell}{s}=\binom{k-1}{t}\binom{t}{s}, $$

we can eliminate $\ell$ to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{k} \displaystyle=-\lambda\mu_{k-1}+\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}\sum_{s=0}^{t}\binom{k-1}{t}\binom{t}{s}(-\lambda)^{t-s}m_{s} \displaystyle=-\lambda\mu_{k-1}+\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{t}\mu_{t} \displaystyle=\lambda\sum_{t=0}^{k-2}\binom{k-1}{t}\mu_{t}, $$

as desired. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.7.

Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . Take $C=C(d),D=D(X),\tau=\tau(X),L(j),w=w(X)$ as in the proof of Theorem 1.5. Theorem 7.1 (with a union bound and keeping track of the dependence on $\mathcal{L}$ ) again gives

$$ \mathbb{P}_{f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)}\left[\left|M_{\ell}(\rho_{f,X,L(j)})-\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}S(\ell,r)\left(\frac{L(j)\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}{\log(HX^{d})}\right)^{r}\right|\geq\varepsilon\text{ for some $1\leq\ell\leq k$ and $0\leq j\leq\tau$}\right]\\
\ll_{k}\frac{\tau\varepsilon^{-2}(\mathcal{L}\log w)^{2k(d-1)}}{w^{1-o(1)}}, $$

uniformly in $\varepsilon>0$ .

Now pick $f\in\mathcal{P}(d,H)$ uniformly at random subject to the constraint $\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)\neq 0$ . Arguing as in the proof of Theorem 1.5 we conclude that with probability at least

$$ 1-O_{d,k}\left(\frac{\tau\varepsilon^{-2}(\mathcal{L}\log w)^{2k(d-1)}}{w^{1-o(1)}}\right), $$

we have

$$ \displaystyle M_{\ell}\left(\rho_{f,X;\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}}\right)=\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}S(\ell,r)\mathcal{L}^{r}+O_{k}(\varepsilon+(\log D)/\tau) $$

for all $1\leq\ell\leq k$ . Set $\tau=\tau(X):=\varepsilon^{-1}\log D$ . Consider the centered and rescaled distribution $\mathcal{L}^{-1/2}\left(\rho_{f,X;\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}}-\mathcal{L}\right)$ . By Lemma 7.4, its $k$ -th moment is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k}{\ell}M_{\ell}\left(\rho_{f,X;\frac{\mathcal{L}\log(HX^{d})}{\mathfrak{S}_{f}(w)}}\right)(-\mathcal{L})^{k-\ell}}{\mathcal{L}^{k/2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k}{\ell}m_{\ell}(\mathcal{L})(-\mathcal{L})^{k-\ell}}{\mathcal{L}^{k/2}}+O_{k}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{k/2-\ell}\right) \displaystyle=C_{k}+O_{k}\left(\mathcal{L}^{-1/2}+\varepsilon\mathcal{L}^{k/2-1}\right). $$

This error term is comfortably $o_{k}(1)$ if (say) $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(X):=\mathcal{L}^{-k/2}$ .

Take a sequence of $X_{i},H_{i},w_{i},f_{i}$ as in the statement of Theorem 1.7, and let $E_{i}$ denote the event that the last centered equation fails for $f_{i}$ . Then, by the assumption $\log\mathcal{L}(X)=o(\log w(X))$ and the growth rate of $X_{i}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Pr[E_{i}] \displaystyle\ll_{d,k}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\tau(X_{i})\varepsilon(X_{i})^{-2}(\mathcal{L}(X_{i})\log w_{i})^{2k(d-1)}}{w_{i}^{1-o_{k}(1)}} \displaystyle\ll_{k}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varepsilon(X_{i})^{-3}\mathcal{L}(X_{i})^{2k(d-1)}}{w_{i}^{1-o_{k}(1)}} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{L}(X_{i})^{3k/2+2k(d-1)}}{w_{i}^{1-o_{k}(1)}} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{w_{i}^{1-o_{k}(1)}}<\infty. $$

Apply the Borel–Cantelli Lemma and take a union bound over $k$ as in the proof of Theorem 1.5. This concludes the proof because the Gaussian distribution is determined by its moments. ∎

# Counting integral points in thin sets of type II: singularities, sieves, and stratification

**Authors:** Dante Bonolis Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: dante.bonolis@duke.edu , Lillian B. Pierce Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: lillian.pierce@duke.edu and Katharine Woo Address: Princeton University, Fine Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544 Email address: khwoo@princeton.edu

## Abstract

Consider an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ for an integer $m\geq 1$ . Let $N(F,B)$ count the number of $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that $F(y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable for $y\in\mathbb{Z}$ . In nomenclature of Serre, bounding $N(F,B)$ corresponds to counting integral points in an affine thin set of type II. Previously, in this generality Serre proved $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma<1$ . When $m\geq 2$ , this new work proves $N(F,B)\ll_{n,F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+1/(n+1)+\varepsilon}$ under a nondegeneracy condition that encapsulates that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is truly a polynomial in $n+1$ variables, even after performing any $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables on $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . Under GRH, this result also holds when $m=1$ . We show that generic polynomials satisfy the relevant nondegeneracy condition. Moreover, for a certain class of polynomials, we prove the stronger bound $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{e(n)}$ , comparable to a conjecture of Serre. A key strength of these results is that they require no nonsingularity property of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . The Katz-Laumon stratification for character sums, in a new uniform formulation appearing in a companion paper of Bonolis, Kowalski and Woo, is a key ingredient in the sieve method we develop to prove upper bounds that explicitly control any dependence on the size of the coefficients of $F$ .

## 1. Introduction

Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial, and define the counting function

$$ N(F,B)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap[-B,B]^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}. $$

Trivially, $N(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ , and this is sharp in the case that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has degree at most 1 in $Y$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $F$ is absolutely irreducible, the best known bound (in such generality) is $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma<1$ due to Serre [Ser97]. A conjecture of Serre on thin sets of type II suggests that for suitable polynomials $F(Y,\mathbf{X}),$ the trivial bound for $N(F,B)$ may be reduced by a full factor of $B$ , and this is the motivation for the present work. As an illustration, here is a special consequence of our main work:

#### Theorem 1.1.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $H(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an irreducible polynomial and define $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ for an integer $d\geq 2$ . Suppose there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[(X_{i})_{i\in I}]$ for a subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . Then there is an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\log(\|F\|+2)^{e(n)}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for all $\varepsilon>0$ .

(Here and throughout, $\|F\|$ denotes the maximum absolute value of any coefficient of $F$ . We follow the convention that $A\ll_{\kappa}B$ implies that $|A|\leq C_{\kappa}B$ with the implied constant $C_{\kappa}$ depending on $\kappa$ .) A strength of Theorem 1.1 is that it requires no assumption of nonsingularity for $F$ . Many previous works on bounding $N(F,B)$ in various contexts, such as [Pie06, HB08, Mun09, HBP12, Bon21, BCLP23, BP24] have relied on $F$ satisfying an appropriate nonsingularity condition. A central aim of the present work is to bound $N(F,B)$ for singular polynomials $F$ .

Our main work goes beyond the cyclic structure of the polynomial in Theorem 1.1. Consider any absolutely irreducible polynomial of the form

$$ F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})=Y^{md}+Y^{m(d-1)}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Y^{m}f_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

in which each $f_{j}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is a polynomial (not necessarily homogeneous) of degree $k_{j}\geq 0$ , and $f_{d}\not\equiv 0$ . If $m=1$ , (1.1) simply specifies that $F$ is monic in $Y$ ; if $m\geq 2$ , this structure imposes that $F$ is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ . It is natural to require that $f_{d}\not\equiv 0$ (since otherwise $y=0$ provides a solution to $F(y,\mathbf{x})=0$ for each $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}$ and so $B^{n}\ll N(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ ); this certainly holds if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible.

Our most general theorem (Theorem 1.2) bounds $N(F,B)$ with an exponent as strong as Theorem 1.1 under two conditions: (i) a nondegeneracy condition that encapsulates that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is truly a polynomial in $n+1$ variables, even after performing any $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables on $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ ; (ii) the condition $m\geq 2$ in (1.1). We furthermore can allow $m=1$ , under the assumption of GRH. Under a stronger nondegeneracy condition, we show the dependence on $\|F\|$ is at most polylogarithmic (Theorem 1.3). In particular, our main theorems require no assumption of nonsingularity. Moreover, we show that in the moduli space of polynomials of the form (1.1) for fixed $m,d,k_{1},\ldots,k_{j}$ (and even among the subspace of singular polynomials), polynomials that satisfy the relevant nondegeneracy condition (i) are generic (Theorem 3.1). We furthermore prove for a certain class of polynomials the stronger bound $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{e(n)}$ , which is comparable to a conjecture of Serre (Theorems 1.4 and 1.5). We next state these general results precisely.

### 1.1. General setting of new work

The first nondegeneracy condition we require takes the following form. Let $M$ be a finite (nontrivial) extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ . We say $M$ is an n-genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for every $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ such that

$$ M=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

$G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has nonzero degree in each of $Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . We say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. (In particular, $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ .) Our first main result is:

#### Theorem 1.2.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial of the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ . Then there exists an integer $h=h(n,\deg F)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\|F\|^{h}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for every $\varepsilon>0$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and the same hypotheses hold with $m=1$ , the same result holds, conditional on GRH.

The proof of this theorem relies on a dichotomy, so that it is a consequence of two main theorems. On one side of the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, we prove a slightly better bound, with a polylogarithmic dependency on $\|F\|$ , under a stronger nondegeneracy condition. The main strategy to prove this result is a polynomial sieve.

Precisely, we say that a finite (nontrivial) extension $M$ of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for all subextensions $M^{\prime}$ satisfying

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset M, $$

$M^{\prime}$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. We say that an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. (In particular, $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ .)

#### Theorem 1.3.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be a strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial of the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ . Then there exists an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\log(\|F\|+2)^{e(n)}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for every $\varepsilon>0$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and the same hypotheses hold with $m=1$ , the same result holds, conditional on GRH.

On the other side of the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, we must consider the case in which $F$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. In this case, a completely different argument achieves a stronger exponent, at the expense of the dependency on the coefficients of $F$ :

#### Theorem 1.4.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Then there exists an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,F}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{e(n)}. $$

The exponent in this case concurs with a conjecture of Serre, which we review momentarily. In this theorem, the dependence on $F$ in the implicit constant is inexplicit. But we show that within the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, either we can apply the polynomial sieve (leading to the inequality stated for $N(F,B)$ in Theorem 1.3) or we can refine the strategy for Theorem 1.4 to attain $N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\|F\|^{h}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{e}$ for some $e=e(n)$ and $h=h(n,\deg F)$ . Taken together, this ultimately verifies the remaining cases of Theorem 1.2. Note that this result does not require the polynomial to have the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ , and hence sidesteps the need to assume GRH when $m=1$ .

### 1.2. Relation to previous results

The special case of Theorem 1.1 in which $H(\mathbf{X})$ is a nonsingular form includes the main theorem of Munshi’s work [Mun09] as formulated and proved by Bonolis [Bon21, Remark 1]. The special case of Theorem 1.2 in which $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=g(Y)-f(\mathbf{X})$ for a fixed polynomial $g$ and a nonsingular form $f$ recovers many cases of the main theorem of [Bon21] (see Example 8.12 and details in Remark 8.13). Theorem 1.3 immediately implies Theorem 1.1, since under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.1, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ is a strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial (as proved in Example 8.7). Finally, the special case of Theorem 1.3 in which $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ defines a nonsingular hypersurface in weighted projective space $\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ (for an integer $e\geq 1$ ) recovers the main theorem of Bonolis and Pierce’s work [BP24] (see Example 8.10 and Remark 8.11).

### 1.3. Relation to Serre’s conjecture on thin sets

Recall Serre’s formulation of thin sets [Ser97, §9.1]: a subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a thin set of type I if there is a Zariski-closed subvariety $F\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $M\subset F(\mathbb{Q})$ . On the other hand, a subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ if there is an irreducible projective algebraic variety $Z$ of dimension $n-1$ and a generically surjective morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ of degree $D\geq 2$ with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ . Any thin set is contained in a finite union of thin sets of type I and type II. Affine thin sets of each type are defined analogously, with $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ replaced by $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . One motivation to show a thin set contains few points comes from specialization of Galois groups: as Serre observed, for $\mathbf{x}$ outside of a thin set, $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ has the same Galois group as $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ [Ser97, p. 122].

#### 1.3.1. Projective setting

Let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set. Define the height function $H(\mathbf{x})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|$ for $\mathbf{x}=[x_{1}:\cdots:x_{n}]\in\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ with $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ and $\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1$ , and the associated counting function for the thin set:

$$ M_{H}(B)=\{\mathbf{x}\in M:H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}. $$

Trivially, $M_{H}(B)\ll B^{n}$ . Serre conjectured in [Ser97, p. 178] that

$$ M_{H}(B)\ll_{M}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c} $$

for some $c$ . If $M$ is of type I this can be interpreted as a statement of the Dimension Growth Conjecture, which predicts that if $Z$ is an irreducible projective variety in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ of degree $D\geq 2$ then $Z_{H}(B)\ll_{Z,\varepsilon}B^{\dim Z+\varepsilon}$ for all $B\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ . This has been resolved in many cases by [Bro03b, BHB06a, BHB06b, HB94, HB02, Sal07], and in all remaining cases by Salberger [Sal23]. A uniform version, in which the implied constant depends only on $n,\deg Z,\varepsilon$ is also known, as long as $\deg Z\neq 3$ ; see [Sal23].

For thin sets of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the conjecture (1.2) has been proved (with $B^{\varepsilon}$ instead of a logarithmic factor) when $n=2$ , and when $n=3$ if the cover has degree at least 3, by Broberg [Bro03a]. (For $n=3$ and degree 2, Broberg proves $M_{H}(B)\ll B^{9/4+\varepsilon}$ .) It has also been proved for the special case of nonsingular cyclic covers of $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ when $n\geq 10$ , by Heath-Brown and Pierce in [HBP12] (which also obtains somewhat weaker nontrivial bounds for $3\leq n\leq 9$ ).

#### 1.3.2. Affine setting

As Serre describes in [Ser97, p. 122], an affine thin set $M$ of type II in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ has a corresponding polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]$ that is absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]$ ) and of degree $D\geq 2$ in $Y$ , for which

$$ M=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Q},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0,\text{$y$ not a pole of any coefficient of $F$}\}. $$

If $F$ satisfies appropriate homogeneity conditions, a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ can be described in an analogous way.

Our study of $N(F,B)$ is thus the study of counting integral points on affine thin sets of type II. Serre made initial progress: if $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is absolutely irreducible and $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , then by [Ser97, Thm. 1, p. 177],

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma} $$

for some $\gamma<1$ , and unspecified dependence of the implicit constant on $F$ . An examination of Serre’s original argument (which is done in [BPW25a]) shows that this bound (with $\gamma=1$ ) can be made to have at most polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is of the form (1.1) for some $m\geq 2$ ; when $m=1$ , this polylog dependence can be established under GRH for reasons similar to why GRH is assumed in Theorem 1.2 for $m=1$ . To prove our main theorems, we require an unconditional version of (1.3) with at most polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ , which applies to any irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ with constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . We prove this in Theorem 2.13.

Serre also attributes to earlier work of Cohen [Coh81, Thm. 2.1] a bound of the strength

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,D}\|F\|^{c}B^{n-1/2}\log B $$

for all $B\geq\|F\|^{3c}$ for some $c=c(n,\deg F)$ . There is a gap in the method described in [Coh81, Thm. 2.1]; we prove in the companion paper [BPW25b] that this gap can be repaired by using the theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials that we develop in the present paper.

If no further condition is placed on $F$ , the upper bound (1.3) is (essentially) sharp. For example, Serre points to the trivial example $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Y^{2}-X_{1}$ , for which

$$ N(F,B)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$x_{1}$ is a square}\}\gg B^{n-1/2}. $$

But Serre’s conjecture (1.2) for counting rational points on projective thin sets also suggests a question for counting integral points on certain affine thin sets of type II: for suitable polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , is there is some $c=c(F)$ such that

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c},\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$?} $$

And, can the dependence of the implicit constant on $\|F\|$ be controlled? These questions motivate our present work.

Previous works such as [Mun09, Bon21, BP24] (or in the function field setting [BCLP23]) improved on Serre’s bound (1.3), and approached (1.5), but only when $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies a nonsingularity condition, and has a special shape. Additionally, Pierce and Heath-Brown [HBP12] have proved Serre’s conjecture (1.5) for $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-f(\mathbf{X})$ when $n\geq 10$ (also obtaining stronger results than (1.3) for $n\geq 6$ and than Theorem 1.1 for $n\geq 8$ ), but only under the assumption that $f$ has nonsingular leading form.

In the present work, we make no assumption of nonsingularity. Theorems 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 provide bounds for $N(F,B)$ that approach (1.5) as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Moreover, Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.5 (stated below) admit the exponent predicted by (1.5).

### 1.4. Singularities, sieves, and stratification:

Our strategy is to count solutions contributing to $N(F,B)$ via a polynomial sieve, as formulated in [BP24]. The unconditional sieve lemma we employ (Lemma 6.1) imposes that $m\geq 2$ in the depiction (1.1) of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ ; under GRH, an analogous sieve lemma also holds true for $m=1$ (Lemma 6.2). Aside from this application of the sieve lemma, the remainder of the paper does not distinguish between $m\geq 2$ and $m=1$ .

After an application of a polynomial sieve lemma, our central concern is to understand for many primes $p$ the local counting function

$$ v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\;(\text{mod}\;p):F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\;(\text{mod}\;p)\}. $$

In particular, it is crucial to estimate for each $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ the associated complete sum

$$ S(\bfu,p)=\sum_{\bfa\;(\text{mod}\;p)}(v_{p}(\bfa)-1)e_{p}(\bfu\cdot\bfa). $$

A celebrated stratification result of Katz and Laumon [KL85] (see also Fouvry [Fou00]) provides a set of nested varieties that control how large $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|$ can be as $\mathbf{u}$ varies. The version of the stratification we require is as follows: there exists a constant $C_{F}\geq 1$ , an integer $N_{F}\geq 1$ , and homogeneous varieties $\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{Z}[1/N_{F}]}\supset V_{1}\supset V_{2}\supset...\supset V_{n}$ , where $V_{j}$ has codimension at least $j$ , such that for any prime $p\nmid N_{F}$ and for $\bfu\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ ,

$$ |S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+j-1}{2}}. $$

Thus in particular if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , then $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+j}{2}}$ . Previous works that employed the polynomial sieve (such as [Mun09, Bon21, BCLP23, BB23, BP24]) only encountered two possibilities: $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n}{2}}$ ( $\mathbf{u}$ is good) or $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+1}{2}}$ ( $\mathbf{u}$ is bad), since in all those works $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ was assumed to be nonsingular. Here we make no such assumption, and we require the full strength of the Katz-Laumon stratification.

To obtain the explicit dependence on $\|F\|$ in Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, we require an even stronger statement of stratification, which makes explicit whether (and how) the following parameters depend on the coefficients of $F$ : $C_{F},N_{F}$ , and the degree, number of irreducible components, and defining polynomials of each stratum $V_{j}$ . This uniform stratification is new: it is proved by two of the authors with Emmanuel Kowalski, in the companion paper [BKW25], and recorded here in Theorem 6.3.

Even with such a uniform stratification in hand, an essential difficulty arises when applying the stratification to bound $N(F,B)$ . This occurs if an irreducible component, say $X_{j}$ , of some stratum $V_{j}$ is degenerate, that is, lies in a proper linear subspace of $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ (and in particular is hence contained in a hyperplane, say $W_{j}$ ). We show that to handle the contribution of a possible degenerate component, it would suffice to prove that aside from a set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ , for each prime $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in W_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

Since there are $O(p^{n-1})$ terms in the sum, this is a statement that $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\ll p^{n/2}$ on average over $\mathbf{u}\in W_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ . The proof of the second moment bound (1.6) is delicate: it is precisely where the assumption that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable becomes relevant (in the proof of Theorem 1.3).

Precisely, we are able to prove that (1.6) holds as long as for a certain change of variables $L\in\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ with integer entries (determined by the hyperplane $W_{j}$ ), the polynomial $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that aside from an exceptional set $\mathcal{E}_{L}$ of primes with $|\mathcal{E}_{L}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F_{L}\|$ , for each prime $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{L}$ ,

$$ \#\{(a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:F_{L}(Y,X_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n})\text{ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-2}. $$

In a key step, we show that (1.7) holds as long as $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is “strongly $n$ -genuine.” Here, and throughout, we say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial if $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. Similarly, we say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. That is to say, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable (resp. strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable) precisely when $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine (resp. strongly $n$ -genuine) for all $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ .

This series of ideas leads ultimately to Theorem 1.3 with at most polylog dependency on $\|F\|$ : if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable then $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L$ , by definition. Thus we can show (1.7) holds, and hence the second moment bound (1.6) can be obtained for all hyperplanes $W$ , and in particular for any hyperplane that contains at least one degenerate component of a stratum $V_{j}$ .
