## 1. Introduction

In 1936, Cramér introduced a probabilistic model for predicting features of the primes. In this model, $\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ is prime}}$ is modeled by a random variable $X_{n}$ with $\mathbb{P}(X_{n}=1)=1-\mathbb{P}(X_{n}=0)=1/\log n$ . We have that almost surely

$$ \lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{n\leqslant X}X_{n}}{\sum_{n\leqslant X}\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ prime}}}=1. $$

In particular, Cramér’s model matches the Prime Number Theorem. It is interesting to test Cramér’s heuristic as a method for modeling finer aspects of the distribution of the primes. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, it is known that Cramér’s model matches the truth for primes in intervals of the shape $[X,X+X^{1/2+\varepsilon}]$ . For $\lambda>2$ , Cramér’s model suggests that

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+(\log X)^{\lambda}}\mathbbm{1}_{n\text{ is prime}}=(1+o(1))\frac{(\log X)^{\lambda}}{\log X} $$

since

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+(\log X)^{\lambda}}X_{n}=(1+o(1))\frac{(\log X)^{\lambda}}{\log X} $$

almost surely. It turns out that the naive conjecture described above is false, and

#### Theorem 1.1 (Maier, [15]).

Fix $\lambda>1$ and set $H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Then, the following holds:

$$ \limsup_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\pi(X+H)-\pi(X)}{H/\log X}>1, $$

and

$$ \liminf_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\pi(X+H)-\pi(X)}{H/\log X}<1. $$

Following Maier’s remarkable result, similar results on the inequidistribution of other arithmetic sequences in short intervals were obtained by Balog-Wooley [1] on numbers representable as sums of two squares, and Tongsomporn and Steuding [24] on primes in Beatty sequences. Later, Maynard [20] combined Maier’s methods with sieve theory to push these results further for prime numbers and numbers representable as the sum of two squares. Additionally, Thorne [23] has shown the function field analogue of Theorem 1.1.

Granville and Soundararajan [8] generalized Maier’s work and showed that a more general class of arithmetic sequences will be poorly distributed in either short intervals or short arithmetic progressions. In particular, they demonstrated that this phenomenon is not specific to the primes.

Friedlander and Granville [5] use Maier’s method show the analogue of Maier’s result for short arithmetic progressions. Specifically, writing $\pi(X,q,a)=\#\{p\leqslant X:p\equiv a\mod q,p\text{ prime}\}$ , it is shown that for fixed $A>2$ , large $X$ there exists $q_{\pm}\in[X,2X]$ such that

$$ \pi(X(\log X)^{A},q_{+},1)>(1+\delta_{A})\frac{X}{\varphi(q_{+})(\log X)^{A-1}}, $$

$$ \pi(X(\log X)^{A},q_{-},1)<(1-\delta_{A})\frac{X}{\varphi(q_{-})(\log X)^{A-1}}. $$

There has been further work on these lines by Friedlander, Granville, Hildebrand, and Maier [6].

Before we state our general result, we shall discuss some special cases of our main theorem. In [25], Vinogradov shows for odd $N$ that

$$ \#\{p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}\in[0,N]:p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3}=N\}=\frac{\mathfrak{S}(N)}{2}\frac{N^{2}}{(\log N)^{3}}, $$

where

$$ \mathfrak{S}(N)=\prod_{p|N}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\bigg)\prod_{p\nmid N}\bigg(1+\frac{1}{(p-1)^{3}}\bigg). $$

One might desire to understand the distribution of pairs $(n_{1},n_{2})$ for which $n_{1},n_{2},N-n_{1}-n_{2}$ are all prime. By the above result, an analogue of Cramér’s model might be to model $\mathbbm{1}_{n_{1},n_{2},N-n_{1}-n_{2}\text{ prime}}$ by a random variable $X_{n_{1},n_{2}}$ with

$$ \mathbb{P}(X_{n_{1},n_{2}}=1)=1-\mathbb{P}(X_{n_{1},n_{2}}=0)=\frac{\mathfrak{S}(N)}{2(\log N)^{3}} $$

Unconditionally, Zhan [26] has an asymptotic the count of $(n_{1},n_{2})$ such that $n_{1},n_{2},$ and $N-n_{1}-n_{2}$ are prime, and that the $n_{i}$ are restricted to appropriate short intervals of length at least $N^{\frac{5}{8}}(\log N)^{c}$ for some $c>0$ . This analogue of Cramér’s model would suggest that one would be able to count such $n_{i}$ in short intervals as short as $(\log X)^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda>2$ .

A special case of our main theorem provides an answer in the negative to the this Cramér-type model provides. Specifically, we show:

#### Corollary 1.2.

Let $N$ be a sufficiently large odd number and $\lambda>\frac{3}{2}$ . Let $N\ll X\leqslant N/6,H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . There exist $\delta_{\lambda}^{+},\delta_{\lambda}^{-}>0$ such that for $X$ sufficiently large, there exist $x^{\pm},y^{\pm}\in[X,2X]$ such that

$$ \#\{p_{1}\in[x^{+},x^{+}+H],p_{2}\in[y^{+},y^{+}+H]:N-p_{1}-p_{2}\textrm{ prime}\}\geqslant(1+\delta_{\lambda}^{+})\mathfrak{S}(N)\frac{H^{2}}{(\log X)^{3}}, $$

$$ \#\{p_{1}\in[x^{-},x^{-}+H],p_{2}\in[y^{-},y^{-}+H]:N-p_{1}-p_{2}\textrm{ prime}\}\leqslant(1-\delta_{\lambda}^{-})\mathfrak{S}(N)\frac{H^{2}}{(\log X)^{3}}. $$

This result can be shown using a combination of Maier’s matrix method and the circle method. Our main theorem, however, can be applied to a broader class of equations that are beyond the reach of the circle method. For instance, we can instead consider primes in four term arithmetic progressions, and show similar irregularities in the distribution of $(x,y)$ such that $x,x+y,x+2y,x+3y$ are all prime.

Next, we introduce the general setting. Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a system of linear forms.

#### Definition 1.

The complexity of a system of forms $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t})$ is the smallest integer $s\geqslant 0$ such that $\{\tilde{\psi_{j}}:[t]\backslash\{i\}\}$ can be partitioned into $s+1$ classes such that $\tilde{\psi_{i}}$ is not contained in the affine linear span of any of the classes, where $\tilde{\psi}$ denotes the homogeneous part of $\psi$ .

We will restrict ourselves to systems of finite complexity, which measures the linear independence of the homogeneous parts of the forms. In [9], Green and Tao show that a system has finite complexity if and only if the $\tilde{\psi_{i}}$ are pairwise pairwise linearly independent. In particular, twin primes and Goldbach’s conjecture both have infinite complexity; as a result, we are not able to say anything about such primes using this technology.

In their seminal work, Green and Tao proved the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for linear patterns with finite complexity. Let us take $\Lambda(n)=\Lambda(|n|)$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus{\left\{0\right\}}$ and $\Lambda(0)=0$ .

#### Theorem 1.3 (Green and Tao, [9]).

Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t})$ be a system of finite complexity. Then the following asymptotic holds:

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in[-X,X]^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}))=(2X)^{d}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}+o_{\Psi}(X^{d}), $$

where

$$ \beta_{p}=p^{-d}\sum_{\textbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\left(\frac{p}{p-1}\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}),p)=1}\right). $$

We note that this asymptotic is not exactly what Cramér’s model predicts, but is properly corrected by the local factors $\beta_{p}$ for the system $\Psi$ . A random model for the primes along the lines of Cramér, correcting for these local factors was found by Granville [7]. In [17], Matomäki, Shao, Tao and Teräväinen, have confirmed that the asymptotic holds in short boxes of length $H\geqslant X^{5/8+\varepsilon}$ :

#### Theorem 1.4 (Matomäki, Shao, Tao, and Teräväinen, [17]).

Let $X^{5/8+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ have finite complexity. Then we have that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in[X,X+H]^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}))=H^{d}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}+o_{\Psi}(H^{d}). $$

We study the limits to equidistribution with the following result.

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $\lambda>1$ , $X$ sufficiently large, and $H=(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Then, there exist $\delta_{\lambda}^{+},\delta_{\lambda}^{-}>0$ such that there exists $\textbf{x}^{\pm}\in[X,2X]^{d}$ such that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in\prod_{i=1}^{d}[x^{+}_{i},x^{+}_{i}+H]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(\textbf{x})\textrm{ is prime}}\geqslant(1+\delta_{\lambda}^{+})\frac{H^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}, $$

and

$$ \sum_{\textbf{x}\in\prod_{i=1}^{d}[x^{-}_{i},x^{-}_{i}+H]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(\textbf{x})\textrm{ is prime}}\leqslant(1-\delta_{\lambda}^{-})\frac{H^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

#### Remark 1.

We note that we expect primes in these patterns to be equidistributed in large enough boxes because it is a linear system. If instead we look at quadratic polynomials, then there are large cone regions where there are no integer solutions. For example, there are no primes of the form $m^{2}+n^{2}$ for $0<m,n\leqslant X$ with $0<\arg(m+ni)<\frac{1}{X}$ , for there are no integral points in the region. However, equidistribution would predict in most sectors of angle $\asymp\frac{1}{X}$ , there are $\asymp\frac{X}{\log X}$ primes.

These irregularities are due to the structure of the lattice points for the quadratic in certain sectors. In our linear case, there are no such obstructions to regularity; the number of lattice points in $\prod_{i}[x_{i},x_{i}+H]$ remains $(1+o(1))H^{d}$ for all $x_{i}$ . Thus, the relative abundance or sparsity of linear patterns of primes is therefore due to the structure of the primes and not immediately due to the fact that they sit inside the integers.

#### Remark 2.

We expect to be able to show the analogue of our result in short arithmetic progressions rather than short intervals à la Friedlander and Granville [5].

#### Remark 3.

For a fixed $\lambda$ and a range $[X,2X]^{d}$ , we note that if worked out, we can get $\delta_{\lambda}^{\pm}$ to grow exponentially with $t$ . In particular, as $t$ grows, we get counts in small boxes that deviate by an arbitrarily large constant factor from the expected count. We are thus able to find deviations that are in a sense more severe than those of Maier.

We end this section with a brief outline of the rest of the paper. In §2, we will set up the main results from which our main theorem follows; in §2.3 we complete the proof of Theorem 1.5 assuming these two results, to whose proofs the rest of the paper will be devoted. In §3, we set up the machinery surrounding nilsequences we shall require in our proof . What remains is then reduced to certain estimates sums of nilsequences along primes in arithmetic progressions with moderately large moduli, which we show in §4; it is here where new ideas are brought in.

## 2. Setup

### 2.1. Notation

In this section, we will specify notation that will be used for the remainder of the paper. We fix a system of form $\Psi=(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ of finite complexity $s$ . We write $[N]=\{1,2,...,N\}.$ Associated to these forms are the local densities $\beta_{p}$ , as defined in Theorem 1.3.

Throughout, $p$ always denotes a prime. Write $P(z)=\prod_{p\leqslant z}p$ . We will use $\mathcal{P}$ to denote the set of prime numbers.

We let $\omega:\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 1}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 1}$ be the Buchstab function, i.e. the unique continuous function such that

$$ \displaystyle\omega(u) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{u},\hskip 7.0pt1\leqslant u\leqslant 2 \displaystyle\frac{d}{du}(u\omega(u)) \displaystyle=\omega(u-1),\hskip 7.0ptu\geqslant 2 $$

Throughout, $\gamma$ shall denote the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

### 2.2. Existence of dutiful moduli

#### Definition 2.

A modulus $Q$ is dutiful if for all $q\leqslant(\log Q)^{\frac{1}{10}}$ , all of the Dirichlet characters $\chi\mod{(qQ)^{{\left\lfloor 20s\log\log Q\right\rfloor}}}$ satisfy that for any $\beta\in[1/2,1]$ such that $L(\beta,\chi)=0$ , the following holds:

$$ \beta\leqslant 1-\frac{1}{(\log Q)^{2}}. $$

#### Remark 4.

We note that the choice of $1/10$ here is somewhat arbitrary. It is chosen for notational simplicity and to simply have fewer variables to keep track of through the proof.

#### Proposition 2.1.

There arbitrarily large $z$ such that $P(z)$ is a dutiful modulus.

#### Proof.

We proceed similarly to the proof of Lemma 1 in [14]. Write

$$ M(z)=(P(z)({\lceil\log^{1/10}P(z)\rceil}!))^{{\left\lfloor 20s\log\log P(z)\right\rfloor}}. $$

We record $\log M(z)=(1+o(1))20sz\log z$ . Take some $z_{1}$ sufficiently large. If $P(z_{1})$ is dutiful, we are done. Otherwise (since $z$ is sufficiently large and $\log M(z)=o(\log^{2}P(z))$ ), there exists some $\tilde{\chi}\mod M(z_{1})$ with $L(\tilde{\beta},\tilde{\chi})=0$ and

$$ 1-\tilde{\beta}\leqslant\frac{c_{1}}{\log M(z_{1})} $$

for some sufficiently small $c_{1}$ . Since $z$ is sufficiently large and $\log M(z)=(1+o(1))20sz\log z$ , there exists $z\geqslant z_{1}$ such that

$$ \frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}<1-\tilde{\beta}\leqslant\frac{c_{1}}{\log M(z)} $$

Therefore, $\tilde{\chi}$ induced $\mod M(z)$ is still an exceptional character to modulus $M(z)$ .

It follows by Theorem 5.28 in [13] (Landau/Page’s theorem) that there are no other exceptional characters $\mod M(z)$ So, for all $\chi\mod M(z)$ , we have that if

$$ 1-\beta\leqslant\frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}, $$

then $L(\beta,\chi)\neq 0.$ The desired result then follows upon noting that for large $z$ ,

$$ \frac{c_{1}/2}{\log M(z)}\geqslant\frac{1}{(\log P(z))^{2}}. $$

∎

### 2.3. Main estimates

To prove Therorem 1.5, we shall rely on the following two propositions, from which we shall prove the Theorem 1.5 in the next subsection.

#### Definition 3.

For a given modulus $Q$ , $\textbf{a}\in(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ is called admissible if

$(\psi_{i}(\textbf{a}),Q)=1$ for all $i\leqslant t$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

Suppose that $Q=P(z)$ is dutiful, and fix $\varepsilon>0$ . Then, for $X\geqslant\exp((\log Q)^{50})$ , admissible $\textbf{a}\in(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
{\bf n\equiv\bf a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(n))=\frac{1}{\#\mathcal{A}}\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}(1+O(z^{-1}))+o{\left(\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\right)}. $$

Here, $\mathcal{A}\subset(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ is the set of admissible tuples $\mod Q$ .

We remark that for almost all $Q\leqslant X^{\frac{1}{3}-\varepsilon}$ , Teräväinen and Shao [21] have shown Proposition 2.2.

We also introduce an estimate for linear patterns of rough numbers. This result follows from general work of Matthiessen [19, Theorem 2.1], though in our specific case of rough numbers, we expect that it should also follow with a little work from results on linear patterns of primes.

#### Proposition 2.3.

Fix $u>1$ , take $z$ large, and let $N=z^{u}$ . Then, we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[N,2N]^{d}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(n),P(z))=1}=(1+o(1))\frac{\#\mathcal{A}}{P(z)^{d}}\left(e^{\gamma}\omega(u)\right)^{t}N^{d}, $$

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of admissible tuples $\mod P(z)$ .

#### Proof.

We note that $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))=1}$ is a multiplicative function. Let us take on the notation of [19]; we note that $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))=1}$ satisfies the all of the conditions to apply Theorem 2.1 except condition (iii). However, this issue is only an obstacle in the proof that the constructed measure is pseudorandom. However, since $\mathbbm{1}_{(.,P(z))}\leqslant\mathbbm{1}_{\text{prime}}$ , we can use the pseudorandom measure defined by Green and Tao in [9] and proceed with the proof of Theorem 2.1 in [19].

Take $\tilde{W}(x)=\prod_{p\leqslant\log\log N}p$ . Then, Theorem 2.1 in [19] gives us that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf n}\in[N,2N]^{d}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(n),P(z))=1}\\
=(1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\sum_{(A_{i},\tilde{W})=1}\frac{\tilde{W}^{t}}{\tilde{W}^{d}\varphi(\tilde{W})^{t}}\sum_{v\in\mathbb{Z}/\tilde{W}\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(v)\equiv A_{i}\mod\tilde{W}} $$

Now let us take $B>0$ large; for $1\leqslant w_{i}\leqslant(\log N)^{B}$ , if both $\mathbbm{1}_{(w_{i},P(z))=1}\neq 0$ and $p\mid w_{i}\implies p\mid\tilde{W}$ , then $w_{i}=1$ . So the sum over $w_{i}$ ’s becomes

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\sum_{(A_{i},\tilde{W})=1}\frac{\tilde{W}^{t}}{\tilde{W}^{d}\varphi(\tilde{W})^{t}}\sum_{v\in\mathbb{Z}/\tilde{W}\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{\psi_{i}(v)\equiv A_{i}\mod\tilde{W}}\\
=(1+o(1))\frac{\omega(u)^{t}}{(\log z)^{t}}\cdot\prod_{p\leqslant\log\log N}\beta_{p}. $$

Now, we can see that

$$ \prod_{p\leqslant\log\log(N)}\beta_{p}=\frac{\#{\mathcal{A}}}{P(z)^{d}}\cdot\frac{P(z)^{t}}{\varphi(P(z))^{t}}\cdot(1+O(z^{-1}+(\log\log N)^{-1}), $$

as both sides can be related to $\prod_{p}\beta_{p}$ . Finally,

$$ \frac{P(z)}{\varphi(P(z))}=\prod_{p\leqslant z}(1-1/p)^{-1}\sim e^{\gamma}(\log z), $$

as desired. ∎

### 2.4. Proof of main theorem

We now prove the main theorem using Maier’s matrix method, assuming Propositions 2.2 and 2.3.

Take $Q=P(z)$ a sufficiently large dutiful modulus, and let

$$ X=Q{\lfloor\exp((\log Q)^{100})/Q\rfloor} $$

so that $Q|X$ . Next, take $U=z^{u}$ , for some $u$ to be determined later. As in the Maier matrix method, we shall estimate the following sum

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\bf n)). $$

in two different ways.

On one hand, we note that the inner sum only contributes if a is admissible. Then, we may estimate the inner sum with Proposition 2.2, and then execute the second sum in the second line with Proposition 2.3. By this, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}\\
\textbf{a}\text{ admissible}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}(Q)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n})) \displaystyle=(1+o(1))\frac{X^{d}}{(\log X)^{t}}\cdot\prod_{p}\beta_{p}\cdot\frac{1}{\#\mathcal{A}}\sum_{\textbf{a}\in[U,2U]^{d}}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(\textbf{a}),Q)=1\forall i} \displaystyle=(1+o(1))\frac{U^{d}X^{d}}{Q^{d}(\log X)^{t}}\cdot(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}\cdot\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

On the other hand, rearranging, we have

$$ \Sigma=\sum_{\mathbf{r}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}}\sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n})), $$

where

$$ R_{\mathbf{r}}=\prod_{j\leqslant d}[Q\mathbf{r}_{j}+U,Q\mathbf{r}_{j}+2U]. $$

Since $\Sigma$ is the average over all $\mathbf{r}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}$ , there must exist $\mathbf{r}^{\pm}\in[(X-U)/Q,2(X-U)/Q]^{d}$ such that

$$ \sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}^{+}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))\geqslant(1+o(1))(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}U^{d}(\log X)^{-t}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}, $$

$$ \sum_{\textbf{n}\in R_{\mathbf{r}^{-}}}\prod_{i\leqslant t}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))\leqslant(1+o(1))(e^{\gamma}\omega(u))^{t}U^{d}(\log X)^{-t}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

The desired result follows from the fact that for any $u$ , there exist $u^{+},u^{-}\geqslant u$ such that $e^{\gamma}\omega(u^{-})<1<e^{\gamma}\omega(u^{+})$ (see Lemma 4 in [15], for example). Finally, let us take $u=101\lambda$ so that $z^{u}\geqslant(\log X)^{\lambda}$ . Let us look at the short boxes of length $U^{+}=z^{u^{+}}$ (resp. $U^{-}=z^{u^{-}}$ ); applying the pigeonhole within the box, we can see that there is a box of length $(\log X)^{\lambda}$ with an exceptionally large (resp. small) number of primes.

#### Remark 5.

We remark that it is not necessary to take $Q=P(z)$ in these arguments; more generally we could take $Q=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{S}}p$ for $\mathcal{S}$ a subset of the primes that grows with $z$ .

## 3. The Green-Tao Machinery

Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be an arithmetic function, and let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t}):\mathbb{Z}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{t}$ be a system of linear forms with complexity $s$ . Assume that

$$ \mathbb{E}f(n)=\delta+o(1) $$

for some constant $\delta>0$ . Consider the following sum:

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{R}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}f(\psi_{i}(\mathbf{r})). $$

The method of Green and Tao in [9] allows us to find asymptotics for the above sum, assuming “nice” properties of $f$ . We later will take $f$ so that we may count either primes or rough numbers. In either scenario, we must assume that $f$ is bounded by a “constant-like” function — a pseudorandom measure.

#### Definition 4.

A $k$ -pseudorandom measure $\nu:[N]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a function that satisfies:

- • $\nu$ is a measure:

$$ \mathbb{E}\nu(n)=1+o(1). $$

- • $\nu$ satisfies the linear forms condition: Let $m\leqslant k2^{k-1}$ and $t\leqslant 3k-4$ . Let $(L_{ij})_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m,1\leqslant j\leqslant t}$ be a matrix of rational numbers of height $\ll k$ where no row is zero or a rational multiple of another. Let $\psi_{i}:(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{t}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ be linear forms given by $\psi_{i}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}L_{ij}x_{j}+b_{i}$ . Then if we consider the natural extension of $\nu$ to $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ , we have that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{t}}(\nu(\psi_{1}(x))\ldots\nu(\psi_{m}(x)))=1+o(1). $$

#### Remark 6.

We would like to note that originally Green and Tao included a correlation condition, but this can be dropped due to the work of Conlon, Fox, and Zhao [3], and Dodos and Kanellopoulos [4].

For such $f$ bounded by pseudorandom measures, we can relate (3) to the Gowers norm of $f$ . In particular, after a technical reduction of rewriting $\Psi$ in $s-$ normal form (which is always possible as described in section 4 of [9]) we can apply the generalized von Neumann theorem:

#### Theorem 3.1 (Green and Tao, Proposition 7.1 [9]).

Let $\nu$ be a $k(s)$ -pseudorandom measure and $f_{1},\ldots,f_{t}:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ are functions $|f_{i}(x)|\leqslant\nu(x)$ . If $\Psi$ is a system in $s$ -normal form. If

$$ \min\|f_{j}\|_{U^{s+1}[N]}\leqslant\delta, $$

then we have that for some $c>0$ ,

$$ \sum_{n\in[N,2N]^{d}}\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))\ll_{\Psi,k(s)}\kappa(\delta)N^{d}+o(N^{d}), $$

where $\kappa(\delta)$ is a function that approaches $0$ as $\delta\rightarrow 0.$

#### Proof sketch.

We proceed as in the proof of Proposition 7.1 in [9]; first we take $\varepsilon=\delta^{c}$ in Corollary A.3 (for $c$ yet to be determined) and transfer the problem to $\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}$ , for $N^{\prime}$ a sufficiently large constant multiple of $N$ . In particular, for $F$ a Lipschitz function of Lipschitz constant $O(\delta^{-c})$ and bounded by $1$ , we want to show that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}F(n)\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))=O(\kappa(\delta)). $$

Next, we expand $F$ under a Fourier expansion: for any $X>1,J=X^{d}$ a Fourier expansion

$$ F(n)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}e(m_{j}n/N^{\prime})+O(\delta^{-c}(\log X)/X) $$

for some coefficients $c_{j}\ll 1$ . We get that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{n\in(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}} \displaystyle F(n)\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n)) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}\mathbb{E}_{n\in(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}e(m_{j}n/N^{\prime})\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))+O_{k(s)}\left(\frac{\delta^{-c}(\log X)}{X}\right). $$

Here we have applied the linear forms condition for $\nu$ to bound the error term from the Fourier expansion. Let us take $X$ growing slowly in $1/\delta$ .

It is observed by Green and Tao, that the individual exponential sum correlation bounds will be implied by showing

$$ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))=O(X^{-d}\kappa(\delta)). $$

This then reduces us to Proposition 7.1” in Appendix A of [9], which states that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})^{d}}\prod_{i\in[t]}f_{i}(\psi_{i}(n))\leqslant\|f_{i}\|_{U^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}/N^{\prime}\mathbb{Z})}+o(1). $$

Now applying our assumption and setting $X=(1/\delta)^{1/2d}$ , $c=1/4d,$ and taking $\kappa(\delta)=\delta^{1/6d}$ , we obtain the above bound. ∎

#### Remark 7.

We note that we will eventually take $\delta(N)$ as function satisfying that $\delta(N)\rightarrow 0$ and $N\rightarrow\infty,$ so this upper bound will become $o(N^{d}).$

In order to achieve our desired estimate on primes or rough numbers, we will want to use the following quantitative inverse theorem for the Gowers norm; a statement of this form was first achieved by Manners [16], but we will use the version obtained by Tao and Teräiväinen in [22]

#### Theorem 3.2 ([22], Theorem 8.3).

Let $\nu$ be a pseudorandom measure such that

$$ \|\nu-1\|_{U^{2k}[N]}\leqslant\delta^{C_{0}} $$

for some constant $C_{0}$ sufficiently large in $k$ . Let $f$ be a $\nu$ -bounded function such that

$$ \|f\|_{U^{k}[N]}\geqslant\delta. $$

Then there exists a $(k-1)$ -step nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ of dimension $O(\delta^{-O(1)})$ and complexity at most $\exp\exp O(\delta^{-O(1)})$ , a Lipschitz function $F:G/\Gamma\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ of complexity at most $\exp\exp O(\delta^{-O(1)})$ , and a polynomial map $g:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\gg\exp(-\exp(O(\delta^{-O(1)})). $$

Thus, it will remain to bound sums of the form $\mathbb{E}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)$ . Our approach is motivated by the splitting of sums into “major” and “minor” arcs in the circle method; for 1-step nilsequences, this is the same process. We take $G/\Gamma$ to be $s$ -step nilmanifold with Mal’cev basis ${\mathcal{X}}$ . Before introducing the factor theorem, let us first let us recall some definitions:

#### Definition 5.

$\gamma\in G$ is $Q$ -rational if $\gamma^{r}\in\Gamma$ for some $0\leqslant r\leqslant Q$ .

#### Definition 6.

$f(n):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ is a (M,N)-smooth if $d(f(n),\text{id}_{G})\leqslant M$ and

$d(f(n),f(n-1))\leqslant M/N$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Here we are using the metric induced on $G$ by ${\mathcal{X}}$ .

#### Definition 7.

We say that a sequence $(g(n)\Gamma)$ is totally- $\delta$ -equidistributed if

$$ \bigg|\mathbb{E}_{P}F(g(n)\Gamma)-\int_{G/\Gamma}F\bigg|\leqslant\delta\|F\|_{\text{Lip}}, $$

for all Lipschitz functions $F:G/\Gamma\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ and $P\subset[N]$ an arithmetic progression of length at least $\delta N.$

#### Theorem 3.3 ([11, Theorem 1.19]).

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a $m$ -dimensional manifold with a $s$ -step filtration and $N\geqslant 0$ , $0\leqslant\delta\leqslant 1/2$ . Let ${\mathcal{X}}$ be a $\delta_{0}$ -rational Mal’cev basis adapted to the filtration and $g\in\mathrm{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G)$ of degree $d$ . Then there exists a number $\delta_{0}\geqslant\delta\geqslant\delta_{0}^{O(1)}$ , a rational subgroup $G^{\prime}\subset G$ with Mal’cev basis ${\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}$ for $G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime}$ , which are $M$ -rational combinations of the basis elements of ${\mathcal{X}}$ , and a decomposition

$$ g(n)=\xi(n)g^{\prime}(n)\gamma(n) $$

such that $\xi,g^{\prime},\gamma$ are polynomial sequences and Let $G/\Gamma$ be a $m$ -dimensional manifold with a $s$ -step filtration and $N\geqslant 0$ , $0\leqslant\delta\leqslant 1/2$ . Let ${\mathcal{X}}$ be a $\delta_{0}$ -rational Mal’cev basis adapted to the filtration and $g\in\mathrm{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G)$ of degree $d$ . Then there exists a number $\delta_{0}\geqslant\delta\geqslant\delta_{0}^{O(1)}$ , a rational subgroup $G^{\prime}\subset G$ with Mal’cev basis ${\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}$ for $G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime}$ , which are $M$ -rational combinations of the basis elements of ${\mathcal{X}}$ , and a decomposition

$$ g(n)=\xi(n)g^{\prime}(n)\gamma(n) $$

such that $\xi,g^{\prime},\gamma$ are polynomial sequences and

- • $\xi(n):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ is $(\delta^{-1},N)$ -smooth,

- • $g^{\prime}(n):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G^{\prime}$ is totally- $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed in $G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime}$ using the metric induced by ${\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}$ ,

- • $\gamma(n):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ is $\delta^{-1}$ -rational and $(\gamma(n)\Gamma)$ is periodic with period at most $\delta^{-1}$ .

Using this factor theorem in [10], Green and Tao showed that the Mobius function is orthogonal to nilsequences; in particular any nilsequence with nontrivial equidistributed part belongs to the “minor arc” and the periodic parts can be bounded using Siegel’s theorem due to the size of the period being small. In our application of Proposition 2.2, however, we need to modify the factor theorem slightly to deal with “major arcs” with larger moduli. We remark that a similar theorem is proved by Matthiesen in [18] (Theoren 6.4).

### 3.1. A $Q$ -factor theorem

#### Theorem 3.4.

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a $m$ -dimensional manifold with a $s$ -step filtration, $N,Q\geqslant 0$ , $0\leqslant\delta_{0}\leqslant 1/2$ , and $0\leqslant a<Q<N^{1/2}$ . Let ${\mathcal{X}}$ be a $\delta_{0}^{-1}$ -rational Mal’cev basis adapted to the filtration and $g\in\text{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G)$ of degree $d$ . Then there exists a number $\delta_{0}\geqslant\delta\geqslant\delta_{0}^{O(1)}$ , a rational subgroup $G^{\prime}\subset G$ with Mal’cev basis ${\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}$ for $G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime}$ , which are $M$ -rational combinations of the basis elements of ${\mathcal{X}}$ , and a decomposition

$$ g(n)=\xi(n)g^{\prime}(n)\gamma(n) $$

such that $\xi,g^{\prime},\gamma$ are polynomial sequences and

- • $\xi(n):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ is $(\delta^{-1},N)$ -smooth,

- • $g^{\prime}(Qn+a):\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G^{\prime}$ is totally- $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed in $G^{\prime}/\Gamma^{\prime}$ using the metric induced by ${\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}$ ,

- • $\gamma:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow G$ satisfies that $\gamma(Qn+a)$ is $\delta^{-1}$ -rational, $(\gamma(n)\Gamma)$ is periodic with period $(Qq)^{d}$ with $q$ at most $\delta^{-1}$ , and $(\gamma(Qn+a)\Gamma)$ is periodic with period at most $\delta^{-O(1)}$ .

We achieve the above theorem using morally the same proof as that of Theorem 3.3 in [11], only with an extra dependency on an exterior $Q$ . In particular, we start with the quantitative Leibman theorem from [11].

#### Theorem 3.5 ([11, Theorem 1.16]).

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a $m$ -dimensional manifold with a $s$ -step filtration. Let $N\geqslant 1$ and $0\leqslant\delta\leqslant 1/2$ . If ${\mathcal{X}}$ is a $\delta^{-1}$ -rational Mal’cev basis adapted to the filtration and $g\in\mathrm{poly}(\mathbb{Z},G)$ , then at least one of the following is true:

- • $(g(n)\Gamma)$ is $\delta$ -equidistributed in $G/\Gamma$ ,

- • There is a nontrivial horizontal character $\eta:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ such that $|\eta|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and $\|\eta\circ g(n)\|_{C^{\infty}[N]}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Assume $g(Qn+a)$ is not totally- $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed on $G/\Gamma$ . Then by Theorem 3.5 there is some $q^{\prime}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and $|\eta|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ such that

$$ \|\eta\circ g(Qq^{\prime}n+a)\|_{C^{\infty}[N]}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}. $$

Let $\psi:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ be our map to Mal’cev coordinates (recall that the dimension of $G$ is $m$ ), then we know that $\eta\circ g(n)=k\cdot\psi(g(n))$ for some vector $k\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $|k|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ . Since $g(n)$ is a polynomial map, we have that

$$ \psi(g(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}t_{j}\binom{n}{j}, $$

for some $t_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . Restricting to an arithmetic progression mod $Q$ , we have that

$$ \eta\circ g(Qq^{\prime}n+a)=k\cdot\psi(g(Qq^{\prime}n+a))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}(k\cdot t_{j})\binom{Qq^{\prime}n+a}{j}. $$

We wish to rewrite the above as

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}\binom{n}{j}, $$

so that we can apply information from the $C^{\infty}[N]$ norm of $\eta\circ g(n)$ . We note that the $C^{\infty}[N]$ is independent of the shift by $a$ , so we can take $a=0$ . We know that $\alpha_{d}=(Qq^{\prime})^{d}(k\cdot t_{d})/d!$ , so we have that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{d}(k\cdot t_{d})/d!\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{d}}{N^{d}}. $$

We note that

$$ \alpha_{d-1}=(k\cdot t_{d})(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}\cdot\frac{d(d-1)}{2d!}(1-Qq^{\prime})+(k\cdot t_{d-1})(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}\cdot\frac{1}{(d-1)!}. $$

However, since $Q\delta^{-O(1)}/N\ll N^{-1/3}$ we can see the contribution from the terms with $(k\cdot t_{d})$ will be inconsequential to $\|\alpha_{d-1}\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}$ and that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{d-1}(k\cdot t_{d-1})\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll_{d}\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{d-1}}{N^{d-1}}. $$

Similarly, we achieve that

$$ \|(Qq^{\prime})^{j}(k\cdot t_{j})\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll_{d}\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}Q^{j}}{N^{j}}, $$

for each $j=1,...,d.$

So, let us pick $u_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that $Q^{j}(k\cdot u_{j})\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|t_{j}-u_{j}|\ll\frac{\delta^{-O(1)}}{N^{j}}$ . We define $\xi(n)$ as the sequence such that

$$ \psi(\xi(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\binom{n}{j}(t_{j}-u_{j}). $$

Next, we pick the vectors $v_{j}$ with denominators of the form $(Qq)^{j}$ with $q\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ and such that $k\cdot u_{j}=k\cdot v_{j}$ . We define $\gamma(n)$ as the sequence such that

$$ \psi(\gamma(n))=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\binom{n}{j}v_{j}. $$

So, we take $g_{1}(n)=\xi^{-1}g\gamma^{-1}(n).$ It is clear via the arguments of [11] that $\xi(n)$ is $(\delta^{-O(1)},N)$ -smooth and $\gamma$ has the correct periodicity properties. So, it remains to construct $g^{\prime}$ totally $\delta^{-O(1)}$ -equidistributed. However, $g_{1}$ is not necessary such; if $g_{1}$ is not totally equidistributed then we can repeat the argument above iteratively, forming $\xi_{1}$ and $\gamma_{1}$ . We note that $\xi(n)\xi_{1}(n)$ will still be $(\delta^{-O(1)},N)$ smooth and $\gamma_{1}(n)\gamma(n)$ periodic. Thus, we repeat the procedure until we have $g^{\prime}(Qn+a)$ totally $\delta^{-O(1)}$ -equidistributed. ∎

## 4. Linear patterns in smooth arithmetic progressions

In this section, we will prove Proposition 2.2. We recall our goal is to show that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}\mod Q\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))=(1+o(1))\frac{1}{\#{\mathcal{A}}}X^{d}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}, $$

where $Q$ is a dutiful modulus, $\textbf{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}\subset(\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ an admissible tuple, and $\beta_{p}$ the local factors associated to $\Psi$ . In particular, we wish to upper bound

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}\mod Q\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))-\frac{Q^{d}}{\#{\mathcal{A}}}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}. $$

We note that since $Q=P(z)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\#{\mathcal{A}}=\#\{\textbf{a}\mod Q:(\psi_{i}(\textbf{a}),Q)=1\forall i\} \displaystyle=\prod_{p\leqslant z}\sum_{\textbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}_{(\psi_{i}(\textbf{x}),p)=1} \displaystyle=Q^{d}{\left(\frac{\varphi(Q}{Q}\right)}^{t}\prod_{p\leqslant z}\beta_{p}. $$

So, it remains to upper bound

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textbf{n}\in[X,2X]^{d}\\
\textbf{n}\equiv\textbf{a}\mod Q\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\left(\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\textbf{n}))-\frac{Q}{\varphi(Q)}\right). $$

Now, we apply the Green-Tao method described in the previous sections; we note that for our choice of $X$ in (1), we can see that $Q=P(z)$ for $z\leqslant(\log X)^{1/50}.$ So, we can use Proposition 8.4 from [22], taking $\varepsilon=1/50$ , to construct a pseudorandom measure on $\Lambda(Qn+b)$ satisfying the desired conditions. We see that this reduces to showing that for $(b,Q)=1$ ,

$$ \bigg|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\\
n\equiv b\mod Q\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-Q/\varphi(Q))F(g(n)\Gamma)\bigg|=o(N/Q) $$

for $F(g(n)\Gamma)$ a $s$ -step nilsequence. We apply Theorem 3.4 and write $g(n)=\xi(n)g^{\prime}(n)\gamma(n)$ . First, we will follow Green and Tao in [10] for when $g^{\prime}$ is nontrivial, i.e. our “minor arc” case.

### 4.1. Totally equidistributed case

Let us assume that $g^{\prime}$ is nontrivial, in which case we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\\
n\equiv b\mod Q\end{subarray}}F(g(n)\Gamma)=o(N/Q) $$

by definition of $g^{\prime}$ being totally equidistributed. Next, let $r=\delta^{-O(1)}$ be the periodicity of $\gamma(Qn+b)\Gamma$ . We can then bound the remaining sum by

$$ \sum_{c\mod r}^{*}\bigg|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\\
n\equiv b\mod Q\\
n\equiv c\mod r\end{subarray}}\Lambda(n)F(\xi(n)g^{\prime}(n)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)\bigg|, $$

where the sum over $c$ is restricted to those moduli that can also be $b\mod Q$ . Additionally, we restrict to progressions of $P$ of difference $r$ and length $\delta^{O(1)}N$ so that $\xi(n)$ will be near constant on $P$ . Then we can see that it suffices to show that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in P\\
n\equiv b\mod Q\\
n\equiv c\mod r\end{subarray}}\Lambda(n)F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(n)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)=o\left(\frac{|P|}{\textrm{lcm}(r,Q)}\right). $$

We now apply Vaughan’s decomposition of $\Lambda$ to reduce the problem to Type I and Type II sums. In particular, if the above sum is $\gg\varepsilon|P|/Qr$ , then at least one of the following is true:

- • For $\gg\delta^{O(1)}K$ integers in $[K,2K]$ with $K\leqslant N^{2/3}$ , (5)

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in P/k\\ kn\equiv b\mod Q\\ kn\equiv c\mod r\end{subarray}}F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(kn)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)\gg\varepsilon\frac{\delta^{O(1)}|P|}{K\textrm{lcm}(r,Q)}, $$

- • There is a $K,W$ such that $N^{1/3}\ll K\ll N^{2/3}$ and $N\ll KW\ll N$ such that for $\gg\delta^{O(1)}K^{2}$ pairs $(k,k^{\prime})\in[K,2K]^{2}$ , such that (6)

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in P/K\\ kw,k^{\prime}w\equiv b\mod Q\\ kw,k^{\prime}w\equiv c\mod r\end{subarray}}F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(kw)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)\overline{F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(k^{\prime}w)\gamma_{c}\Gamma}\gg\varepsilon\delta^{O(1)}\frac{|P|}{K\textrm{lcm}(r,Q)}. $$

Let us first consider the Type I case, although the arguments for both will be similar. Then we find that after pigeonholing to a specific residue of $k\equiv\tilde{k}\mod Qr$ , for $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-1}K$ integers in $[K,2K]$ ,

$$ \sum_{n\in P/k}F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(k(Qrn+b)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)\gg\varepsilon\delta^{O(1)}|P|/KQr. $$

Let us write $g_{k}(n)=g(kn)$ and $g_{k,b}(n)=g(k(n+b))$ ; this will still be a polynomial sequence. The lower bound (5) implies that $g_{k,b}(n)$ is not equidistributed on progressions of length $\delta^{O(1)}Q$ , in particular, by the argument in [10, §3], there is a character $\eta_{k}:G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $|\eta_{k}|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}$ with

$$ \|\eta_{k}\circ g_{k}(Qrn)\|_{C^{\infty}[N/k]}\ll\delta^{O(1)}. $$

Now, we pigeonhole again to fix a character $\eta$ . If

$$ \eta\circ g^{\prime}(n)=\alpha_{d}n^{d}+...+\alpha_{0}, $$

then we know that

$$ \eta\circ g_{k}(Qrn)=(Qr)^{d}\alpha_{d}n^{d}+...+\alpha_{0}. $$

Thus, we have that for $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-1}K$ integers $k\equiv\tilde{k}\mod Qr$ , we have that

$$ \|q_{j}Q^{j}r^{j}\alpha_{j}k^{j}\|\ll\left(\frac{\delta^{O(1)}K}{N}\right)^{j}. $$

By Lemma 3.3 of [10], which uses that for $t=4^{j}$ , most admissible integers can be represented as the sum of $t$ $j$ th powers, this implies that there are $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-1}K^{j}$ such integers $m$ in $[K^{j}/Q]$ such that for $k_{j}\equiv t\tilde{k}^{j}\mod Qr$ , $m$ will satisfy that

$$ \|q_{j}Q^{j}r^{j}(Qm+t\tilde{k}^{j})\alpha_{j}\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll\delta^{O(1)}(K/N)^{j}, $$

for some $q_{j}\ll\delta^{O(1)}$ . Then by Lemma 3.4 in [10], we have that there exists a $q_{j}^{\prime}\ll\delta^{O(1)}$ such that

$$ {\lVert q_{j}q_{j}^{\prime}Q^{j+1}\alpha_{j}\rVert}_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll\delta^{O(1)}Q/N^{j}. $$

Now, if $\alpha_{j}=\frac{a_{j}}{q_{j}q_{j}^{\prime}Q^{j+1}}+\beta_{j}$ , with $\beta_{j}\leqslant\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-j}N^{-j}$ , then we return to the earlier inequality (7) and see that this implies

$$ {\left\lVert\frac{ma_{j}}{q_{j}^{\prime}}+\frac{t\tilde{k}^{j}a_{j}}{q_{j}^{\prime}Q}+O(\delta^{O(1)}(K/N)^{j})\right\rVert}_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ll\delta^{O(1)}(K/N)^{j}. $$

Since $(b,Q)=1$ , we can see that the $\tilde{k}$ chosen above by the pigeonhole principle will satisfy that $\tilde{k}^{j}\neq 0\mod Q$ . So, since $Q\leqslant N^{1/3}\leqslant N/K$ , we have that $a_{j}$ must be divisible by one value of $Q$ . Thus, we have that for (5) to hold, we must have

$$ \alpha_{j}=\frac{a_{j}^{\prime}}{q_{j}q_{j}^{\prime}Q^{j}}+O(\delta^{O(1)}(QN)^{-j}), $$

for each $j$ . Now, we recall that $g^{\prime}(n)$ was defined such that $g^{\prime}(Qn+a)$ is totally- $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed. We see that the above relation contradicts this assumption, and hence if $g^{\prime}$ is nontrivial, (5) can not occur.

Next, we treat the Type II case, which follows a similar argument. Under the assumption of (6), we get that after pigeonholing in residues of $k,k^{\prime}$ mod $Qr$ , for $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-2}K^{2}$ pairs $(k,k^{\prime})\in[K,2K]^{2}$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{n\in P/K}F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(k(Qrn+b)\gamma_{c}\Gamma)F(\xi_{P}g^{\prime}(k^{\prime}(Qrn+b))\gamma_{c}\Gamma)\gg\varepsilon\delta^{O(1)}\frac{|P|}{KQ}. $$

Next, we write $g_{k}(n)=g(kn)$ and $g_{k,k^{\prime},b}(n)=(g_{k}(n+b),g_{k^{\prime}}(n+b))$ , which will be a polynomial sequence on $G/\Gamma\times G/\Gamma.$ Again, we have that this will not be $\delta^{O(1)}$ -equidistributed on progressions of length $\delta^{O(1)}$ , so we get a character $\eta_{k,k^{\prime}}:G\times G\rightarrow\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with

$$ \|\eta_{k,k^{\prime}}\circ g_{k,k^{\prime},b}(Qn)\|_{C^{\infty}[N/K]}\ll\delta^{O(1)}. $$

As a result, we have that

$$ \|q_{j}Q^{j}(k^{j}+k^{\prime j})\alpha_{j}\|\ll\delta^{O(1)}(K/N)^{j}, $$

for $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-2}K^{2}$ pairs $(k,k^{\prime})$ with $k,k^{\prime}$ having fixed residues mod $Qr$ . We can pigeonhole and find a $k^{\prime}$ such that it occurs in $\gg\delta^{O(1)}Q^{-1}K$ pairs $(k,k^{\prime})$ . This reduces us to equation (7) and the rest of the proof follows as above. Hence, if $g^{\prime}$ is nontrivial, we have that (4) holds. This completes the “minor arc” case.

### 4.2. Periodic case

We can see that for the proof of Proposition 2.2, it remains to show that (4) holds for the case when $g^{\prime}=1$ , i.e. the “major arcs”. By partial summation (to remove the smooth part $\xi(n)$ from the decomposition in Theorem 3.4), we are reduced to showing the following.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Suppose that $Q=P(z)$ is a dutiful modulus, $X$ as in (1), $N\gg X^{1/10}$ and $M\gg\frac{N}{(\log N)^{O(1)}}$ . Then, for any $q\ll(\log X)^{O(1)}$ , $G/\Gamma$ a $s$ -step nilmanifold, and any $(qQ)^{d}$ -periodic polynomial sequence $\gamma:\mathbb{Z}\to G$ , we have that for some absolute $\delta>0$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+M\\
n\equiv a(Q)\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-Q/\varphi(Q))F(\gamma(n)\Gamma)\ll\frac{N}{\varphi(Q)}(\log Q)^{-\delta}. $$

We prove this at the end of the section, after preparing some technical results that shall be necessary in the proof.

#### Lemma 4.2.

We have that for any Dirichlet character $\chi\mod q$ of conductor $q_{1}$ not divisible by the square of an odd prime, and any $q$ -periodic $s$ -step nilsequence $n\mapsto F(\gamma(n)\Gamma)$ , and any $\varepsilon>0,$

$$ \sum_{x(q)}\chi(x)F(\gamma(x)\Gamma)\ll q^{1+\varepsilon}q_{1}^{-c2^{-s}}. $$

for some absolute $c>0$ .

#### Proof.

By the forward direction of the inverse theorem for the Gowers norm 11 1 See, for example, the proof of Proposition 1.4 in Appendix G of [12] for $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ ; one can check that the loss is only polynomial during the differencing., for any $\eta_{s}>0$ , if we know:

$$ \bigg|\sum_{x(q)}\chi(x)F(\gamma(x)\Gamma)\bigg|\geqslant q^{1+\varepsilon}q_{1}^{-\eta_{s}}, $$

we have that

$$ {\left\lVert\chi\right\rVert}_{U^{s}[q]}\gg q^{\varepsilon}q_{1}^{-O(\eta_{s})}. $$

This is false, however, for sufficiently small $\eta_{s}$ , since the following bound holds (which then can be inputted into the definition of the Gowers norm):

$$ \frac{1}{q}\sum_{x(q)}\chi(x+h_{1})\dots\chi(x+h_{s})\overline{\chi}(x+h_{s+1})\dots\overline{\chi}(x+h_{2s})\\
\ll q_{1}^{-1/2+o(1)}q^{o(1)}+\mathbbm{1}_{{\left\{h_{1},\dots,h_{s}\right\}}\equiv{\left\{h_{s+1},\dots,h_{2s}\right\}}(q_{1})} $$

(see, for example, [2, §B]). Here, we write $\mathbbm{1}_{{\left\{h_{1},\dots,h_{\ell}\right\}}\equiv{\left\{h_{\ell+1},\dots,h_{2\ell}\right\}}(q_{1})}$ to be the indicator function that the multisets $H_{1}={\left\{h_{1}\mod{q_{1}},\dots,h_{\ell}\mod{q_{1}}\right\}}$ , $H_{2}={\left\{h_{\ell+1}\mod{q_{1}},\dots,h_{2\ell}\mod{q_{1}}\right\}}$ are the same. Thus, we derive that

$$ {\left\lVert\chi\right\rVert}_{U^{s}[q]}\ll q_{1}^{-2^{-s}}. $$

∎

We shall also require the following consequence of log-free zero density estimates.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $1/2>\eta>0$ and fix a $q>0$ . Suppose that $\mathcal{S}\subset{\left\{\chi\pmod{q}\right\}}$ is a set of nonprincipal characters such that all $\chi\in\mathcal{S}$ , $L(s,\chi)$ has the following zero-free region:

$$ L(\sigma+it,\chi)\neq 0,\mathrm{for}|t|\leqslant q^{10},\sigma\geqslant 1-\eta. $$

Then, for $N$ sufficiently large, $M\gg N(\log N)^{-O(1)}$ , and $\frac{\log q}{\log M}$ sufficiently small, we have

$$ \sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}}\bigg|\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}((\Lambda(n)-q/\varphi(q))\chi(n)\bigg|\ll M^{1-\eta}. $$

#### Remark 8.

We have taken $X=Q\lfloor{\exp((\log Q)^{100})/Q}\rfloor$ , so by the definition of dutiful moduli, we have that for all $q\leqslant(\log X)^{1/10}$ , and any Dirichlet character $\chi\mod{(qQ)^{{\left\lfloor 20s\log\log X\right\rfloor}}}$ , we have that $L(\beta,\chi)\neq 0$ for

$$ \beta\in\bigg[1-\frac{1}{(\log X)^{2}},1\bigg]. $$

So, we will take $\eta=(\log X)^{-2}$ in the application of the above lemma.

#### Proof.

First, we note that the contribution of the principal character can be handled by the prime number theorem, so we assume $\chi$ is nonprincipal. For such $\chi$ , we have that

$$ \frac{q}{\varphi(q)}\bigg|\sum_{n\leqslant N}\chi(n)\bigg|\leqslant q\ll M^{1-\eta}. $$

Thus it remains to bound

$$ \sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}}\bigg|\sum_{N\leqslant n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)\bigg|. $$

For $T=q^{10}$ , by Perron’s formula (see Proposition 5.25 of [13]), we have

$$ \sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)=\sum_{\rho_{\chi}}\frac{(N+M)^{\rho_{\chi}}-N^{\rho_{\chi}}}{\rho_{\chi}}+O\bigg(\frac{N}{T}(\log Nq)^{2}\bigg), $$

where $\rho_{\chi}=\sigma_{\chi}+i\gamma_{\chi}$ runs over nontrivial zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ with $|\gamma_{\chi}|\leqslant T$ . We have

$$ \bigg|\frac{(N+M)^{\rho_{\chi}}-N^{\rho_{\chi}}}{\rho_{\chi}}\bigg|\ll(1+|\gamma_{\chi}|)MN^{\sigma_{\chi}-1}, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\bigg|\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)\bigg| \displaystyle\ll Mq^{10}\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\rho_{\chi}}N^{\sigma_{\chi}-1} \displaystyle=Mq^{10}\bigg(2N^{-\frac{1}{2}}N(1/2,T)+2\log N\int_{1/2}^{1-\eta}N^{\sigma-1}N(\sigma,T)d\sigma\bigg), $$

where

$$ N(\sigma^{\prime},T)=\#\{\sigma+it:L(\sigma+it,\chi)=0,|t|\leqslant T,\sigma\geqslant\sigma^{\prime}\}. $$

The desired result then follows upon using the log-free zero density estimate

$$ N(\sigma,T)\ll(qT)^{c(1-\sigma)}, $$

where this bound accounts for a possible Siegel zero (as our zero-free region assumed will not in general rule out Siegel zeros). ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

First, let us recall that $Q=P(z)$ and write

$$ r=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p>z\\
p^{\ell}||q^{d}\end{subarray}}p^{\ell},\text{ and }R=\frac{(qQ)^{d}}{r}. $$

$$ \frac{Q}{\varphi(Q)}=\frac{R}{\varphi(R)}\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{q}}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{p}\bigg)^{-1} $$

Since $z\gg\log Q$ , $\#\mathcal{P}_{q}\ll 1$ , we have that

$$ \prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{q}}\bigg(1-\frac{1}{p}\bigg)^{-1}=1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}. $$

By a similar analysis, we obtain that

$$ \frac{Q}{\varphi(Q)}=\frac{R}{\varphi(R)}\bigg(1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}\bigg)=\frac{rR}{\varphi(rR)}\bigg(1+O{\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}\bigg). $$

Therefore, after splitting into residue classes modulo $R$ , it suffices to show that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+M\\
n\equiv b(R)\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))F(\gamma(n)\Gamma)\ll\frac{M}{\varphi(R)}(\log Q)^{-\delta} $$

for some $\delta>0$ . By orthogonality and the fact that $(r,R)=1$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle E \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+M\\
n\equiv b(R)\end{subarray}}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))F(\gamma(n)\Gamma) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\varphi(R)}\sum_{\chi_{1}(R)}\overline{\chi_{1}}(b)\frac{1}{\varphi(r)}\sum_{\chi_{2}(r)}\overline{\chi_{2}}(R)A(\chi_{2})\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))\chi_{1}\chi_{2}(n), $$

where we define

$$ A(\chi_{2})=\sum_{x(r)}\overline{\chi_{2}}(x)F(\gamma(Rx+b)\Gamma). $$

Let $C=\log^{\frac{1}{10}}Q$ . Applying Lemma 4.2, for some $\delta>0$ . the contribution of those $\chi_{2}$ with conductor at least $C$ and not divisible by an odd prime square is

$$ \ll\frac{1}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}|A(\chi_{2})|\bigg|\sum_{N\leqslant n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-R/\varphi(R))\chi_{1}\chi_{2}(n)\bigg|\ll\frac{M}{\varphi(R)}\frac{r}{\varphi(r)}C^{-\delta}. $$

$$ E\ll\frac{1}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal{S}_{\text{ld}}}\bigg|\sum_{N<n\leqslant N+M}(\Lambda(n)-rR/\varphi(rR))\chi(n)\bigg|+\frac{Mr}{\varphi(R)\varphi(r)}C^{-\delta}. $$

# On Manin’s Conjecture for Châtelet surfaces

**Authors:** Katharine Woo Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 Email address: katywoo@gmail.com

## Abstract

We resolve Manin’s conjecture for all Châtelet surfaces over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction

- 2 Outline

- 3 Background and notation

- 4 Upper bounds

- 5 Initial reductions

- 6 The cuspidal contribution – the finite image case

- 7 The cuspidal contribution – the Grössen case

- 8 The Eisenstein contribution

- 9 Level of distribution

- 10 Large moduli and Hooley’s $\Delta$ -function

- 11 The asymptotics

- 12 Analysis of the leading constant

- A A special case of the leading constant

- References

## 1. Introduction

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ , and let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Q}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree $3$ or $4$ . A Châtelet surface $X_{\Delta,f}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is defined as a proper smooth model of the affine surface:

$$ x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=f(z). $$

The purpose of this paper is to prove Manin’s conjecture for all Châtelet surfaces, including when $\Delta<0.$

Châtelet surfaces were first studied by Châtelet in [6, 7], who was interested in parameterizing their rational points over number fields (see [15]). Later, these surfaces were the first examples of surfaces that are not homogeneous spaces for which the Hasse principle, weak approximation, and other interesting problems about rational points were resolved. For certain pairs $(\Delta,f(z))$ , $X_{\Delta,f}$ may fail the Hasse principle due to a Brauer-Manin obstruction. In [10, 11], Colliot-Thélène, Sansuc, and Swinnerton-Dyer show that the Brauer-Manin obstruction is the only possible cause of why such a surface may fail the Hasse principle; these results hold not only over $\mathbb{Q}$ , but over any number field.

We first present Manin’s conjecture, as applied to Châtelet surfaces. There exists a map $\psi:X_{\Delta,f}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{4}$ , whose image is a singular del Pezzo surface of degree four (as described by Browning in [4]). This map then induces a height function on $X_{\Delta,f}$ by pulling back the natural height $H$ on $\mathbb{P}^{4}$ via $\psi.$ We define the point-counting function:

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\#\{x\in X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q}):H(x)\leq B\}. $$

Manin’s conjecture, originally written as [1, Conjecture C’] by Batyrev and Manin and stated over $\mathbb{Q}$ explicitly by Browning as [5, Conjecture 2.3], predicts the behavior of $\tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ as $B\rightarrow\infty$ ; additionally, in [43], Peyre gives an interpretation of the constant in terms of local densities and the Brauer group. In the following conjecture, the exponent is worked out in [4, Lemma 1] by Browning.

#### Conjecture 1.1 (Manin’s conjecture for Châtelet surfaces).

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy that $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ and let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree 3 or 4 that decomposes as a product of $r$ irreducible polynomials $f=f_{1}\ldots f_{r}$ . Let $X_{\Delta,f}/\mathbb{Q}$ be a Châtelet surface defined by $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=f(z)$ . Assume that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ . Then as $B\rightarrow\infty$ ,

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)\sim C_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}, $$

where $C_{\Delta,f}>0$ and

$$ \rho_{\Delta,f}=2+\#\{1\leq i\leq r:\sqrt{-\Delta}\in\mathbb{Q}[z]/(f_{i}(z))\}. $$

#### Remark 1.2.

This formulation of Manin’s conjecture over $\mathbb{Q}$ is equivalent to the same statement under the assumption that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense, thanks to the fact that if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ then $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense. Indeed by [11, Proposition 9.8.(iii)], if $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ then $X_{\Delta,f}$ is birational to a geometrically integral nonconical cubic surface in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ with a pair of conjugate singular points. Then by [17, Theorem A] of Coray and Tsfasman, $X_{\Delta,f}$ must be unirational and thus $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski-dense.

Moreover, the question of when $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset$ is settled by the seminal result of Colliot-Thélène, Sansuc, and Swinnerton-Dyer [11]; it demonstrates that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$ if and only if there is either a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to the existence of rational points. Furthermore, as discussed in [11], a Brauer-Manin obstruction to the Hasse principle may occur only when $f(z)$ is the product of two irreducible quadratics. There is a finite and effective computation for determining when $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset;$ this computation uses auxiliary varieties that we will introduce in (1.2).

Numerous instances of Manin’s conjecture for Châtelet surfaces have been resolved. In [4], Browning established an upper bound of the correct order of magnitude for Châtelet surfaces with $\Delta>0.$ In [37], Iwaniec and Munshi derive a lower bound when $f(z)$ is an irreducible cubic polynomial and $\Delta$ can be either positive or negative. In their seminal result, de la Bretèche, Browning, and Peyre [23] introduced the use of the torsor method, among other tools, to prove Manin’s conjecture for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ when $f$ decomposes as a product of distinct linear factors. Later, de la Bretèche and Browning [20] showed Manin’s conjecture for the case that $\Delta=1$ and $f(z)$ contains an irreducible cubic factor. In [25], the asymptotic for Manin’s conjecture is established for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ where $f$ is an irreducible quartic or a product of two irreducible quadratic factors over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ by de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum; these factorization cases are often regarded as the trickiest cases. Finally, Destagnol [28] resolved Manin’s conjecture for $\Delta=1$ by proving the asymptotic for $x^{2}+y^{2}=f(z)$ where $f$ is a product of two linearly independent linear factors and an irreducible quadratic factor, the remaining unknown factorization. In the above cases, the techniques are amenable to replacing $x^{2}+y^{2}$ with any positive-definite quadratic form of class number one.

Châtelet surfaces belong to a wider class of surfaces; indeed, Châtelet surfaces are singular del Pezzo surfaces of degree four. Manin’s conjecture was established by Batyrev and Tschinkel [2] for all del Pezzo surfaces of degree $\geq 7$ and nonsingular del Pezzo surfaces of degree 6, as these are toric varieties. Additionally, Manin’s conjecture is known for many more examples of del Pezzo surfaces of lower degree, as is discussed by Browning in [5, Chapter 2].

In [4, Lemma 2], Browning shows that

$$ \tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1,\max(|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|,|x|,|y|)\leq B\Big\}, $$

where $F(u,v)$ denotes the homogenization of $f(z)$ . We modify this height function slightly to better suit our techniques. Define:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B):=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\#\Big\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1,\max(|tu^{2}|,|tv^{2}|,\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|)\leq\nu_{\Delta,f}B\Big\}, $$

where $\|.\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{C}$ and

$$ \nu_{\Delta,f}=\begin{cases}\left(\max_{\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]^{2}}|F(\mathbf{y})|\right)^{1/2},&\Delta>0\\
1,&\Delta<0.\end{cases} $$

This new height is bounded up to a constant (depending on $\Delta$ and $f$ ) both above and below by the natural height on $X_{\Delta,f}$ induced by $\psi$ and hence $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)\asymp\tilde{N}(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ ; however, this choice simplifies our computations.

#### Theorem 1.3.

Let $\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}$ be a squarefree integer satisfying that $\sqrt{-\Delta}\not\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{Z}[z]$ be a separable polynomial of degree 3 or 4. Let $X_{\Delta,f}/\mathbb{Q}$ be the corresponding Châtelet surface. Then as $B\rightarrow\infty$ , there exists a constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ such that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=c_{\Delta,f}B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1}+O_{\Delta,f}(B\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-1-10^{-10}}). $$

Moreover, if $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero then there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}.$

#### Corollary 1.4.

Manin’s conjecture holds for all Châtelet surfaces over $\mathbb{Q}.$

#### Remark 1.5.

Observe that if there is a Brauer-Manin obstruction or a local obstruction to the existence of rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ , then we automatically know that $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=0$ . Hence, Theorem 1.3 can be upgraded to $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ if and only if there is a Brauer-Manin or local obstruction.

In Theorem 1.3, we do not assume a priori that $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})\neq\emptyset.$ Our proof of the aforementioned asymptotic result gives an explicit, albeit complicated, expression for $c_{\Delta,f}$ . Notably, $c_{\Delta,f}$ is closely related to auxiliary varieties; these varieties appear in the work of Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc in [9] when $f(z)$ is the product of two irreducible quadratics. Since our expression for $c_{\Delta,f}$ is complicated, we determine when it vanishes but do not pursue an adelic interpretation along the lines of Peyre’s prediction [43]. In Appendix A, we show that the constant matches Peyre’s prediction in a simple, but novel case.

Let $f(z)=f_{1}(z)\ldots f_{r}(z)$ be a decomposition into irreducible factors and let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ satisfy that $\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1$ . We define the auxiliary variety:

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},\ldots,f_{r},\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}}:=\{(z,(x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{r}):x_{i}^{2}+\Delta y_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}f_{i}(z)\neq 0\}. $$

The relationship between $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}$ and $X_{\Delta,f}$ will be expanded upon further in §12. For now, let us define the following condition:

- (A) There exists a tuple $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{r}$ satisfying $\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1$ such that

$$ X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{v})\neq\emptyset $$

for all places $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ .

We will show that if condition (A) holds then our constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ is nonzero (see Proposition 12.5). Additionally, if $f(z)$ is irreducible, then a consequence is that $c_{\Delta,f}$ is nonzero if there are no local obstructions to rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ .

In this way, Theorem 1.3 gives an analytic proof of the existence of many rational points on $X_{\Delta,f}$ via direct counting if condition (A) holds. Now, by the work of Colliot-Thélène, Coray, and Sansuc, and an application of Harari’s “formal lemma” [32], one can interpret condition (A) in terms of the Brauer-Manin obstruction and local obstructions of $X_{\Delta,f}$ . In particular, this allows us to conclude that if $c_{\Delta,f}$ is zero, then $X_{\Delta,f}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$ as well.

Finally, we remark on the possible application of these techniques to achieve an analytic proof of weak approximation for $X_{\Delta,f}$ . That $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}$ is a binary quadratic form corresponding to principal ideals is not of much relevance to our proof; indeed one can recreate the entire argument with a positive-definite or indefinite binary quadratic form. Adding arbitrary congruence conditions on $(u,v)$ will also be of little consequence for the analytic techniques. These points will be expanded on and are necessary ingredients in forthcoming work on del Pezzo surfaces of degree one, where both arbitrary congruence conditions and arbitrary positive-definite binary quadratic forms are required. So, at least in the case when $f(z)$ is irreducible, the methods can be adapted to establish weak approximation for $X_{\Delta,f}$ .

Finally, we highlight the new ingredients that allow us to push beyond $\Delta=1$ . In §2, we provide a detailed outline of our proof. First, we decompose our count into contributions from Eisenstein series and cusp forms. Consider the following function for $\Delta$ a positive squarefree integer:

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
I\textrm{ is principal}\end{subarray}}\exp(2\pi iz\cdot N(I)). $$

This function is a modular form of weight one and has a decomposition into Eisenstein and cuspidal components. If $\Delta=1$ , then the fact that $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ has class number one implies that $\theta(z)$ is purely Eisenstein, i.e. the cuspidal part is zero. We will find that in general the cuspidal contribution is negligible in comparison with the Eisenstein contribution.

When $\Delta<0$ , i.e. the indefinite case, a similar picture forms with careful analysis; the main additional obstacle in this case is that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has an infinite unit group. To mitigate this difficulty, we restrict our point-count to mildly-short boxes and intervals of length scaled by $\ell=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ This restriction allows us to estimate accurately the count

$$ \#\{|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}|\leq B:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v)\} $$

and convert our sum into a question about principal ideals $I$ with norm $t^{2}F(u,v).$ Of course, summing over short intervals and boxes complicates our estimates and sometimes adds an extra factor of $\ell^{-O(1)}$ , where this exponent can be made explicit. Fortunately, the error terms achieved by previous results on Manin’s conjecture, whose techniques we mimic, achieve savings of $\log(B)^{-10^{-5}}$ which will be more powerful than $\ell^{-O(1)}.$ Once the sum is written in terms of principal ideals of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ , we can again decompose the count in terms of Eisenstein and cuspidal contributions as before; this is equivalent to decomposing the Maass form into Eisenstein and cuspidal ingredients.

Second, we demonstrate that the cuspidal contribution is always negligible in comparison with the Eisenstein contribution. Let $C(z)$ denote the cuspidal part of $\theta(z)$ and let $\lambda_{C}(n)$ denote its Fourier coefficients. Our cuspidal contribution reduces to estimating sums of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\left|\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v))\right|, $$

and of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{d\mid t}\mu(d)\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{C}\left(t^{2}F(u,v)/d^{2}\right). $$

In the first case, we study correlation sums of the absolute values of its Fourier coefficients $\lambda_{C}(n)$ along polynomial values; although we sacrifice cancellation in the sign of $\lambda_{C}(n)$ , we still gain a saving of a power of log. In particular, we use a Nair-type sieve [42] to reduce the problem to computing the first few Sato-Tate moments of the corresponding $L$ -functions (see Rankin’s [44] work on the moments of the Ramanujan $\tau$ -function). We remark that this method was used by Holowinsky [35] to study correlation sums of Fourier coefficients of cusp forms with quadratic polynomials. Heath-Brown [34] also used this technique to study the equidistribution of solutions to certain Châtelet surfaces and his work inspired our proof techniques. While this technique handles most cases, there are delicate issues concerning the cuspidality of the base change lift of $C(z)$ to the splitting field of $f(z)$ ; in these cases, the absolute values are too expensive of a sacrifice.

Fortunately, in the above exceptional cases, we can appeal to the more robust method of handling the second sum. We determine that since $C(z)$ is a cusp form, we can derive savings for the sum

$$ \sum_{d\leq X}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq X/d}\lambda_{C}(at^{2}). $$

Moreover, our cusp forms are induced from class group characters of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ This extra structure allows us to track explicitly the dependency in the above bound on $a$ . Thus, we can derive a polylogarithmic saving on

$$ \sum_{|u|,|v|\leq B^{1/2}}\sum_{d\leq B/\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\mu(d)\sum_{t\leq B/d\max(|u|,|v|)^{2}}\lambda_{C}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

The inner sum is controlled by the poles of the symmetric square $L$ -function of $C(z)$ (see [45] for a discussion of the poles); if there is no pole, then the desired cancellation follows from the inner sum. If $C(z)$ is dihedral and the symmetric square $L$ -function has a pole, then an asymptotic for the inner sum is well-understood and the cancellation follows from the Möbius sum.

For the Eisenstein contribution, we follow the methods of [23, 20, 25, 28, 33] that resolved the $\Delta=1$ case. The third new feature is that for more general $\Delta$ , due to Gauss genus theory (see [30]), the Eisenstein Fourier coefficients now contain an extra summation over genus characters. This extra complication can still be handled by the aforementioned techniques for the $\Delta=1$ case and we achieve an explicit expression for the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}.$

The fourth and last new ingredient is the analysis of the vanishing of the leading constant $c_{\Delta,f}$ . This is resolved in §12 and involves the auxiliary varieties introduced in (1.2). In particular, our leading term brings us to a non-negative sum which is approximately of the form

$$ \sum_{(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})/\sim}\prod_{p}\mu_{p}(X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})). $$

where if $\mu_{p}(X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p}))\geq 0$ is zero then $X^{*}_{\Delta,f_{1},...,f_{r},\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})=\emptyset.$ Here, the sum over $(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{r})/\sim$ is over a sufficient and finite set of auxiliary varieties. Consequently, we show that if $c_{\Delta,f}=0$ then there is a local obstruction for every auxiliary variety.

## 2. Outline

In this section, we outline our proof strategy; our goal is to highlight the new techniques and convey the essential ideas, without the technical detail provided in the rest of the paper. By leaving out some of the more notationally-heavy complications, we hope to provide a clear roadmap for the rest of the paper. We warn the reader that in this section some of the claims are vague (and will be made precise in later sections) and some are technically false (but morally true and the modifications needed to correct the statements will be given later).

Let us start with the case when $\Delta>0$ . If $\Delta=1$ , Theorem 1.3 is known; so assume that $\Delta>1$ (for example, we can take $\Delta=5$ ). The main challenge to overcome is when $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has class number greater than one. From our definition (1.1), we see that:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},B)=\sum_{0\leq t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

where $r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)=\#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}:x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=n\}.$ Consider the binary theta series

$$ \theta(z)=\sum_{n}r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)\exp(2\pi inz)=\sum_{x,y}\exp(2\pi iz(x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}), $$

which is a modular form of weight one in $M_{1}(\Gamma_{0}(-\Delta),\chi)$ (see [36, §22.3]), where $\chi$ denotes the real quadratic character for $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ We can decompose $\theta(z)$ in terms of its Eisenstein and cuspidal contributions $\theta(z)=E(z)+C(z)$ . Note that since $\theta(z)$ is a weight one modular form, the Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein component and the cuspidal component are expected to be of the same magnitude.

The Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein part can be written explicitly in terms of genus characters, i.e. the class group character of order $\leq 2$ . As such, we have a nice description of the Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein part:

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi(d). $$

For the cuspidal part, we can write $\lambda_{C}(n)$ as a fixed linear combination of Fourier coefficients $\lambda_{\Psi}(n)$ , where $\Psi$ is the automorphic cuspidal representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ given by a class group character $\psi$ of order $\geq 3$ . The critical fact that we can restrict to those $\psi$ of order $\geq 3$ follows from Gauss genus theory for binary quadratic forms, as discussed by Fomenko in [30]. We can describe these coefficients $\lambda_{\Psi}(n)$ explicitly:

$$ \lambda_{\Psi}(n)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})=n\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}). $$

From this decomposition of $r_{x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}}(n)$ , we can see that Theorem 1.3 follows from gaining asymptotics on

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}(1\star\chi)(t^{2}F(u,v)) $$

and sufficient upper bounds on

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{\Psi}(t^{2}F(u,v)). $$

Note that we have left out the $\gcd$ -conditions here.

Before analyzing the two sums above, let us discuss what happens when $\Delta<0$ . There are two challenges involved in the indefinite case: again, we run into issues when $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ has class number greater than one; we also must handle the fact that there are infinitely many solutions to the equation $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=1.$ To handle the second issue, we restrict to counting in short boxes.

Let $\ell,L=w(B)$ , a small value going slowly to zero as $B\rightarrow\infty.$ We eventually take $w(B)=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}.$ Define the box

$$ \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L):=\mathbf{x}_{0}+[0,L]^{2}, $$

and the interval

$$ \mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell):=\{\exp(2\pi i\theta^{\prime}):\theta^{\prime}\in[\theta,\theta+\ell]\}. $$

Then we consider the restricted counting function:

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)):=\#\left\{((x,y),(u,v),t)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{+}:\begin{array}[]{cc}x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\\
(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\\
\|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}\|\leq B,\\
\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell),\\
\gcd(x,y,t)=\gcd(u,v)=1\end{array}\right\}. $$

In other words, we restrict $(u,v)$ to a mildly shorter box $(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ and constrain the argument $\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell).$ Here we define the argument as

$$ \arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})=\frac{|x+y\sqrt{-\Delta}|}{|x-y\sqrt{-\Delta}|}\bmod|\varepsilon|^{2}, $$

where $\varepsilon$ is the fundamental unit to Pell’s equation $x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}=1.$ Our strategy is to produce an asymptotic for $N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))$ ; this asympotic would then recover an estimate for $N(X_{\Delta,f},B)$ by splitting the region $\{|x|,|y|\leq B,|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}\}$ into short boxes and arguments in $\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)$ , and then summing over $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ and $\theta$ . This computation is done in §5.7.

By restricting to the shorter box and interval, we can make precise the count

$$ \#\{|x\pm y\sqrt{-\Delta}|\leq B:x^{2}+y^{2}=t^{2}F(u,v),\arg(x+y\sqrt{-\Delta})\in\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)\}. $$

In particular, we can find an explicit constant

$$ \kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\theta)=c_{\Delta}\cdot\max(-\log|F(\mathbf{x}_{0})|,0)\cdot\frac{|\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)|}{4\pi} $$

satisfying that

$$ N(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))=(\kappa(\mathbf{x}_{0},\theta)+O(w(B)))\\
\times\sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}\#\{I\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}):I\textrm{ a principal ideal and }N(I)=t^{2}F(u,v)\}\\
+E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell)), $$

where $E(X_{\Delta,f},\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L),\mathcal{I}(\theta,\ell))$ is a linear combination of remainder terms of the form

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))| $$

for $\Xi$ a cuspidal automorphic representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ given by an unitary nontrivial Hecke Grössencharacter $\xi$ on $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})$ of infinite order (see Definition 3.2).

For the main term, we again use a decomposition into Eisenstein and cuspidal components. In particular, we can express

$$ \#\{I\subset\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}):I\textrm{ principal and }N(I)=n\}=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{\psi\in\hat{C}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta})}\\
N(\mathfrak{a})=n\end{subarray}}\psi(\mathfrak{a}), $$

where $C$ is the class group of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-\Delta}).$ Again, from Gauss’s genus theory, the Eisenstein contribution comes from the class group characters of order $\leq 2$ ; the Fourier coefficient for the Eisenstein part is approximately

$$ \lambda_{E}(n)\approx(1\star\chi)(n). $$

Similarly, the cuspidal Fourier coefficient is a linear combination of sums $\lambda_{\Psi}$ where $\Psi$ is the representation given by $\psi$ a class group character of order $\geq 3.$ This matches the process completed in the positive definite case.

In the end, Theorem 1.3 reduces to estimating the sum

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

and providing a suitable upper bound on the sums

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v)), $$

$$ \sum_{t\leq B}\sum_{|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}}|\lambda_{\Xi}(t^{2}F(u,v))|. $$

where $\Xi$ is the representation of $\text{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ induced by a Hecke character $\xi$ . Additionally, (2.3) will only be used when $\xi$ is a class group character of order $\geq 3$ (and hence has finite image), whereas (2.4) only occurs when $\xi$ is a Hecke Grössencharacter (which has infinite image). We remark that it is likely that with more careful analysis we could remove the absolute values in (2.4); however, we achieve the necessary savings with the absolute values added.

Our method for estimating the Eisenstein contribution follows closely the previous approaches when $\Delta=1$ ; indeed, when $\Delta=1$ , $\theta(z)=E(z)$ and so the whole sum is contained in the Eisenstein part. We particularly mimic the proofs of de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [25] and the proof of Heath Brown in [33]. However, we must consider when $(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)$ lies in a short box – fortunately, all of the techniques are either amenable to this issue or we achieve a savings that is far larger than the loss incurred from summing over $|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}$ instead of the smaller region.

Using estimates on lattice points in convex regions, we establish a near-optimal level of distribution result for squarefree binary forms in §9. Write $F(x,y)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}F_{i}(x,y)$ as the decomposition into irreducible forms. We show that

$$ \sum_{d_{i}\leq D_{i}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
d_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}1-\frac{BL^{2}}{t}\cdot\frac{\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\}}{(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{2}}\right|\ll D+\sqrt{\frac{BD}{t}}\exp(\sqrt{\log\log(B)}), $$

where $D=D_{1}\ldots D_{r}.$ This result allows us to take $D\leq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-\varepsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ and still obtain a reasonable bound. This level of distribution result is obtained in [25] for $F(x,y)$ irreducible or a product of two irreducible quadratics; we closely follow their techniques. Also, Marasingha [39] studies a general level of distribution result for squarefree binary forms and achieves a savings for $D\leq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-A}$ for any large enough integer $A>0$ . We remark that if $F(x,y)$ has linear factors then the shape of the above bound is slightly different.

This step is the primary obstacle to studying $F(x,y)$ of higher degree; for $\deg(F)\leq 3$ , the level of distribution is sufficient and for $\deg(F)=4$ , it is almost sufficient (up to a power of $\log(B)$ ). For $\deg(F)>4$ , the level of distribution would be a power of $B$ away from necessary and this gap can not be covered by the argument as written below.

The other main input into our proof comes directly from de la Bretèche and Tenenbaum in [22] when $F(x,y)$ is irreducible or the product of two irreducible quadratics; we describe their idea in detail in §10 and discuss how to handle other factorizations of $F(x,y)$ . Define the twisted Hooley $\Delta$ -function:

$$ \Delta(n,\chi):=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\mathbb{R}\\
0\leq v\leq 1\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\
d\in[D,e^{v}D]\end{subarray}}\chi(d)\right|. $$

Applying Nair’s sieve and [22, Theorem 1.1], we achieve that for $D\geq\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{-10^{-5}},$

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|u|,|v|\leq(B/t)^{1/2}\\
\exists d_{i}\sim D_{i}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}\Delta(F(u,v),\chi)\ll\frac{B}{t}\cdot\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-5}}. $$

Note that since we take $L=w(B)=\log(B)^{-10^{-10}}$ , this bound is still $\ll\frac{BL^{2}}{t}\log(B)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-7}}.$ This procedure handles the large moduli.

Together, these results allow us to re-express the Eisenstein contribution as:

$$ BL^{2}\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{1}{t}\sum_{(a_{i})\bmod\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1+\chi(a_{i}))\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod\Delta:F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\equiv a_{i}\bmod\Delta\}\\
\times\sum_{d_{i}\leq D_{i}}\frac{\chi(d_{1}\ldots d_{r})\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}\bmod d_{1}\cdots d_{r}:d_{i}\mid F_{i}(\mathbf{x})\}}{(d_{1}\cdots d_{r})^{2}}\\
+O\left(\sum_{t\leq B}\frac{B}{t}\log(B/t)^{\rho_{\Delta,f}-2-10^{-5}}\right). $$

However, the above expression is an oversimplification – in particular, it assumes that $(1\star\chi)(n)$ is a totally multiplicative function, which it is not. Instead, we must substitute the identity that

$$ (1\star\chi)(mn)=\sum_{c\mid\gcd(m,n)}\mu(c)\chi(c)(1\star\chi)(n/c)(1\star\chi)(m/c). $$

Consequently, we re-express our main term as:

$$ \sum_{(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)}(1\star\chi)(F(u,v))=\sum_{(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r})}^{\prime}\mu(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\chi(c_{1}\cdots c_{r})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(u,v)\in(B/t)^{1/2}\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}_{0},L)\\
c_{i}\mid F_{i}(u,v)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1\star\chi)(F_{i}(u,v)/c_{i}). $$

Here the sum over $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r})$ is restricted to a finite set of possible vectors where the entries divide the pairwise resultants of the irreducible factors of $f(z)$ .

Proceeding as before with our level of distribution result and bounds on the large moduli with the twisted Hooley $\Delta$ -function, our main term is actually of the form:
